own fieldsAttributeself.hp = 3read / writeAn attribute created in setup (self.hp = 3) becomes an Attribute. Keeping values.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
destroy()No parameters—Removes it. With no drawing, visible hardly matters. .active becomes False.
cancel_process()No parametersselfCancels timers / tweens / sounds / mode; the Entity stays alive. The mode becomes None without @exit_mode. See scope.
goto_mode(fn)Parameters: fn (the chapter's function)—Forces exit + entry, even if it is already in that mode. See Mode.
after / everyParameters: delay or interval (seconds), fn (function)HandleTimers on this Entity — they survive a mode change; they die on destroy / cancel_process. See scope.
tweenParameters: target (Attribute or Point), to (the same type as the current value)HandleInterpolates an Attribute / Point on this Entity (number, tuple, Vec2, Color…). See tween.
setup(self)Parameters: self (this object)—After the constructor. The own fields are born here: self.hp = 3. Write setup, not __init__: an __init__ that does not call super().__init__(**kwargs) raises TypeError when the object is created.
on_update(self, dt)Parameters: self (this object), dt (number)—Every frame, on this Entity. See Frame.
on_destroy(self)Parameters: self (this object)—Once, from inside destroy(). It does not fire on a mode change.
Subclassing Shape / Sprite / SpatialFx / Text

Parameters on the class line become the defaults of that type. The pose (center, layer) stays on the instance. It works the same for a spatial effect — class Energy(Orb, radius=16, color="gold", group="energy") — and for a text: class Scoreboard(Text, font_size=32, color="gold", group="hud"), and Scoreboard("0", top_left=(20, 580)).

class Bolt(Circle, radius=8, color="gold", group="bolt"):
    def on_update(self, dt):
        self.move_by(0, 560 * dt)
Bolt(center=(x, y))

class Ship(Sprite, source="playerShip1_blue.png", height=48, group="ship"):
    def setup(self):
        self.hp = 3
Ship(center=(x, y))
Goes on the classDoes not
color visual groupcenter layer
Size: radius width/height length/anglePose per instance (center=)
Sprite: source= frame= height=class Bolt(Circle): radius = 8 — TypeError on the class: it goes on the class line
Text: font_size font color background glow align width groupThe text and the position (center top_left … box layer stack angle)
—Widgets, Entity, Endless: no class parameters (an error with the fix); pass them on the instance
SpatialFx: the type's parameters (radius amount color length…), group soft_edgePoints (center p1 p2 origin); Fire's style= — it picks another class: write Fire(style=…)

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
class Bolt(Circle): radius = 8parameters on the class line, not attributes in the body. A value in the body with a Scena name (radius = 8, visible = False, group = "x") raises TypeError when the class is defined, with the fix: the class line (class Bolt(Circle, radius=8)) or setup (self.visible = False).—
def __init__(self): in a subclassa replacement for Scena's constructor. What the object does when it is born goes in def setup(self):, which Scena calls with the object ready. An __init__ of your own (for your own parameters) takes **kwargs and calls super().__init__(**kwargs); without that call, creating the object raises TypeError with the fix.—

Where else to look — Place · Appearance · Move · Geometry

Appearance

How an object looks on the screen: its color and material (solid color, gradient, image), how it blends with what is behind it, the lasting effects (visual, add-ons, filters) and the passing ones (transients). Color, Gradient and Texture only appear once applied to an object — in .fill, .visual or set_color.

Color / Gradient / Texture → Color / Gradient
Choosing colors (ramp, palette) → Palettes and ramps
Blend → Blend
.glow / .shadow / .tail → Add-ons
Neon / Halo / … → Visual
Death / hit / knock → Transients
Blur / DropShadow → Filters

Color / Gradient / Texture

Three ways to paint: a solid color (Color or just its name, "coral"), a gradient (Gradient) or an image (Texture). On their own they do not appear: they go in .fill, .visual, set_color or canvas.background. RGB is 0–1. A name that is almost right ("blu"): a warning + the closest color ("blue"). An unknown name: a warning + magenta, with Did you mean. To choose colors (ramps, palettes): Palettes and ramps.

Wherever the framework asks for a color (color=, set_color, Glow("cyan"), canvas.background = "navy", Text(..., color=) / background=), any of these forms works:

FormExample
Name"coral" · "dark red" · "sky blue"
Hex"#33ccff" · "#RRGGBBAA"
RGB 0–1(0.2, 0.4, 0.8) · (0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 0.5)
ColorColor("cyan") · Color(0.2, 0.4, 0.8)
 
c = Circle(color="coral")
c.set_color("tomato")
c.fill = Gradient("sunset", angle=-90)
c.fill = Texture("tex2.png", fit="tile", tile_size=40)
Color("cyan")
Color(0.2, 0.4, 0.8)
Color("#33ccff")
Color.from_hsv(0.55, 0.8, 0.9)
Color.random()
Color("red").jitter()
c.set_color("navy")
c.set_alpha(0.8)
gold = Color("gold").lighter(0.15)

Color harmonies: triadic, analogous, shades, contrast_color, muted_version.

Color reference

Immutable: lighter / with_alpha / jitter return a new Color. A color is shared (every shape with the default color uses the same one), so color.alpha = 0.5 raises AttributeError with the fix: color.with_alpha(0.5) or shape.set_alpha(0.5).

A color compares by value, however it is written: ball.color == "red", == "#ff0000" and == (1, 0, 0) are True, and print shows the channels. In a set or dict of strings it is not found (its hash is the value's, not the string's): ball.color in {"red", "blue"} gives False. Compare with a list (in ["red", "blue"]) or use Color("red") as the key; Scena warns when it sees .color in {"…"}.

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.rgbtuple(1, 0.8, 0, 1)readTuple (r, g, b, a) in 0–1.
.alphanumber0.8readAlpha 0–1. A different alpha: with_alpha(a) (a new Color) or shape.set_alpha(a).
.hsl / .hsv / .brightnesstuple or number(0.5, 0.8, 0.6)readRead-only. HSL/HSV: (h, s, l|v, a).

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
Color(name) / Color(r, g, b[, a]) / Color("#RRGGBB")Parameters: r, g, b, a (numbers 0–1), or a color name / "#RRGGBB"ColorConstructor. Color(None) is “no color” (false in an if).
Color.from_hsl(h, s, l[, a]) / Color.from_hsv(h, s, v[, a])Parameters: h, s, l|v, a (numbers 0–1)ColorFactories. The hue h wraps around; S / L / V / alpha are clamped. HSV: saturation and brightness apart — good for vivid colors.
Color.from_rgb(r, g, b[, a]) / Color.from_name(name[, a])Parameters: r, g, b, a (channels 0–1) · name, aColorShortcuts, the same as Color(...).
ColorNames.is_known(name) / ColorNames.get(name)Parameters: name (name, str)True/False · (r, g, b)Does the name make a color? It takes the same spellings as Color(name) (capitals, hyphens, joined or apart, dark / light / faded in front: "lightcyan" is "light cyan"; a near typo becomes the closest color, with a warning). get returns the 0–1 tuple; an unknown name: a warning + magenta, like Color.
Color.random(saturation=, value=, alpha=)Parameters: saturation / value (number or (lo, hi)), alphaColorA random hue in HSV. Vivid by default: S=0.65, V=0.85. A range: saturation=(0.3, 0.9).
jitter(hue=, saturation=, value=)Parameters: hue / saturation / value (number, ± half)ColorA nearby color (HSV). Default hue=0.04 (~±14°) — reds stay red. Widen it for “warm tones”. A gray stays gray (only the value varies).
with_alpha(alpha)Parameters: alpha (number 0–1)ColorA copy with another alpha.
lighter(amount=0.1) / darker(amount=0.1)Parameters: amount (number)ColorA copy with the lightness (HSL) amount higher / lower; hue and saturation stay. amount defaults to 0.1.
saturate(amount=0.1) / desaturate(amount=0.1) / hue_cycle(amount=0.1)Parameters: amount (number)ColorA copy. amount defaults to 0.1. saturate on a gray returns the same gray (gray has no hue).
vibrant_version(amount=0.5) / whiter_version(amount=0.4)Parameters: amount (number)ColorMore neon (HSV; a gray stays gray, only lighter) · a mix toward white. Defaults 0.5 / 0.4.
Color.interpolate(color1, color2, t, color_space=)Parameters: color1 (Color), color2 (Color), t (number), color_space (ColorSpace)ColorA mix. t is usually 0–1. Default ColorSpace.OKLAB (even to the eye — plain RGB passes through gray/brown in the middle). Also: HSL / HSV (the shortest way around the hue circle; a gray end takes the other end's hue, so white → blue stays bluish) · RGB.
a.lerp(b, t)Parameters: b (Color), t (number)ColorInstance shortcut for Color.interpolate (OKLAB). Used by lerp / tween.
complementary()No parametersColorThe opposite color on the circle.

Gradient reference

Gradient(*colors, type="linear", size=, angle=0)

A name without =: the colors in order (a preset, two colors, or a ramp). The rest by name.

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
*colors1st, 2nd…str or Color"rdyl"A preset name, or the ramp. One color: dark → light.
typename=str"linear"linear · radial · sweep.
anglename=number0Degrees. Linear and sweep. 0 = from left to right; 90 = from bottom to top (the first color at the bottom); -90 = from top to bottom. The same on a shape and on a Wallpaper. The sky presets ("sunset", "day") start at the top: angle=-90.
sizename=number or Nonefits the objectIn design units. Linear: the distance from the center to each end of the gradient. Radial: the radius. Sweep ignores it.

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.typestr"linear"readRead-only. "linear" · "radial" · "sweep". The same value passed in type=.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
darker(amount=0.1)Parameters: amount (number)GradientA new, darker ramp: each stop with Color.darker(amount). amount defaults to 0.1 (how much the HSL lightness goes up/down). Type, size and angle stay the same. Use: g2 = Gradient("ocean").darker(0.2) · brick.visual = g.darker().
lighter(amount=0.1)Parameters: amount (number)GradientA new, lighter ramp: each stop with Color.lighter(amount). amount defaults to 0.1. Same geometry as the ramp. Use: g2 = Gradient("navy", "cyan").lighter(0.15).
mean_color()No parametersColorWeighted average of the stops (RGB integral along the ramp). Use: c.line = g.mean_color().darker(0.2).
set_alpha(alpha)Parameters: alpha (number 0–1)GradientAlpha on every stop (mutable, in place: it changes the shapes that use this Gradient). Unlike darker / lighter, which return a copy. shape.set_alpha(a) gives the shape a new Gradient and leaves the others alone.

A material: it must be applied in .fill, .visual, set_color or canvas.background. On a Shape with an area, visual = Gradient(…) / set_color(Gradient(…)) / Paint(Gradient(…)) fills it and draws an outline with mean_color().darker(0.2) (the line_width thickness does not change). Paint(g, line=False) or Fill leave the outline out. Texture / ProceduralFill stay fill only.

Texture("tex2.png")
Texture("tex2.png", fit="cover")
Texture("tex2.png", fit="tile", tile_size=40)

Texture reference

Texture(source, filename=, image=, fit="cover", tile_mode=, scale=1, tile_size=, angle=0, color=, shift=)

A name without =: 1st in order (a file or an image). The rest by name. Lookup: Image files.

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
source1ststr"tex2.png"The image file (PNG / JPG). Lookup: Image files.
filename / imagename=str / Skia imageNoneInstead of source: the path by name, or a Skia image already loaded. Rare — the usual way is the 1st argument.
fitname=str"cover"How the image fills the shape: "cover" (covers it all, crops what is left over) · "contain" (fits whole, leaves a border) · "stretch" (stretches on both axes) · "tile" (repeats in tiles of tile_size). The same names as the Wallpaper.
tile_sizename=number or (w, h)40With fit="tile": the size of each tile, in design units. With another fit it is a TypeError (it would change nothing).
scalename=number1Extra zoom on the image (greater than 0): 2 shows the image at twice the size.
anglename=number0Turns the image, in degrees, counterclockwise (like the Gradient's angle): inside the shape, or on a Wallpaper around the center of the screen (with fit="tile", around the world's (0, 0) point). Turned, a "cover" image leaves the corners empty; tile_mode="mirror" fills them.
shiftname=HueShift or RecolorHueShift(amount=0.33)Changes the colors of the pixels: HueShift turns the hue; Recolor swaps one band of color for another. See Add-ons / Visual.
colorname=colorimage averageIt does not paint the image: it is the color the visuals use as the “object's color” (the glow of a Neon, for example). Left out: the average of the visible pixels.
tile_modename=str"decal"What shows outside the image: "decal" (nothing, transparent) · "clamp" (stretches the last row of pixels) · "repeat" (repeats) · "mirror" (repeats, mirroring). Left out: "repeat" with fit="tile", otherwise "decal". In tile, "clamp" becomes "repeat".

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.fitstrreadRead-only. The same value passed in fit=.
.tile_modestrreadRead-only. The same value passed in tile_mode=.
 
pond = Rect(center=(300, 120), width=240, height=60)
pond.fill = WaterFill()                     # water seen from the side
pond.fill = WaterFill(kind="top", speed=0.5)  # seen from above, slower
torch = Circle(center=(100, 200), radius=30)
torch.fill = FlameFill()
torch.fill = WaveFill("teal", amount=0.8)   # liquid of any color
torch.fill = AuroraFill(color="lime")
torch.fill = SwellFill()
Procedural reference

Ready-made animated fills. They go in .fill (or set_color); the outline stays your own. They are the material behind the visuals Water / Flame / Swell / Wave / Aurora — use the visual when you want the whole effect (border, glow), and the fill when you want only the inside.

FactorySignatureReturnsMeaning
WaterFill(kind="side", amount=1.0, speed=1.0)Parameters: kind ("side" / "top"), amount (number), speed (number)ProceduralFillWater. "side" = a platform seen from the side (surface on top); "top" = a pond seen from above.
FlameFill(amount=1.0, speed=1.2)Parameters: amount (number), speed (number)ProceduralFillFire rising inside the shape.
SwellFill(amount=1.0, speed=1.0)Parameters: amount (number), speed (number)ProceduralFillAn abstract flow (not water seen from the side).
WaveFill(color=None, amount=1.0, speed=1.0)Parameters: color (color), amount (number), speed (number)ProceduralFillA body of liquid of any color.
AuroraFill(color=None, amount=1.0, speed=0.9)Parameters: color (color), amount (number), speed (number)ProceduralFillVertical aurora bands, of any color.
ProceduralFill(kind=, amount=1.0, speed=1.0, seed=0.0, color=None)Parameters: kind (shader name), amount, speed, seed (numbers), color (color)ProceduralFillThe class behind the factories. Prefer the factories; an unknown kind raises ValueError with the list.

amount is the intensity (0 = off, 1 = default); speed multiplies the animation's time. Fill(…) takes only a solid color: for a visual with a procedural fill, Paint(WaterFill()).

plate = Rect(center=(200, 150), width=120, height=60)
plate.visual = Fill("red")                  # fill only, no outline
plate.visual = Stroke("navy", width=4)      # outline only
plate.visual = Paint(Gradient("sunset"))    # ramp + a darker outline
plate.visual = Paint("coral", line=False)   # color without an outline
Paint / Fill / Stroke reference

Simple color visuals, for wherever a visual would go (shape.visual = …, set_defaults(visual=…)). They are not animated visuals: they only decide fill, outline and thickness.

ClassSignatureReturnsMeaning
Paint(material, alpha=None, *, color=, line=True)Parameters: material (color, Gradient, Texture or ProceduralFill), alpha (0–1), color (the same as material, by name), line (True/False)PaintFill and outline at once, like set_color: the material paints the inside and the outline gets a contrasting tone. With no arguments: steel blue + a contrasting outline. line=False removes the outline.
Fill(color="steel blue", alpha=None)Parameters: color (solid color), alpha (0–1)FillFill only. Gradient / Texture / a visual raise TypeError — use Paint(Gradient(…)).
Stroke(color="black", width=None)Parameters: color (solid color), width (number)StrokeOutline only; width changes the line_width.

Visual and Recipe are the classes behind every visual in the catalog (they are there for isinstance(v, Visual)). You do not build them: pick a ready-made visual.

Color names

The CSS color names work too ("beige", "saddle brown", "midnight blue"), joined or apart. dark / light / faded in front are always Scena's modifier: "dark slate gray" is "slate gray" darkened.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Color(255, 128, 0)ValueError: RGB is 0–1. Divide by 255, or use hex ("#ff8000").0–255

Palettes and ramps

Tools to choose colors that go together (they paint nothing). Colormap is a continuous ramp: ask for the color at any point t from 0 to 1. Palette is N colors taken from the ramp, read by an index that wraps around. Both return Color and use the same presets as Gradient.

tints = Palette("plasma")              # 6 colors from the preset
hud.fill = tints[wave_number]          # wrapping index

ramp = Colormap.from_colors("red", "blue")
halfway = ramp.get_color(0.5)          # the midpoint (OKLAB)
Colormap

A color ramp that you sample (it draws nothing on its own). It is the table behind Gradient("plasma") and Palette("plasma"). Create the ramp, then ask for a color at t (0–1). Default interpolation: ColorSpace.OKLAB.

ramp = Colormap.from_colors("red", "blue")
ramp.get_color(0.0)          # red
ramp.get_color(0.5)          # the midpoint (OKLAB)
ramp.random()                # a random color on the ramp

Colormap.from_colors("red", "yellow", "blue")
Colormap.from_preset("plasma")
Colormap([(0.0, "navy"), (0.4, "cyan"), (1.0, "white")])
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
Colormap.from_colors(*colors, color_space=)Parameters: colors (name / Color / RGB), color_space (ColorSpace.OKLAB)ColormapA ramp with evenly spaced colors (2 → the ends; 3+ → equal steps). OKLAB by default.
Colormap.from_preset(preset, color_space=)Parameters: preset (name), color_space (ColorSpace.OKLAB)ColormapThe same presets as Gradient, or a color name (dark → light). OKLAB by default.
Colormap([(t, color), …], color_space=)Parameters: colors (list of pairs: position 0–1, color), color_space (ColorSpace.OKLAB)ColormapExplicit stops. OKLAB by default.
get_color(t)Parameters: t (number 0–1)ColorThe color at position t on the ramp.
random()No parametersColorShortcut for get_color(random.random()) — a random color between the stops.
Palette

Discrete samples of a ramp. It draws nothing on its own — it returns Color. The same presets as Gradient. Default: 6 points, OKLAB interpolation. The index wraps around (modulo); get_next() moves its own cursor forward.

Palette(*source, steps=6, color_space=ColorSpace.OKLAB)

A name without =: a preset, a list of colors, or colors in order. steps and color_space by name.

tints = Palette("plasma")              # 6 colors from the preset
tints = Palette("plasma", steps=8)

# a list or loose arguments — the same ramp
Palette(["red", "yellow", "blue"])
Palette("red", "yellow", "blue", steps=5)

# wrapping index: any counter works
hud.fill = tints[wave_number]

# or in sequence, without keeping an index
def spawn():
    Circle(fill=tints.get_next())

# from a Gradient / Colormap you already made
accents = Palette(Gradient("sunset"), steps=4)
Parameter / methodSignatureReturnsMeaning
steps=integer, default 6—How many colors the palette takes from the ramp, evenly spaced from start to end.
color_space=ColorSpace, default OKLAB—How the in-between colors are mixed. ColorSpace.OKLAB (the default) gives steps that look even to the eye; RGB passes through grayish tones in the middle. Also HSL / HSV.
Palette(preset)Parameters: preset (str), steps=6, color_spacePaletteSamples the preset (the same table as Gradient). With no arguments: "plasma".
Palette(["red", "yellow", "blue"])Parameters: list or *colors, steps, color_spacePaletteA ramp with these colors, then steps samples. Also: stops [(t, color), …], a Colormap or a Gradient.
palette[i]Parameters: i (int)ColorThe sample at the index. It wraps around: palette[6] == palette[0] if steps=6. A slice (palette[:3]) does not wrap.
get_next()No parametersColorThe next sample; its own cursor, wrapping. for color in palette goes through once (it is not this cursor).
reset(index=0)Parameters: index (int)PaletteMoves the get_next cursor (modulo). Chainable.
random()No parametersColorOne of the samples, at random (discrete). Colormap.random() samples the continuous ramp.
len(palette) / .colorsNo parametersint / listHow many samples. .colors returns a copy.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Color.random() · ramp.random() · palette.random() · color.jitter()Color.random() = any hue (vivid). ramp.random() = a continuous sample of this ramp. palette.random() = one of the N samples. color.jitter() = a variation near one color.the same draw
Palette("plasma")It samples the shared preset table (like Colormap.from_preset)It does not build a Gradient — Gradient paints; Palette returns Color
palette[i]A wrapping index (never IndexError on an int)A plain list — a slice does not wrap; for is finite

Blend

Blend chooses how an object's colors combine with what is already drawn behind it: on top ("normal", the default), adding light ("add", for lasers and glows), darkening ("multiply", for shadows)… The same setting on Shape and Sprite: .blend = "add".

On a Shape, it blends fill and line. On a Sprite, it blends the image (the PNG). Reading it returns the same string. It does not link with @=.

# Shape: a stroke of light (adds to the background)
ray = Line(p1=(120, 80), p2=(280, 240), color="cyan")
ray.set_alpha(0.3)
ray.blend = "add"

# Sprite: a brighter PNG over what is below
ship.blend = "add"

# Ink / shadow (multiplies the colors)
stain.blend = "multiply"

ship.blend = "normal"          # back to normal

"add" brightens even an opaque PNG (it adds the RGB where they overlap). A PNG with alpha (glass, holes) takes part in the mix. sprite.alpha is another setting: it makes the image transparent (0–1) without changing the formula — the two combine.

Everyday

NameDoes
"normal"Default. The source on top, honoring alpha.
"add"Adds the colors. Laser, shot, glow, light particles. Blows out to white where they overlap.
"multiply"Multiplies. Darkens. Shadow, ink, tinted glass.
"screen"The inverse of multiply. Brightens. Smoke, soft glow (blows out less than add).

Contrast

NameDoes
"overlay"Multiply on a dark destination, screen on a light one.
"hard-light"Like overlay, with the source as a hard light.
"soft-light"A soft version of hard-light.

Darker / lighter

NameDoes
"darken"Keeps the darker channel of source and destination.
"lighten"Keeps the lighter channel.

Comparison

NameDoes
"difference"Absolute difference. Invert / compare.
"exclusion"Like difference, with less contrast.
"subtract"Subtracts the source from the destination. Today it paints the same as "difference".

Dodge / burn

NameDoes
"color-dodge"Brightens the destination according to the source. A strong glow.
"color-burn"Darkens the destination according to the source.

HSL (the source's color, the rest from the destination)

NameDoes
"hue"The source's hue; the destination's saturation and lightness.
"saturation"The source's saturation; the rest from the destination.
"color"The source's hue + saturation; the destination's lightness.
"luminosity"The source's lightness; the destination's color.

An unknown name: TypeError with the list. It does not link with @=. Use =. look_like / save_visual / restore_visual copy the blend. A visual (Halo, Neon…) may rewrite the fill's blend while it is on; visual = None gives yours back. sprite.alpha / set_alpha fade only the image — on a Shape, set_alpha changes the alpha of the fill/line. See Appearance and clicks.

Add-ons

Add-ons are five effects added on top of an object's appearance, each in its own property: a glow around it (.glow), a shadow (.shadow), a motion trail (.tail) and, on Sprite only, a turned hue (.hue) and grayscale (.gray). Each is turned on with an assignment and lives alongside the visual and the other add-ons.

PropertyWhat it doesOnShortcuts
.glowA halo of light around the body.Shape, Sprite, TextTrue = a glow in the object's color · a color ("cyan") · Glow(…) / CheapGlow(…) to tune it
.shadowA shadow offset down and to the right.Shape, SpriteTrue · a color · Shadow(…)
.tailGhost copies behind the object as it moves.Shape, SpriteTrue · a color · Tail(…)
.hueTurns the PNG's colors around the hue circle (red → green → blue).Spritea number of turns (0.33 = a third: red becomes green) · True = 0.33 · HueShift(…)
.grayTakes the color out (a disabled button, a character turned to stone).SpriteTrue = all gray · a number from 0 to 1 (0.5 = half gray) · Grayscale(…)

To turn one off, assign False or None. Reading the property returns the settings object (Glow, Shadow…) or None. visual = None removes only the visual: the add-ons stay. save_visual() / restore_visual() save and bring back the add-ons too. CheapGlow also goes in .glow (there is no .cheapglow); assigning Glow / Shadow to .visual raises TypeError with the hint.

ship.glow = True
ship.glow = "cyan"
sting.glow = CheapGlow("tomato", radius=8)
ship.shadow = Shadow("navy")
sprite.hue = 0.33
sprite.gray = True          # gray (a disabled button); 0.5 = half
bolt.tail = True
# no angle=: it follows the motion
ship.tail = Tail(color="gold", size=1.4, amount=1.15)
bolt.tail = Tail(angle=180)
ship.tail = Tail(
    angle=lambda: ship.angle + 180,
    size=lambda: 1.4,
    amount=lambda: 1.15,
)
Text("GO", glow=True)

tail = True and Tail(…) without angle= follow the motion (a trail behind the velocity; it fades when the object stops). Tail(angle=180) locks the direction (90 = up). angle / size / amount take lambda: — evaluated again every frame. Do not use ship.visual = Glow().

Reading the parameters. radius= and offset= in design units; sigma= is how much it blurs (bigger = softer); amount= is the intensity (1 = default); alpha= is the opacity, from 0 to 1.

Visual

A visual is a ready-made look, almost always animated, that changes how an object is drawn — neon, hologram, metal, water, an energy shield. Each object has one visual at a time, in .visual: ship.visual = Neon(). It works with no arguments, in the object's color. The exceptions have their own palette: Metal() is chrome and Shield() is the lime-green bubble, whatever the object's color (and the object's color does not change); Metal("gold") / Shield("cyan") give the color. None removes the visual and goes back to the look from before (the add-ons stay). save_visual / restore_visual bring back the look on the screen (add-ons included).

There are body visuals (Neon, Gel, Sphere, Aurora, Metal, Halo(style="fill")…) and outline visuals (Rim, Laser, Ink, Halo, ElectricBolt, Tracer…). Without color=, a body visual follows the object's color and an outline visual follows the object's outline (.line). The object's color (color=, set_color) gives an outline derived from it — darker on a light color, lighter on a dark one —, and that is the one the outline visual follows: Circle(color="red") with Laser() gives a pinkish laser; for a red laser, Laser("red") or .line = "red". color= in the constructor paints the visual and stays on the object: on a body visual it becomes the object's color, on an outline visual it becomes only the outline (Rim("red") is the same as .line = "red" and then Rim(); once the visual is removed, the inside keeps its own color). Left out, it follows the object (or its own palette, in Metal and Shield). Writing .fill / .line, .line_width, .blend or .dash before or after putting on the visual gives the same drawing. A visual that sets its own thickness, blend or dash (Rim, Halo, Shield, Bolt…) keeps its own while it is on — the Rim's border changes with Rim(width=) — and the value you wrote shows when the visual comes off (visual = None). The rule: a visual that takes color= shows set_color — set_color / .color = recolor every visual that takes color=, whether it was made with a color or not (Neon("red"), Laser, Rim, Halo(style="line")…, Metal, the Shield bubble); a visual without color= keeps the color and warns. A visual is not a transient. A glow on many objects: .glow, not N× Neon.

Each effect states whether it works on Shape, Sprite or both (the chips below and the tag on the panel). In the signature, a name without = is the 1st, 2nd… in order (Neon("cyan")). A name with = goes by name (amount=1.2).

ship.save_visual()
ship.visual = Neon("tomato")
ship.color = "lime"
ship.glow = True
after(0.4, ship.restore_visual, name="bonus")

visual = None ≠ restore_visual(): None goes back to the look without a visual (the add-ons stay); the save / restore pair goes back to exactly the saved look (with the add-ons). One slot per object; use name= in the after to renew the duration.

Reading the parameters. color= tints the effect; left out, it follows the object's color. amount= is the intensity: 1 is the default, 0 turns it off, 2 is strong. speed= is the animation's pace: 1 normal, 2 twice as fast, 0 freezes it. width= is a thickness in design units. Visuals that paint a color of their own (glow, border, body) take color= as the 1st argument; procedural materials (Flame, Swell, Water) and pixel operators (Grayscale, HueShift, Recolor, EmissiveBloom) do not — change the color with set_color on the object.

Transients

Transients are short effects on an object: flashing when it takes damage, growing suddenly and going back to size, fading out when it dies, appearing when it is born. You call the verb (ship.flash(0.12)), it ends on its own and the lasting look (.visual) does not change. Each kind of effect has a channel: a new effect on the same channel replaces the previous one, and different channels run together. It works on Shape and Sprite.

The first number = the duration. The rest by name — including style= (when there is one) and on_done= (a callback when it ends or is cancelled). Tabs below: the signature and parameters of each verb.

ship.flash(0.12)
ship.pop(scale=1.2)
ship.knock(distance=16, angle=30)
ship.dissolve_out(0.4, style="vortex", on_done=ship.destroy)
ship.dissolve_out(0.45, style="wipe", angle=0)
ship.dissolve_out(0.35, style="fade")

The first number is always the duration in seconds. Color, scale, intensity, amount, style go by name: pop(scale=1.4), flash(intensity=0.6), dissolve_out(style="noise"). Dissolve style: noise · vortex · wipe · fade. Do not use visual = Neon() just for a flash. A new effect on the same channel replaces the one in progress and calls the old one's on_done right away (the same on_done as a normal end — it is not told that it was cut short). Trigger at the end: When it ends.

ChannelMethodsWhen it ends
lifedissolve_out burn_out fade_out implode dissolve_in fade_indeath: visible=False (hides, does not destroy: to remove it, on_done=shape.destroy); spawn: shows it at the start; on_done
flashflash blinkclears; on_done
textflash_text(text, duration=1, *, on_done=None) — only Text and widgets. Shows text for duration seconds in place of the usual text (scoreboard.flash_text("+100", 0.5))shows the usual text again (if the text is linked to a field, it stays linked); on_done
pulsepulse_outlineclears; on_done
poppopclears; on_done
knockknockclears; on_done
sparkspark_burstclears; never hides; on_done
—clear_transientscancels them all; calls each one's on_done

Reading the parameters. The 1st number is always the duration, in seconds. intensity= / amount=: 1 is the default. on_done= is the function called at the end (or when another effect on the same channel interrupts it).

Filters

A filter works on an object's pixels after they are drawn — it blurs, casts a shadow, thickens, makes them glow. It goes in one of two properties: fill_filter acts on the inside, line_filter on the outline (or on a Line's stroke). It works on Shape, Sprite and Text.

For ready-made effects, prefer what already exists: the common glow and shadow are the add-ons .glow / .shadow; an animated look is a visual; an effect on the whole screen is a Post. The filter is the fine tuning of a single object. None removes the filter. One instance can go on many objects (halo = GlowFilter(…) on a whole fleet costs less than one per object). Two filters together: one's input= takes the other, or ComposeFx(outer, inner). A visual or a SpatialFx here raises TypeError.

c.fill_filter = Blur(sigma=4)
c.fill_filter = DropShadow(offset=12, sigma=8)
c.fill_filter = None

Reading the parameters. radius=, offset= and sigma= in design units (sigma is how much it blurs). input= chains: the filter acts on the result of another one (Blur(sigma=2, input=DropShadow())).

The filter goes in fill_filter (inside) or line_filter (outline). To make many objects glow, use the .glow add-on or a single shared GlowFilter — not a Halo visual on each one.

Where else to look — Draw · World · Sound

Reactive

Reactive is how you make one value follow another without writing code every frame. c.radius = ship.hp copies the number once; c["radius"] @= lambda: ship.hp links: from then on the radius follows the HP by itself, whenever the HP changes. To run an action when something changes (play a sound, switch levels), use @when / @on_change; to act after some time, Schedule.

Link a field / replace contents (<<) → Link
What can go on the right → What can be linked
A lambda in a for loop → Lambda
A lambda in the constructor → Formulas in constructors
The game's score (st) / HP on the Entity → Keeping values
What else controls a field → Persistent drivers

Link

Three operators put a value in a field. = copies the current value. @= links the field to a formula: Scena redoes the math whenever something the formula reads changes. << copies the values of another object into this one, without swapping the object. @= always takes brackets on the left — c["radius"] @= lambda: … — because c.radius would already be the number, not the field.

st.score = 0
st.lives = 3
st["hud"] @= lambda: f"Stars {st.score}"          # @= creates the field if missing

c.radius = 10
c.radius = other.radius
c["radius"] @= lambda: player.hp * 10
hero["grounded"] @= lambda: "bottom" in hero.touching_sides
line["p1"] @= lambda: rect.top_left
turret["angle"] @= lambda: dial.value
ship["scale"] @= lambda: 1 + 0.2 * st.pulse

# the whole mouse is a point (direct link). .x / keyp still need a lambda — see Frame
cursor["center"] @= mouse
c.center["x"] @= lambda: 1200 if keyp("D") else 800

# copy now
Circle(center=player.center, radius=player.hp)
# live link
Circle(center=lambda: player.center, radius=lambda: player.hp * 10)

# << : replaces the contents; the object on the left stays the same
pos = Vec2(0, 0)
pos << Vec2(50, 50)          # same pos; new values
c.center << other.center     # other stays in the game
# c.absorb(other)            # this one does remove other

c["radius"].unlink()
c.unlink_all()
Rules
CaseMeaning
=Copies the current value. No link afterwards.
<<Replaces the contents inside the object on the left (A << B). A is still the same object (whoever kept it sees the new values). It does not link. A linked field: the same LinkedAttributeError as =. Across types, it copies what the target can be: ellipse << hero.box fills the box (like Ellipse(box=)), rect << square; anything else refuses with the fix (Circle(box=region)). It is not absorb (that one copies and destroys the other).
["field"] @=Links. Right side: something reactive from Scena, or a callable. A bare number or expression: TypeError — use lambda: player.hp * 10.
ConstructorBare argument = copy. Callable = link. Details: Formulas in constructors.
ship.field @=Not the same as the bracket: Python reads ship.field first. On a scalar field (ship.hp, p.x) that is already a float — Python's own TypeError, with no Scena message. Prefer ship["field"] @= lambda: ….
.unlink() / unlink_all()c["radius"].unlink() frees that field from its formula; c.unlink_all() frees every linked field of the object (and of its parts, like center.x).
Linked field + = / <<LinkedAttributeError. Unlink first. In the pose verbs / tween: the same, unless force=True (warns and frees it) — Move. The same family of error applies when another persistent driver already controls the field.
WidgetThe 1st argument is the field the widget reads and writes (Slider(st["volume"]), linked both ways). It is not @=.
A lambda that reads nothing Scena tracksTypeError — the formula must name something reactive (see What can be linked). It does not freeze silently.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
A << Ba copy of the values of B into A. A is still the same object. B stays where it was.@= (it does not link) · A = B (swaps the Python reference) · absorb (copies and destroys the other)
c.absorb(other)c << other followed by destroy(other).<< alone

What can be linked

On the left of @= goes the field that will change; on the right, the formula — usually a lambda:. The formula must read at least one thing Scena tracks (a field, an object, st, clock, keyp, mouse): that is how Scena knows when to redo the math.

The right side must name something Scena tracks. A plain Python variable does not say when it changes: @= refuses it with TypeError.

What is reactive (it can appear on the right and trigger updates):

  • Point, Vec2, Shape (Circle, Rect, Line, …), Sprite, Entity — and their fields (c.radius, ship.center, hero.hp…)
  • st (and any State) — st.score, st.lives…
  • clock, keyp, mouse — frame input (always inside lambda:)
  • mic.level, audio.level, h.level (from a play_sound) and their .spectrum() — sound measurements, updated once per frame (Microphone)
  • A standalone field: Attribute(0.0)

Fields you create on an Entity join this world by themselves — Keeping values.

Canonical forms

The two everyday spellings. The expression on the right returns something that fits the target, and names at least one reactive object:

# thing["field"] @= lambda: expression that fits the field
dst["xyz"] @= lambda: src.abc

# Point: a lambda that returns the pair
circle1["center"] @= lambda: (a.x * 2 + 10, b.abc / 2)
# a pair of lambdas (one per axis) — the constructor spelling:
# Circle(center=(lambda: a.x * 2 + 10, lambda: b.abc / 2))

The general rule, day to day:

thing["field"] @= lambda: obj1.field_a + obj2.field_b

Concrete examples:

c["radius"] @= lambda: ship.hp * 0.1
hud["text"] @= lambda: f"Wave {st.wave}"
cursor["center"] @= mouse
twin["angle"] @= (lambda h=host: h.angle)

In a for loop, each lambda needs its own object: lambda h=host: h.angle — see Lambda.

Inside the formula, use the dot. The lambda already keeps the math alive: Scena reads st.score in the code and redoes the math when the field changes. Brackets inside it (lambda: st["score"] * 2, f"{st['score']}", c["radius"]) would give the field, not the number: @= (and a constructor's lambda) refuses with TypeError, pointing at the line and the dot spelling. A bracket alone on the right, with no lambda, is the direct link: c["radius"] @= st["size"].

Shorter forms, also valid

They work, but they are not the suggested path. Without lambda, both sides must already be objects Scena tracks (a field, a Point, a Vec2) — Python does not compute the expression first:

thing1 @= src                  # if thing1 and src are Scena objects (Point, Vec2, field)
dst["xyz"] @= src["abc"]       # if xyz and abc are reactive fields
line["p1"] @= rect.top_left    # links straight to the Point on the right, no math
orbit.center @= earth.center

A number or an already-computed expression (host.angle, player.hp * 10) becomes a float before @= sees it — TypeError. Use lambda:.

Named function

When the math has several cases, write a def and link the function (no parentheses). Scena reads the function's code once to learn what it depends on — just like a lambda:

def score_text():
    if st.won:
        return "You win!"
    if st.dead:
        return f"Game over — stars {st.stars}"
    return f"Stars {st.stars}   Lives {st.lives}"

scoreboard["text"] @= score_text       # no () — links the function, not its result
scoreboard["text"] @= lambda: score_text()   # also valid: Scena follows the function

It also works right in the constructor: Text(score_text, top_left=(20, 580)) makes the same link.

You can use if, local variables, len / min / round, math, Scena functions and other functions from the same file (up to 3 levels deep). Scena refuses with TypeError what it cannot see by reading the code — otherwise the link would sit still without warning:

  • for / while / [… for … in …] — the items only exist when it runs. Do it in update().
  • Reading a group (len(group["enemy"])) — use update() or a group formula.
  • Changing a Scena object inside the formula (c.radius = 5) — the formula only reads and returns.
  • An index that changes into a list of objects (balls[st.i].radius) — name the object.
  • Calling a function from another file, getattr / eval, a def or lambda inside the formula, try.

Does not work — a plain Python variable does not tell Scena when it changes; neither does a bare number:

x = 10
c["radius"] @= lambda: x * 2  # TypeError: the formula names nothing reactive

# also TypeError — host.angle has already become a float
# twin["angle"] @= host.angle

# right: brackets on the field, or a lambda that names the Shape
twin["angle"] @= host["angle"]
twin["angle"] @= lambda: host.angle

# right: put it in st (or an Attribute) and name that
st.x = 10
c["radius"] @= lambda: st.x * 2

You can create a reactive value by hand, without a Shape:

from scena import Attribute, State

pulse = Attribute(0.0)           # a standalone field, outside any object
hud = State(name="hud")          # another set of fields, like st
hud.level = 0

ring["scale"] @= lambda: 1 + pulse
label["text"] @= lambda: f"{hud.level}"

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
lambda: x + c.radius with a plain xvalid: it updates when c.radius changes (and reads x again at that moment). @= only refuses when the formula reads only plain variables and nothing Scena tracks.frozen
c.radius @= lambda: …an error: c.radius is already a float, so Python raises its own TypeError, with no Scena message. A scalar needs brackets: c["radius"] @= …. A compound value (c.center, a Vec2, an Attribute) accepts thing @=, but the path we teach is the same bracket + lambda.another spelling of the bracket
c["glow"] @= … (visual)a refusal: visuals, add-ons and filters (.visual, .glow, .shadow…) do not link. Use = and on_update / @when. Color and visibility do link: Linked color and visibility.a reactive field
Frame input in @=clock / keyp / mouse always inside lambda: (lambda: clock.time, lambda: keyp("D"), lambda: mouse.x) — never a bare number, nor once / dx. See Frame.the current value
A widget linked to a formulaa control the user's gesture does nothing to: the formula is in charge.a free control
r["damage"] @= lambda: r.width * 2 (a field of the object reading its own size)a known limit: an own field cannot read the size of its own object (width, radius…) nor its computed points (corners, the center of a Polygon) — those come from the whole object, and the new field is part of it. CircularReferenceError with the explanation. Use a property on the class (@property def damage(self): return self.width * 2) or compute it in update(dt). The object's own fields (r.charge), the center of a Rect or Circle and the fields of other objects can be read.a circular reference of your own

Lambda

lambda: keeps the math for Scena to redo later. In a for loop, pin the object: lambda b=ball: b.center.

Without lambda, Python computes right away and Scena gets a number. With lambda:, Scena keeps the math and redoes it when the source changes:

c["radius"] @= lambda: player.hp * 10
cursor["center"] @= lambda: mouse

The lambda looks up the name when it updates, not when you wrote the line. In a for loop, the name ball moves from one circle to the next. In the end, every lambda sees the last one — and every line follows it.

# wrong — all 20 lines follow the last ball
for i in range(20):
    ball = Circle(center=canvas.game_view.center, radius=16)
    Line(p1=(50, 50), p2=lambda: ball.center)

# right — b=ball keeps this ball now
for i in range(20):
    ball = Circle(center=canvas.game_view.center, radius=16)
    Line(p1=(50, 50), p2=lambda b=ball: b.center)

In the body use b.center, not ball.center. The center stays live; only which ball is fixed. If the name never changes (a point1 created once), lambda: point1 is enough — everyone is meant to follow the same point.

A callback that writes an attribute (after, on_done, …): a lambda only takes an expression — an assignment with = does not fit. Use setattr:

# wrong — SyntaxError (a lambda takes no assignment)
# after(1.0, lambda: player.active = True)

after(1.0, lambda: setattr(player, "active", True))
ship.dissolve_out(0.4, on_done=lambda: setattr(ship, "active", False))

If you want the spelling player.active = True

def wake():
    player.active = True
after(1.0, wake)

Formulas in constructors

An object can also be born linked: pass a lambda: instead of a value and the parameter follows the formula, like an @= written right after. A value without lambda is copied once. The geometry parameters (position, size, angle) and the color accept a lambda — layer and tag do not.

Without lambda, Python computes right away and the object is born with that number / point. With lambda:, Scena keeps the math and redoes it when the source changes — the same as an @= afterwards:

# copy now — player can move; this Circle stays where it was born
Circle(center=player.center, radius=player.hp)

# live link — follows the player and the HP
Circle(center=lambda: player.center, radius=lambda: player.hp * 10)

A point takes a lambda that returns the pair, or a pair of lambdas (one per axis). The pair is a constructor spelling; after creation use c["center"] @= lambda: (…, …) or link each axis.

Circle(center=lambda: player.center)
Circle(center=(lambda: a.x * 2 + 10, lambda: b.abc / 2))
p = Point(0, 300)
p["x"] @= lambda: mouse.x                 # one axis linked, the other copied
Line(p1=(50, 50), p2=lambda: ball.center)

The rule is the same in every geometry constructor: callable → link; anything else → copy. A point without lambda (center=player.center) copies — it does not follow. To follow, use lambda: (or @= afterwards).

Who accepts a lambda

General rule: geometry parameters and the color accept lambda formulas. The others do not.

ConstructorParameters that linkDo not link (copy / refuse)
Shape — Circlecenter, radius, perimeter_point, p1, p2, angle, spread, colorlayer, group, box, use_center
Shape — Rect / Square / Ellipsethe model's geometry: center, width, height, angle, top_left, p1, p2, vec, length, color, …corner_radius (does not link), layer / group, box, anchor
Shape — Linecenter, angle, length, p1, p2, vec, dx, dy, dist, colorlayer / group; relations (parallel_to=, circle=…) already watch by themselves — they are not the author's lambda
Shape — Polygoneach vertex in points= (you can mix: some lambda, some copied)the number of vertices (locked at construction)
Shape — Concavethe model's geometry (the Rect's), rim and colorscoop (locked at construction), layer / group, box
Shape — RegularPolygon / Trianglecenter, radius, side, vertex, angle (Triangle: also base_ratio)n= (RegularPolygon; sides: an integer, locked at construction)
Pointthe whole point: Point(lambda: …); one axis: Point(lambda: mouse.x, 0); a pair: Point((lambda: src.x, 10))Point(other_point) copies (does not follow)
Vec2each component: Vec2(lambda: a.x, lambda: a.y); the whole vector: Vec2(lambda: v1 + v2)the result of math already done (Vec2(v1.x, v1.y) copies the floats)
Sprite / Svgonly center=width / height / size (numbers at creation), frame, hitbox, file, color / visual. fps= / cols= / atlas= go in the Sheet. Afterwards: sprite["width"] @= / ["angle"] @= / ["scale"] @=
Textcenter=, color=text= is a string, or a field (st["score"]) that the Text then shows — not a formula. font_size, top_left=. Afterwards: hud["text"] @= lambda: …
Trackcenter, radius, begin, end; each point in points=stroke, smooth, floating
SpatialFx (Fire, Rain, …)center, radius; for directed fire also width, length, anglecolor, style, layer / group
Boxthe same as the Rect's geometry (center, width, height, p1, p2, …)Box is not an Entity. Box(graphic) is a copy, taken now
Entity()—no geometry in the constructor. Own fields afterwards: self.hp = 3 (copy) or self["hp"] @= lambda: … (link)

Visuals, add-ons and the place in the game never link in the constructor: visual=, glow=, layer=, group=. visible is not even a constructor argument (only for Point and Track): write obj.visible = False on the next line. Color links: Rect(color=lambda: …, line_width=lambda: …), Text(…, color=lambda: …, background=lambda: …), Sprite(…, flip_x=lambda: …) — see Linked color and visibility. Widget: the 1st argument is the Attribute it reads and writes, not a lambda.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Circle(center=player.center) “follows” the playera copy of the point, taken now. To follow: center=lambda: player.center (or c["center"] @= lambda: player.center afterwards).the same as @=
Sprite(width=lambda: …)a refusal — size in the constructor is a number. Link it afterwards: sprite["width"] @= lambda: ….the Sprite's center=lambda: (that one is valid)
In a for loop, Line(p2=lambda: ball.center)every line following the last ball — pin it: lambda b=ball: b.center. See Lambda.—

Linked color and visibility

Color, visibility and mirroring link too: color, fill, line, line_width (shapes and Text), the Text's background, the Sprite's alpha, visible and flip_x / flip_y. The @= is the = redone whenever the source changes: under a visual, a linked color gives the same result as .color = ….

A health bar made only of formulas: its length and its color follow st.health.

st.health = 100
st.facing = 1
ramp = Colormap.from_colors("red", "lime")

bar = Rect(center=(120, 580), width=200, height=12)
bar["width"] @= lambda: 200 * st.health / 100
bar["fill"] @= lambda: ramp.get_color(st.health / 100)

alert = Text("LOW HEALTH", center=(400, 300), color="red")
alert["visible"] @= lambda: st.health < 20

hero = Sprite("hero.png", center=(400, 200))
hero["flip_x"] @= lambda: st.facing < 0
  • While linked, writing directly raises LinkedAttributeError: bar.fill = …, set_color, set_alpha, visual = Paint(…), a visual with its own color (Neon("red")), fade_out() on a linked visible. bar["fill"].unlink() frees it.
  • On a shape, color writes the fill and the outline: linking color and also fill or line raises on the second link. On a Text, color is only the fill.
  • A formula can read another object's color, but a color is not a link source: b["color"] @= a["color"] raises. Link both to the same formula.
  • A Point links none of these (Scena paints and shows the markers); a Track does not link visible; a Text does not mirror. Visuals, add-ons and filters (visual, glow, shadow…) do not link.
  • The formula's value follows the rule of =: a name, hex or tuple becomes a Color; a negative line_width reads 0 and an alpha stays between 0 and 1, as in any formula.
  • In the constructor, a lambda links: Rect(color=lambda: …, line_width=lambda: …), Text(…, color=lambda: …, background=lambda: …), Sprite(…, flip_x=lambda: …).

Keeping values: st and Entity fields

Two places for your values: st, for the values of the game as a whole (score, lives, wave, options), and fields on the Entity itself, for what belongs to it (HP, grounded, ammo). In both, the field is born on the first write (st.score = 0, ship.hp = 3) and Scena already tracks it: @= formulas, @when and widgets can read from it.

Sprite, Circle, Rect, Line, Text, SpatialFx — and Entity() with no drawing — are Entities. Geometry already exists (center, radius, width…); what you invent is an own field. Score, wave, a game-wide flag: st. HP, grounded, ammo: on the Entity that owns them.

An own field (hp, grounded, wave) becomes an Attribute on the first write. From then on Scena tracks the field: widgets, @=, @when and @on_change can read from it.

st.score = 0                  # creates the field
st.lives = 3
st["hud"] @= lambda: f"Stars {st.score}"   # @= creates the field if missing

ship = Sprite("ship.png")     # a Sprite is an Entity
c = Circle()                  # so is a Circle
director = Entity()           # no drawing, same fields

ship.hp = 100                 # creates the field — already tracked
c["radius"] @= lambda: ship.hp * 10

# @= on the bracket also creates it, if the name does not exist yet
hero["grounded"] @= lambda: "bottom" in hero.touching_sides

ship["shield"] @= lambda: st.lives * 10
st reference

st already exists — it is a State. It holds the fields of the game as a whole. The ship's HP lives on the ship, not here.

You do not construct it. from scena import * already brings the object. Widgets, @=, @when and @on_change read from here. For another separate set (HUD, debug), create another State: hud = State(name="hud"). name is only the label in error messages — it is not a key.

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
st.score = 0valuest.score = 0read / writeCreates (or writes) the field. st.score reads the value that is there now, like an Entity field: st.mic is None, type(st.score) and best = st.score (a copy) work as with a plain variable.
st["score"]fieldSlider(st["volume"])readThe field: the place where the value lives. It is what links and tracking take: widgets (Slider(st["volume"])), Text(st["score"]), @on_change(st["wave"]), @when(st["alive"]), tween(st["t"], …), @=. Always outside a lambda: inside one, st.score. Used as a number (if st["alive"]:, st["score"] + 1, in an f-string), it raises TypeError with the dot spelling. .value reads the value; .unlink() removes a formula.
st["hud"] @=linkst["hud"] @= lambda: …read / writeLinks that field. @= creates the field if missing (starting value 0). Reading a field that does not exist raises an error.
st.keys() / st.exists("score")names / boolreadLists the fields; tells whether one has been created.
.namestr"st"readA diagnostic label. The global one is "st".
State(name="hud")Statehud = State(name="hud")—Another set of fields, just like st. An empty name raises ValueError.
CaseMeaning
st.keyReads the value. st.key = … writes it. st.f **= 2, st.pos += Vec2(1, 0), st.pos << (3, 4), st.pos.do_rotation(90), st.pos.x = 5 and st.items += [x] write to the same field and notify whatever is linked. st.items.append(x) changes the list without notifying the links (write st.items += [x]); that is why a formula that reads inside a list or dict in st (st.inv["gems"], ", ".join(st.items)) gives a warning when it is linked, and the way that notifies is to write the whole value (st.inv = {**st.inv, "gems": n}) or keep each number in its own field (st.gems). On a field with a formula (st["pos"] @= …), changing the Vec2 in place raises, like st.pos = …. A Vec2 that another st field or one of your fields already holds, or that has a formula, comes in as a copy: st.start = st.pos keeps where it was, and does not move along with st.pos.
Slider(st.volume)TypeError with the fix: st.volume is the current number, and the widget needs the field, st["volume"]. The same for Text, @on_change, @when, until, tween and @= with a Vec2 (c["center"] @= st.pos, st.pos @= …). With a number, st.x @= … gives Python's own TypeError (unsupported operand type(s) for @=): write st["x"] @= …. A string in Text(st.player_name) gives no error: it shows the current name and does not follow it; to follow it, Text(st["player_name"]). Before 0.8.0, st.key returned the field: st.mic is None was always False and best = st.score followed the score.
st["key"] @=The same spelling as geometry. Creates the field if missing (starting value 0). Reading it (st.key, st["key"] on the right) requires that it exists.
Entity fields: create, read and link
CaseMeaning
ship.hp = 100Creates (or writes) the field. It is already a reactive source.
ship["hp"] @= lambda: …Links. Creates the field if missing (default 0).
ship.hp @= …Python's TypeError — use brackets. See Rules.
ship.aim = Vec2(50, 0)A Vec2 in an own field can change whole or in place, and whatever reads ship.aim in a formula sees both: ship.aim = vec_from_angle(30, 50), ship.aim << (80, 0), ship.aim += (10, 0), ship.aim *= 2, ship.aim.x = 70, ship.aim.do_rotation(90). Linking the vector: ship["aim"] @= lambda: … or ship.aim @= lambda: …, the same link (ship["aim"].unlink() drops it, ship["aim"].is_linked tells); a field that holds no vector yet refuses the bracket: write ship.aim = Vec2(0, 0) first. A list or a dict: ship.items += [x] and ship.d |= {…} notify; ship.items.append(x) changes the list without notifying the links, as in st.
ship.foe = enemyAn object in an own field (or in an st field, st.foe = enemy): a formula that reads through it, lambda: ship.foe.radius * 2 or lambda: st.foe.center.x, follows the object the field holds now. After ship.foe = other, it follows other and stops listening to the previous one. With None along the way, guard the read: lambda: st.foe.radius if st.foe else 0. An own field must hold the object when the formula is linked (an st field may be None).
print(ship.hpt)A missing name on read → AttributeError. A typo shows up here, not at = / @=.
Color and visibility (.color, .fill, .visible, .flip_x…)Not an own field, but it links: @= redoes the = when the source changes (Linked color and visibility). Visuals and add-ons (.visual, .glow) refuse @=: use = and on_update / @when.
ship.x = 10Graphic and SpatialFx have no .x / .y — AttributeError, with no field created. Read ship.center.x. Move with move_to / move_by. Link with ship.center["x"] @=. Point.x still exists. A bare Entity still keeps e.x as an own field.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
st.score and ship.hp are the same idea (a tracked field)different places: the whole game vs this object. Reserved names (visible, layer, center…) do not become own fields.creating ship.score in place of the game's score

Advanced

Persistent drivers

Besides @=, other things also write a field every frame. Only the @= formula is exclusive — the others add up, in any order.

A persistent driver is something that writes the pose (or a field) without the author calling a one-shot verb every frame: the @= formula, mouse dragging (draggable), the wheel (wheel_rotate), a tween / move_to(..., time=) / move_along in flight, or a standing collision resolve(). Only the formula is exclusive: a field linked with @= accepts no other driver (and vice versa), in either order. The others coexist: a move_by(time=) before or after resolve() gives the same result (it stops at the wall), and a draggable shape can have a movement in flight.

DriverWhat it claimsIf you @= on topHow to release
@= (formula)the linked field itself—.unlink() / unlink_all()
draggable / on_drag_tothe parts the drag's move_to writes (e.g. center)LinkedAttributeError right awaydraggable = False (or clear the callbacks)
wheel_rotatethe parts of rotate_by (includes angle)LinkedAttributeErrorwheel_rotate = False
tween / move_to(time=) / move_alongthe target, for the Handle's durationLinkedAttributeError at the @= (not on the next frame)handle.cancel() or wait for the end (with loops="forever", only cancel())
resolve(a, b)usually the center of each sideLinkedAttributeError at the @= or at the resolve itselfunresolve(a, b)
 
c.draggable = True
# LinkedAttributeError — the center already has a driver (draggable)
# c["center"] @= lambda: src

c.draggable = False
c["center"] @= lambda: src          # now ok

h = c.move_to(400, 200, time=2.0)
# LinkedAttributeError — "move_to(time=2) pushes it"
# c["center"] @= lambda: src
h.cancel()
c["center"] @= lambda: src

resolve(ball, "wall")
# LinkedAttributeError if ball.center is already linked
unresolve(ball, "wall")

enemy.draggable = True
enemy.move_by(200, 0, time=2, loops="forever")   # ok: they coexist
# holding the enemy with the mouse freezes its patrol;
# letting go → it carries on from where the enemy was dropped

Rule: an @= formula against any other driver on the same part → a hard error, in either order (the message names the line where the object was created, e.g. the Sprite made at game.py:151). The other drivers never refuse each other. Holding with the mouse freezes the movements (tween / move_*(time=)) on the parts the drag (or the wheel) writes; on release they carry on, before on_drag_to — so a “go back home” (move_to(home, time=0.3)) in on_drag_to works. While you hold it, the drag also beats what your on_update writes to the object (a per-frame gravity move_by): every frame it goes back under the cursor; on release, your code is in charge again. This is not handle.pause(): h.paused stays yours alone. Redeclaring the same kind (a second tween on the same key, a new @= on the same field) → warns and replaces. force=True still exists only on the one-shot verbs of Move / tween — not on the draggable / wheel_rotate flags.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Linking from the draggable center (Line(p1=lambda: c.center) or line["p1"] @= c.center) gives an errorOK — whatever reads the center does not compete with the drag; only what writes to it doeslinking into a draggable center
A linked radius + draggableOK — the drag does not write radiuslocking the whole Circle
move_to / confine in your on_updatea one-shot call by the author — not a persistent driverthe same as draggable / tween
