World

What belongs to the whole screen, not to one object: the background, effects over the whole picture, bursts that last an instant, the camera, the window and quality, layers and groups.

Background → Background
Vignette / Bloom → Post · flash / explosion_at / fade_out → Impacts
Zoom / pan / frame_to → Camera
FPS / quality → Presentation
layer= → Layers
group["wasp"] → Groups

Background

The screen's background, drawn behind everything. It has a base — a color, a gradient, a sky or an image; always exactly one — and extras stacked on top: stars, clouds, haze, dust. Each background shows up as soon as you create it; keep what it returns to change its parameters, hide it or take it away. A color, a Gradient or a Texture becomes the base when you assign it to canvas.background.

SkyGradient("night")
Stars()
Stardust()
Chromadust()
Nebuladust()
cl = Clouds(amount=0.45)
cl.amount = a * b + 0.5
cl.enabled = False
cl.remove()
canvas.background.remove(cl)   # same
canvas.background.clear()      # extras only; the base stays
canvas.set_fly(Tunnel())
Wallpaper(Gradient("black", "navy", angle=90), pan_response=0.05)
Wallpaper("bg1.jpg", tile_mode="mirror", pan_response=0.15)

Space dust: Stardust (two colors), Chromadust (a palette that cycles; reflect=True makes it go back and forth), Nebuladust (three colors in patches). They are not the SpatialFx Starburst, the Chroma post or Nebula (bands).

canvas.background

Assigning replaces the base. Every background (Wallpaper, SkyGradient, Stars, Tunnel…) already shows up when created. Gradient / Color / Texture must be applied here (or inside a Wallpaper). An image file: Wallpaper("bg1.jpg"). Constructor parameters are attributes of the instance you can assign, and take effect on the next frame — the exceptions for Wallpaper / SkyGradient are below.

canvas.background = "navy"
canvas.background = (0.1, 0.1, 0.15)
canvas.background = Color("black")
canvas.background = Gradient("sunset", angle=-90)
Wallpaper("bg1.jpg", fit="cover")
canvas.background.base = Color(0.05, 0.05, 0.08)

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
canvas.backgroundstackcanvas.backgroundread / writeReading it gives the whole background (base + extras), the live one — not a copy. Assigning a color, Gradient or Texture replaces only the base; assigning what you read (canvas.background = canvas.background) changes nothing. To keep the background and go back to it later, keep the base: saved = canvas.background.base … canvas.background = saved.
.baseWallpaperColor("navy")read / writeThe wallpaper. There is always one.
.enabledboolFalseread / writeHides the extras only. The base still draws.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
.add(field)Parameters: field (a background: Stars, Clouds…)the backgroundStacks an extra. If it is already on the stack, does nothing. It is for a background made with Stars.temp(…) (made without stacking) or taken away with remove. Returns the instance.
.remove(field)Parameters: field (a background: Stars, Clouds…)—Takes an extra away. Calling it again does nothing. Same as field.remove(). The base does not leave this way.
.clear()No parameters—Takes away the extras only. The base stays.
.reset_base()No parameters—The base goes back to the default black.
list(canvas.background)Parameters: the stack (canvas.background)listExtras only, not the base.
canvas.set_fly(Tunnel())Parameters: field (a background, or None)—Clears the extras and keeps that one background. None = just clear.
Wallpaper

The base of the background: a color, a gradient, an image or a Texture covering the whole screen. Creating a Wallpaper already makes it the base (canvas.background.base).

Wallpaper(source, filename=, image=, fit="cover", tile_mode=, scale=1, tile_size=, underlay=, pan_response=0, zoom_response=0, rotation_response=0, scroll=(0, 0), enabled=True)

Name without =: 1st in order (color, gradient, texture or file). The rest by name. No args: opaque black. A string with . or / is a file; otherwise it is a color. Image parameters only apply to a file. Creating a Wallpaper already makes it the base. Search: Image files.

Wallpaper("navy")
Wallpaper(Gradient("black", "navy", angle=90), pan_response=0.05)
Wallpaper("space.jpg", tile_mode="mirror", pan_response=0.15, zoom_response=0.3)
Wallpaper("bg2.png", fit="contain")
Wallpaper(path, fit="tile", tile_size=200, tile_mode="mirror")
ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
source1stcolor or Gradient or file or TextureblackWhat the base is made of. A color name, tuple, Color, Gradient, Texture, file ("bg1.jpg") or Image. A Texture keeps here what it does on a shape: angle, shift and set_alpha. A Visual / SpatialFx / filter raises TypeError. E.g. Wallpaper("navy").
filenamename=strNoneInstead of source: the file path.
imagename=ImageNoneInstead of source: a skia.Image already loaded.
fitname=str"cover"Image only: cover · contain · stretch · tile.
tile_modename=str"decal"Image only: what shows beyond the image's border when the camera moves or zooms out. "decal" (nothing; the underlay shows) · "clamp" (stretches the last row of pixels) · "repeat" (repeats) · "mirror" (repeats mirrored, with no seam). Left out: "repeat" with fit="tile", otherwise "decal". In tile, "clamp" becomes "repeat".
scalename=number1Image only: extra zoom. Must be > 0.
tile_sizename=number or pair of numbers¼ of the shorter sideImage / fit="tile" only: the cell, in design units. With another fit it is a TypeError.
underlayname=colorblackImage only: color of the bands left over in fit="contain" and of everything beyond the border with tile_mode="decal". None = does not paint what is left over.
pan_responsename=number0Response to the camera's pan. 0 = stuck to the screen. 1 = 1:1 with the world.
zoom_responsename=number0How much the camera's zoom affects the pattern.
rotation_responsename=number0Fraction of the camera's rotation.
scrollname=point(0, 0)Drift in design units / s, independent of the camera.
enabledname=boolTrueHides the drawing without taking it off the stack.
fitBehavior
coverScales evenly until it covers; crops the rest.
containScales evenly until it fits; letterbox with underlay.
stretchStretches on both axes.
tileRepeats a cell of tile_size.

A camera that moves: in cover / contain / stretch the image ends at the border. With pan_response, zoom_response or rotation_response, the camera gets there: pass tile_mode="mirror" (the image goes on mirrored, with no seam) or "repeat". Without tile_mode, the underlay (black) shows beyond the border. E.g. Wallpaper("bg1.jpg", tile_mode="mirror", pan_response=0.1).

Assigning a color / tuple / Gradient / Texture already wraps it in a Wallpaper. An image: the constructor itself. fit= on a color raises TypeError. Reading .fit / .tile_mode on an image source gives back the same string. Afterwards: source, the camera settings (pan_response / zoom_response / rotation_response / scroll) and enabled are attributes of the instance you can assign. filename / image / fit / tile_mode / scale / tile_size / underlay stay fixed in the source — to change them, replace .source or build another Wallpaper. wp.remove() on the base raises TypeError; replace canvas.background.base.

SkyGradient

A sky in a vertical gradient (top, horizon, ground), as the base of the background. horizon is the height of the horizon line, from 0 (bottom) to 1 (top). Creating one already makes it the base; the last Wallpaper / SkyGradient created wins.

SkyGradient(palette="day", top=, middle=, bottom=, horizon=0, fade=0.003, pan_response=0, zoom_response=0, rotation_response=0, scroll=(0, 0), enabled=True)

Name without =: 1st in order (the preset). The rest by name. No args: "day". palette / top / middle / bottom stay fixed at construction — to change the ramp, replace the base. horizon / fade / the camera settings / enabled take effect live. sky.remove() raises TypeError.

SkyGradient("night")
SkyGradient("sunset")
SkyGradient("day", horizon=0.42)
SkyGradient(top="navy", middle="sky blue", bottom="navy")
ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
palette1ststr"day"day · dawn · sunset · dusk · night · space · overcast · desert · forest · toxic · ember · ice · underwater. Any top / middle / bottom skips the preset and fills in the rest from day.
topname=colorfrom the presetColor of the zenith (top of the screen).
middlename=colorfrom the presetColor of the atmosphere, at the horizon.
bottomname=colorfrom the presetColor below the horizon (solid). With horizon=0 it does not show.
horizonname=number0The horizon line (0–1, y-up from the bottom). 0 = sky all the way down (middle at the bottom). Line it up with Ground.
fadename=number0.003Blends middle → bottom below the line. 0 = a sharp cut. The same parameter as in Ground.
pan_responsename=number0Response to the camera's pan. 0 = stuck to the screen. 1 = 1:1 with the world.
zoom_responsename=number0How much the camera's zoom affects the pattern.
rotation_responsename=number0Fraction of the camera's rotation.
scrollname=point(0, 0)Drift in design units / s, independent of the camera.
enabledname=boolTrueHides the drawing without taking it off the stack.

canvas.background = Neon() / Rain() / Blur() raise TypeError. A material is not placed on its own: assign it or use Wallpaper(…). SkyGradient.remove() / a wallpaper that is the base: TypeError — replace .base.

Reading the parameters. amount= is density or brightness (1 = default); speed= is the background's own motion (0 = still); alpha= is the opacity, from 0 to 1. The camera settings, on every background: pan_response= 0 keeps the background stuck to the screen and 1 makes it move along with the world (values in between give parallax); zoom_response= / rotation_response= do the same for zoom and rotation; scroll=(dx, dy) is a constant drift in units per second; enabled=False hides it. res_scale= (on the cloud and dust backgrounds: Clouds, ChurningClouds, Stardust, Chromadust, Nebuladust, FilamentField) is the internal resolution (1 = full; lower = cheaper and blurrier).

Post

A Post is an effect over the whole picture of the world, applied after everything is drawn: vignette, bloom, film grain, a CRT screen, light. It stays on while it is in the canvas.effects stack — creating it already stacks it. Keep what it returns to change its parameters, hide it or take it away. For a burst that lasts an instant (a flash, a shake, an explosion at a point, darkening the screen), use an Impact.

Vignette()
bloom = Bloom(intensity=0.8)
bloom.intensity = 1.0
bloom.enabled = False
grain = Grain()
grain.remove()
canvas.effects.remove(grain)   # same
canvas.effects.clear()
canvas.effects

Creating an effect already puts it on the stack. .add is for putting back an effect taken away with remove, or one made with Bloom.temp(…) (which creates it without stacking). The order in which the effects apply is fixed, not the order you created them in: blurs first, then added light, color, overlays, distortions and, last, the special (shader) effects. Constructor parameters are attributes of the instance you can assign, and take effect on the next frame. Impacts (flash, *_at, cover) do not go on this stack.

bloom = Bloom(intensity=0.8)
bloom.intensity = 1.0
bloom.enabled = False          # stays on the stack, does not draw
bloom.remove()
canvas.effects.remove(bloom)   # same
canvas.effects.clear()
canvas.effects.add(bloom)      # puts it back
list(canvas.effects)

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
canvas.effectsstackcanvas.effectsreadThe list of the Posts that are on. Creating a Post already puts it here; do not assign canvas.effects = ….
.enabledboolFalseread / writeFalse turns all the Posts off at once. Each effect also has .enabled.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
.add(effect)Parameters: effect (post)the effectStacks it. If it is already on the stack, does nothing. It is for an effect made with Bloom.temp(…) (made without stacking) or taken away with remove. Returns the instance.
.remove(effect)Parameters: effect (post)—Takes it off the stack. Calling it again does nothing. Same as effect.remove(). The Python object lives on; .add puts it back.
.clear()No parameters—Takes away every post.
list(canvas.effects)Parameters: the stack (canvas.effects)listIn construction order.

ColorWash: after construction the palette is .colors (not color / color2 / color3). Haze.kind only picks defaults at construction — change amount / speed / bias.

Hide a post with enabled, not visible. add(Neon()) is the wrong family.

Reading the parameters. amount= / intensity= is the strength (0 turns it off). speed= is the animation's pace (0 freezes it). target= / center= is a point or an object; left out, it follows the mouse. Sizes in “screen pixels” depend on the window size.

Impacts

Impacts are bursts that last an instant, fired by the canvas: you call one, it happens and goes away on its own — there is nothing to keep or take away. On the whole screen (flash, shake, glitch), at a point (explosion_at and the other *_at) or as a cover that darkens the screen (fade_out / fade_in). The same effect on an object is a Transient; something that stays in a place is a SpatialFx; an effect that lasts on the screen is a Post.

canvas.flash(0.6)
canvas.shake(10)
canvas.explosion_at(x, y)
canvas.fireworks_at(hero)
canvas.zap_at(info.point, style="fork")
canvas.hit_at(info, angle=90)
canvas.debris_at(x, y, color="peru")
canvas.fade_out(0.5, on_done=load_next)
canvas.fade_in(0.5)

*_at take (x, y) or a point (tuple, Point, Vec2, Graphic, info); None does nothing. After a point, the other parameters go by name (amount=, radius=). The cover is drawn after the widgets (over the HUD too) and holds until fade_in; it runs even with clock.paused (it is a screen transition, not game time); canvas.covered is 0…1 (read-only). No then= — only on_done. Iris: fade_out(…, style="iris", center=hero) — center= is a point, copied now (left out = center of the frame).

Reading the parameters. The place comes first: x, y or a point (tuple, Point, object, a collision's info); the rest goes by name. amount= is the strength (1 = default); radius= is in design units; shake= / flash= turn on or off the shake and the flash that come with the effect.

Camera

The camera chooses which part of the world shows in the window: shifting the view (pan), moving closer (zoom) and rotating. It does not move the objects — only the view; widgets and the ui layer stay still in the window. Without time= the change is immediate; with time= it animates and returns a Handle, with the same parameters as Move (ease=, loops=, yoyo=…).

canvas.set_origin("center")
canvas.pan_to(200, 80)                      # x, y
canvas.pan_to((200, 80))                    # tuple
canvas.pan_to(Vec2(200, 80))                # Vec2
canvas.pan_to(boss)                         # Point / Graphic (center)
canvas.pan_by(40, 0)                        # dx, dy
canvas.pan_by((40, 0))                      # tuple
canvas.pan_by(Vec2(40, 0))                  # Vec2 — not Point
canvas.pan_to(200, 80, time=0.8, ease="ease_out")
canvas.pan_to(door, speed=300)               # same speed, near or far
canvas.zoom_to(2.0, about=(mouse.x, mouse.y), time=0.6)
canvas.pan_to(400, 300, time=1.0, loops="forever", yoyo=True)
await parallel(
    canvas.pan_to(boss, time=1.0),
    canvas.zoom_to(2.2, time=1.0),
)
canvas.frame_to(focus, pad=0.1, time=1.2)
canvas.reset_view(time=0.5)

canvas.frame_to(group["fleet"].box, pad=0.15)  # None = stays still
# margin in units (not a fraction): canvas.frame_to(box.outset(40))

Following an object. There is no canvas.follow, and time= / speed= will not do it (the destination is read once, at the moment of the call, and the camera goes to where the target was). Call pan_to every frame in update, with slack (deadzone) and lag (chase; to follow at a fixed speed, approach instead of chase):

def update(dt):
    look = (canvas.pan_x, canvas.pan_y)
    tx, ty = deadzone(look, hero.center, size=(160, 90))
    canvas.pan_to(chase(look, (tx, ty), rate=6.0))

The size of the design space (canvas.width / height) and canvas.playfield: Place › Screen regions.

canvas (camera) reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
canvas.zoomnumber1readUniform scale. 1 = no zoom.
canvas.pan_x / .pan_ynumber80readThe world point now at the center of the window.
canvas.rotationnumber1readRotation of the view, in degrees.
canvas.game_viewBoxcanvas.game_viewreadWhat the camera sees now, in the world. With the camera still at the start: from (0, 0) to (canvas.width, canvas.height), center in the middle. A new Box on every read. With the camera rotated it is the upright (unrotated) rectangle that holds the view: its corners are off the screen. See Place.
canvas.ui_viewBoxcanvas.ui_viewreadThe whole window, from (0, 0) to (width, height), for the HUD. It does not move with the camera. A new Box on every read.
canvas.cull_offscreenboolTrueread / writeDoes not draw what is out of view. Default True. The objects keep running update and colliding. False draws everything: Presentation.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
set_origin(where, *, time=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=)Parameters: where (str), time, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done—Pan only. "corner": (0, 0) at the bottom-left corner. "center": in the middle of the window. Zoom and rotation stay. With time=, backgrounds and layers with pan_response follow the camera during the animation, with no jump at the end. No force=.
zoom_to / zoom_byParameters: factor (number), time, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done, about—Absolute / multiplies. about= is the anchor point (world): (x, y), Point, Vec2 or Graphic (center). Left out: the center of the view — the pan does not change. Time parameters: time= / ease= / loops= / yoyo= / then= / on_done= / about=. No force=.
pan_tox, y · (x, y) · Vec2 · Point · Graphic; time, speed, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done—Puts a world point at the center. Forms: two numbers; a tuple (x, y); Vec2; Point; Graphic (uses its center). Time parameters: time= or speed= (world units per second; the duration is the distance from the current view to the destination ÷ speed) / ease= / loops= / yoyo= / then= / on_done=. Does not take angle + distance. No about= / force=.
pan_bydx, dy · (dx, dy) · Vec2; time, speed, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done—Shifts the content. Forms: two numbers; a tuple (dx, dy); Vec2. Not a Point or a Graphic. Takes the same time parameters as pan_to, speed= included (the length of the shift ÷ speed). Does not take angle + distance. No about= / force=.
rotate_to / rotate_byParameters: angle (degrees), time, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done, about—Rotates the view, in degrees. about= optional (default: the center of the view); the same kind of point as for zoom. With time=: the short arc in rotate_to; rotate_by uses the sign as written. Takes the time parameters and about=. No force=.
frame_to(target, *, pad=0, rotate=False, time=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=)Parameters: target (a shape, Box, rectangle or None), pad (number), rotate (True/False), time, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done—Frames the target. Target: a shape / Box / tuple (left, top, w, h), or None (nothing to frame: stays still; with time= a Handle that moves nothing for the whole time — it still takes all three motions). pad is a fraction of the target on each side (0.1 → 10%; size × (1+2p)) — the same family as playfield.pad. Negative tightens the framing. Room in design units: frame_to(box.outset(40)), not pad=. A collapsed Box (width/height 0) frames tight, with no error. rotate=True lines up with the target's angle. The destination is read at the start. No force=.
reset_view(*, time=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=)Parameters: time, ease, loops, yoyo, then, on_done—Takes the camera back to the start: zoom 1, rotation 0, origin at the corner. With time=, backgrounds and layers with pan_response follow the camera during the animation, with no jump at the end. No force=.

time= / ease= / loops= / yoyo= / then= / on_done=: the same as the verbs in Move. about= only on zoom_* / rotate_*. No force= (the camera is not an Entity). Without time=: immediate, returns canvas. With time=: a Handle. yoyo=True needs loops > 1 (or "forever"); with loops=1 it raises an error.

Three motions

The camera has three independent motions: pan, zoom and rotation. Two verbs of the same motion do not add up: the second cancels the first. Different motions run together.

MotionUsed by
panpan_to / pan_by / set_origin. Also zoom/rotation when there is an about=.
zoomzoom_to / zoom_by.
rotationrotate_to / rotate_by.
all threeframe_to / reset_view.
  • Different motions together: pan_to(…, time=1) and zoom_to(…, time=1) (without about=).
  • The same motion: the second call cancels the first.
  • about= pins a world point to the screen — that is pan. Do not mix it with another pan_to (the last one wins).
  • The destination is read at the moment of the call: about= / pan_to / frame_to do not chase a shape.
  • then= only from inside a mode (like the script's tween).

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
canvas.pan_to(hero, time=0.5) follows the heroa destination read at the moment of the call: the camera goes to where the hero was. To follow, pan_to every frame (above). shake is hit feedback, not pan. frame_to(group["…"].box) takes None (an empty group) without a guard.canvas.follow

Presentation

How the game is shown: the window mode (canvas.display), how many frames per second (canvas.framerate), the quality of the effects (canvas.fx_quality) and whether what is out of view gets drawn (canvas.cull_offscreen). By default the window is "windowed" and Scena tunes the rest on its own (FX Auto): it starts at "high" quality at ~60 fps and lowers the quality if the computer cannot keep up. Writing framerate or fx_quality turns that tuning off.

init(width=1000, height=700, window_scale=1.0)
init(width=1000, height=700, display="fullscreen")
canvas.display = "maximized"
canvas.display = "windowed"

canvas.framerate = "vsync60"   # default: locked to the monitor, ~60
canvas.framerate = "vsync30"   # locked to the monitor, ~30
canvas.framerate = "vsync"     # every monitor refresh (144 on a 144 Hz one)
canvas.framerate = 30          # fixed clock at 30 fps
canvas.framerate = "max"       # no cap (bench)

canvas.fx_quality = "high"
canvas.fx_quality = "medium"

canvas.cull_offscreen = False  # draws everything, even what is out of view
canvas.display

The mode of the system window. String. Default "windowed". Assigning sets that mode (it does not toggle). You can assign it before run() (it applies when the window opens) or during the game (it changes at once, like the shortcuts). Read it back to sync a checkbox. Only these three values — no "full" / "max".

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
"windowed"str"windowed"read / writeDefault. A window in the design's aspect, centered on the desktop. No black bars: the window is the design rectangle. Dragging resizes it with the aspect locked. Starting size: window_scale.
"maximized"str"maximized"read / writeFills the desktop (the taskbar stays). The content does not stretch: black bars fill what is left. The title bar's Maximize button is the same mode. Shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+M.
"fullscreen"str"fullscreen"read / writeCovers the monitor: no border, no taskbar. Black bars fill what is left, as in maximized. Ctrl+Shift+F again goes back to the previous mode (e.g. maximized). Shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+F.

init(display=) does the same as assigning canvas.display. Widgets stay in the design rectangle (not on the bars). The design never stretches.

canvas.framerate

How frames are delivered. String or number. Default "vsync60". Assigning turns FX Auto off; with Auto on, reading returns the current step ("vsync60" or "vsync30"). You can assign it before run(). A wrong value raises an error at once and changes nothing ("vsinc" → Did you mean 'vsync'?). Debug shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+4 (vsync → vsync60 → vsync30 → 60 → 30 → max; the HUD shows the real rate).

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
"vsync60"str"vsync60"read / writeDefault. Locked to the monitor, at the rate closest to 60: every monitor refresh on a 60 Hz monitor, every other one on a 120 Hz monitor, 72 per second on a 144 Hz monitor. Each frame appears exactly when the monitor redraws (the vblank), always at the same pace, and dt becomes an exact multiple of the monitor's period.
"vsync30"str"vsync30"read / writeLocked to the monitor, at the rate closest to 30 (twice the interval of "vsync60"). It is FX Auto's last resort when the computer cannot keep up (at "low", or at the current quality when what weighs is the game's logic).
"vsync"str"vsync"read / writeOne frame per monitor refresh: the full rate (120 on a 120 Hz monitor). Smoother, but the work per second goes up with it.
a numbernumber30read / writeA fixed clock at that rate (finite, > 0). It does not follow the monitor: motion can stutter for a while when that rate is close to the monitor's. Prefer a "vsync…".
"max"str"max"read / writeNo cap: as many frames as the computer can make. For measuring performance.
canvas.fx_quality

The quality of the visual effects. String or FxQuality (FxQuality.LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH / MAX — the same values as the strings). Default "high". Shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+3 (cycles low → medium → high; max is left out).

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
"high"str"high"read / writeDefault. Screen effects (Post) at half resolution; effects on objects in full.
"medium"str"medium"read / writeScreen effects at half resolution; SpatialFx and heavy effects in a simpler version. Also: "med".
"low"str"low"read / writeScreen effects at ¼ resolution; light versions of everything.
"max"str"max"read / writeEverything at full resolution. For diagnosis; it is not part of the shortcut's cycle.
canvas.cull_offscreen

Skip drawing what the camera does not see. bool. Default True. Scena tests each object: if its box (with room for glow, outline and effects) does not touch the view, it is not drawn that frame. Only drawing changes: out of view, the object keeps running update, moving and colliding. You can assign it before run() or during the game (an options screen can change it).

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
TrueboolTrueread / writeDefault. Tests the objects and skips the ones out of view. Layers with parallax (pan_response other than 1), widgets, the background and screen effects are always drawn.
FalseboolFalseread / writeDraws every visible object; whatever is outside the window simply does not appear.

The test costs almost nothing. An object standing still keeps its box until it changes; one that only moves carries its box along. On a layer where nothing (or almost nothing) was out of view, Scena waits a few frames before testing again. So a one-screen game stays practically the same, and a world bigger than the window gets much faster. Measured: a level of 1500 tiles draws in 3 ms instead of 8; the level of tutorial 27 runs ~9% faster; a bullet hell with shots that leave the screen, ~7%. False is there for comparing.

set_fx_auto

set_fx_auto(enabled=True, refresh_hz=None, params=None)

Turns FX Auto on or off: the automatic tuning of quality and fps. On by default ("high" quality at ~60 fps). It measures how long each frame takes and, if the computer cannot keep up, lowers the quality (high → medium → low, at "vsync60") and then the fps (low at "vsync30"). If what does not fit is the game's logic (update, processes, collisions) and not the drawing, lowering the quality would not help: it goes straight to "vsync30" at the current quality (high@30), and only if frames actually miss the vsync. Shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+2.

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
enabled1stboolTrueFalse turns the tuning off: quality and fps stay where you put them.
refresh_hzname=number or NoneNoneThe monitor's rate for the plan (60, 120…). None measures it on its own.
paramsname=tuning objectNoneAn escape hatch for performance tests. Leave it out.

canvas.framerate and canvas.fx_quality turn FX Auto off (the same as Ctrl+Shift+2). Benches should call set_fx_auto(False) (and usually canvas.framerate = "max"). The design's size: init(width=, height=), read-only in canvas.width / .height. window_scale=1 is the largest windowed window (aspect locked, desktop showing around it) — it is not maximize. Maximize / fullscreen: canvas.display. There is no canvas.maximized / canvas.fullscreen / toggle_fullscreen().

Layers

Layers decide the drawing order: what is on a higher layer appears in front. Three already exist: default (where everything is born), top (in front of the world) and ui (fixed to the window, for the HUD). Create others by number (layer=10: just the position) or by name (canvas.layers.create: with parallax, and a way to hide everything at once). above / below return the number next to a layer.

Circle(center=(100, 100), radius=20, layer=10)   # z=10, created on the spot
Sprite("cloud.png", layer=below("default"))      # behind default
far = canvas.layers.create("far", pan_response=0.15, below="default")
Sprite("mountain.png", layer="far")    # moves at 15% of the camera
Text("SCORE")                          # ui layer (window)
Rect(center=(80, 700), width=120, height=36, layer="ui")
canvas.layers["top"].post_fx = False   # top stays sharp; ui already comes after the post
Layer by number

layer=<int>

The first use creates the layer with z equal to the number (neutral, visible). The same number puts things on the same layer. The z is frozen — the position is its name. A namespace apart from strings: 10 ≠ "10". canvas.layers.create(10) → TypeError (strings only). No parallax parameters — for that, give it a name. Ceiling: z ≤ 100. bool is not accepted. The default layer has the value 0.

above / below

above(name) · below(name)

Global functions (like chase). name is a str or an int and must exist. Returns an int to use in layer=. above() refuses at once (ValueError) a number that lands on top or above it (ceiling: z ≤ 100). below() has no floor.

CallTypeMeaning
below("default")int-1One step below the anchor layer.
above("default")int1One step above.
above(10)int11A numeric anchor works too (once layer 10 exists).
canvas.layers.create

canvas.layers.create(name, z=, pan_response=, zoom_response=, rotation_response=, scroll=, below=, above=)

The name without =: 1st in order (str only). The rest by name. The camera response freezes at creation; only the scroll speed changes later (layer.scroll).

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
name1ststrThe layer's name. E.g. canvas.layers.create("spawn"). Int → TypeError.
pan_responsename=number10 = stuck to the screen. 1 = follows the world. >1 = foreground.
zoom_responsename=number1How much the camera's zoom affects this layer.
rotation_responsename=number1The fraction of the camera's rotation.
scrollname=point(0, 0)Drift in design units / s, independent of the camera. It adds to pan_response. To start still: create it with a speed and then set layer.scroll = (0, 0) (scroll=(0, 0) at creation leaves the layer neutral).
zname=integer0Order. Or below= / above= — just one. z ≤ 100.
below / abovename=str/int or NoneRelative order: the target's z minus / plus 1. default and top are reserved and neutral. E.g. below="default". Two layers created with below="default" end up at the same z; layers with the same z draw in creation order (the newest on top). To stack them, chain: create("backdrop", below="road").
visiblename=boolTrueWhether the layer is visible when created. Later: canvas.layers["name"].visible.

A parallax layer is decoration: no game physics. Collision / SpatialFx on ui raise an error. top ≠ HUD. A number ≠ a string with the same digits (10 ≠ "10"); a numeric z is frozen; no pan_response on a numeric layer — give it a name.

Endless world

Endless fills the part of a layer that the camera shows: it cuts the axis into cells (slots), builds each cell a little before it comes on screen and destroys the ones left far behind. For runners, flappy games, a ship in a cave, a sky of clouds that never ends. It decides when and where; you decide what.

canvas.layers.create("buildings", pan_response=0.5)
canvas.layers.create("course", below="default")     # a layer of its own, behind the player
Endless("buildings", ["building1.png", "building2.png"], height=300, bottom=80, gap=(40, 200))

def pipes(slot):
    if slot.i < 2:
        return []                                    # empty cell
    middle = slot.rng.uniform(230, 650)              # same cell, same numbers
    return [Rect(top_left=(slot.left, middle - 90), width=70, height=middle - 170, group="wall"),
            Rect(top_left=(slot.left, 800), width=70, height=710 - middle, group="wall")]

course = Endless("course", pipes, step=260)

def update(dt):
    canvas.pan_to(bird.center.x + 120, canvas.pan_y)   # the camera moves
    canvas.playfield.set(canvas.game_view.outset(60))
    st.score = max(0, course.index_at(bird.center.x) - 1)

Pieces: an image path (with height=: the size of each one), a list of paths (one per cell, picked at random) or a function fn(slot) that returns an object, a list of objects or [] (an empty cell). The function builds in the cell's absolute coordinates (slot.left, slot.right…). Endless never moves the pieces.

Random draws: swap random. for slot.rng. (and chance(p) for slot.chance(p)). Each cell has its own draw: going back to a cell builds the same piece. The global random would give a different piece on the way back, without warning. seed= with a number repeats the same world in every run; without seed, a new world every run (.seed tells which one came up).

Endless reference

Endless(layer, pieces, axis=, step=, gap=, start=, seed=, bottom=, left=, group=, height=, width=, size=)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
layer1ststr or intA layer of its own, created with canvas.layers.create(...). default / top / ui raise an error: pieces created mid-game would paint over the player. A parallax layer: decoration only (nothing collidable).
pieces2ndpath, list of paths or functionWhat goes in each cell. A mixed list (image + function) raises an error: vary it inside the function with slot.rng.choice([...]).
axisname="x" / "y" / "xy""x"Horizontal (runner), vertical (a ship climbing) or a grid (a map seen from above).
stepname=number, pair or functionNoneThe cell's size. Required with a function. "xy": a pair (width, height). Varied widths: step=lambda slot: slot.rng.choice([160, 320]). Without step (images only): the image's size + gap.
gapname=number or (min, max)0Space after each image; a pair is drawn per cell. Only for images without step.
startname=number or pairNoneWhere cell 0 starts. Default: the edge of the screen when the Endless is born (the first screen comes already full).
seedname=int or NoneNoneSame number = same world. None = a new world every run.
bottomname=numberNoneImages with axis="x": the y of their base. Default: the bottom of the screen.
leftname=numberNoneImages with axis="y": the x of their left side. Default: the left of the screen.
groupname=str or listNoneThe images' group. The function gives its pieces their group.
height · width · sizename=numberNoneThe size of each image, as in Sprite(path, height=…). Without it, the image gets the size of a Sprite with no size (48 on the longer side). A strip of scenery almost always wants the screen's height=. The function gives its pieces their size.

MemberReturnsMeaning
.pieceslistThe live pieces it built, in axis order.
.index_at(x)int (or (i, j))The cell that holds x (with "xy": index_at((x, y))). Score per stretch, checkpoints, difficulty.
.seedintThe seed in use — pass it in seed= to repeat the run.
.active = False—Freezes the filling (the pieces stay).
.destroy()—Stops and destroys its pieces. In an Act, change_act does this for you.

slot (what the function receives)

FieldReturnsMeaning

slot.left · slot.right · slot.bottom · slot.topnumberThe edges along the endless axis, in world coordinates (left/right in "x", bottom/top in "y", all four in "xy"). The other axis is yours.
slot.boxBoxThe cell ("xy").

Two ways to make an endless game

Every endless game has two frames of reference: the world (ground, pipes, coins, towers) and the screen (the player's ship, enemy formations). The camera decides which one stays still; whatever lives on the other one costs a ride-along line per frame (group[...].move_by).

The camera movesThe camera stays still
Genresrunner, platformer, flappy, ship in a cavevertical shooter with enemy waves
World thingsbuilt once at the slot's coordinates; they do not moveride-along: group["ground"].move_by(0, -v * dt)
Screen thingsride-along: group["onscreen"].move_by(dx, 0)screen = world: Tracks with fixed points work
Parallaxon its own (pan_response)the layer's scroll (layer.scroll changes the speed)
Endlessgame and decorationdecoration only; the game arrives over time (every)
Clearing what leavescanvas.playfield.set(canvas.game_view.outset(m)) every framethe default playfield is enough
Stopping at game overstop the camera: everything stopsclouds.scroll = (0, 0)

The ride-along works because offsets add up: a move_along in progress plus a move_by every frame give the sum of the two.

# Still camera (vertical shooter): the sky moves, the waves arrive over time.
canvas.layers.create("clouds", scroll=(0, -180))

def cloud(slot):
    x = slot.rng.uniform(0, 600)
    return Sprite(slot.rng.choice(["cloud1.png", "cloud2.png"]), center=(x, slot.bottom))

Endless("clouds", cloud, axis="y", step=240)

def boss_arrived():
    canvas.layers["clouds"].scroll = (0, 0)          # the scenery stops

Keeping what changed

Going back to a cell builds everything again: a coin you took comes back. To keep it, use slot.i as the key:

taken = set()

def stretch(slot):
    made = [Rect(top_left=(slot.left, 40), width=800, height=40, group="ground")]
    if slot.i not in taken:
        coin = Circle(center=(slot.left + 400, 120), radius=12, group="coin")
        coin.stretch = slot.i
        made.append(coin)
    return made

@collide("hero", "coin")
def took(hero, coin):
    taken.add(coin.stretch)
    coin.destroy()

Who owns each piece: what the function returns belongs to the Endless (it destroys it when the cell falls behind, going by the cell's position). What the function creates and does not return is yours — an enemy that walks away should not be returned. A piece you destroy (a coin taken) only comes back when its cell leaves the screen and comes back. Other objects on the same layer are not touched.

Terrain: what must match at the seam between cells (the height of the ground) is a function of the world x — neighboring cells ask about the same x. slot.rng is for decisions inside the cell (a tree here, a tower there).

A still camera + Endless on a game layer: the window does not move, so it fills the first screen and stops. Moving the pieces (the conveyor-belt habit) takes them off screen and nothing new arrives — Scena warns once. With a still camera, move the camera, or use a layer with scroll for decoration only. Create the Endless in the Act that uses it.

Groups

A group is a tag. Whatever has the tag is in the group; group["wasp"] is a live view of that set — whoever joins later shows up on the next read.

A name no object uses is an empty group, not an error: after renaming a tag in only one place, group["shots"].destroy() does nothing. Check the name (Scena warns when the name is close to that of a group that exists).

wasp = Sprite("x.png", group="wasp")   # joins the "wasp" group
wasp.hp = 1
group["wasp"].move_by(0, 10)            # acts on all of them
foe = group["wasp"].nearest(player.center, where=lambda w: w.hp > 0)
group["wasp"].destroy()

An object joins a group through a tag: in the constructor (group=) or later (tag). The group has no .add / .remove.

for x in (100, 200, 300):
    Circle(center=(x, 100), radius=10, group="wasp")
ship = Sprite("ship.png", group=["player", "hurt"])
ship.tag("shielded")
ship.untag("hurt")
ship.tagged("player")               # True
copy = ship.clone()                 # copies the tags
elite = ship.clone(group="elite")   # replaces them

An Entity can be in several groups. group= on clone replaces the tags (it does not mix them); leaving it out copies the current ones; group=None = none. Clone a clean template, not an object already tagged. There is no id: the tag is the only name for finding an Entity later (group["hero"].first). A destroyed object leaves its groups at once: group["wasp"] read right after destroy() no longer holds it.

Count, test, pick by position and iterate. The order is the order in which members joined the group — not their position on screen.

for x in (100, 200, 300):
    Circle(center=(x, 100), radius=10, group="wasp")
group["wasp"].hp = 3
w = group["wasp"][1]

group["wasp"].count           # or len(group["wasp"])
group["wasp"].empty
w in group["wasp"]
leader = group["wasp"].first  # or [0]
newest = group["wasp"].last   # or [-1]
i = group["wasp"].index(w)    # 0 = the first to join
mid = group["wasp"][1:3]      # a list, not a group

for w in group["wasp"]:
    w.hp -= 1

The for uses whoever was in the group when the loop began: you can destroy a member midway without breaking it; whoever joins midway only shows up on the next read. A member that leaves and comes back goes to the end. .index(w) and .first / .last use this live rank — if someone ahead leaves, the ones behind move up. For a formation, sort (sorted(group["wasp"], key=lambda w: float(w.center.x))) or keep a fixed number in an own field (w.slot = i, or phase= on move_along).

group["wasp"].move_by(0, 10) calls the same method on each member, with the same arguments. It is the for, written short.

for w in group["wasp"]:
    w.move_by(0, 10)

group["wasp"].move_by(0, 10)   # the same thing
group["wasp"].hp = 3           # writes to all of them
group["wasp"].tag("shielded")  # the group's own: tags all of them

What comes back depends on what the method returns for one member:

If each one returns…The group returns…
the object itself — an instant action, such as move_by without time=the group (you can chain)
something else — a Handle, a copy, a channel…a list with each one's result
 
# with time=: each one returns a Handle → a list
handles = group["wasp"].move_by(0, 80, time=0.4)
await parallel(*handles)

# with speed=: each one works out its own duration (the far one takes longer)
handles = group["wasp"].move_to(400, 120, speed=250)

# move_along always returns a Handle → a list
handles = group["wasp"].move_along(track, time=4)
await parallel(*handles)

# clone returns a copy → a list of copies
copies = group["wasp"].clone()

Reading an attribute: one member → the value; several → a list of values. Writing (group["wasp"].hp = 3) puts the same value in all of them. A member without the method (or the name) raises an error. In an empty group there is no member to call: the method does nothing and returns None — neither the group nor a list (with time= or speed=, it returns a single Handle; with speed= that Handle finishes on the next frame, since there is no distance to cover); reading any field (center, angle, hp…) raises AttributeError saying the group is empty — there is no member to read from. For the position of a group that may become empty, use centroid or box (None if empty). If you are going to use the return value (e.g. await parallel(*handles)), test group["wasp"].empty first.

.destroy(), .tag(), .untag(), .nearest(), .filter(), .index(), .first / .last belong to the group (see the reference); they are not “call it on each one and collect”.

The same arguments for everyone. A different phase, destination or time per member: write the for. There is no group.every / group.on_update: the fleet's loop lives in update or in a Director.

Find a member, count the ones that pass a test, measure the fleet.

foe = group["wasp"].nearest(player.center, where=lambda w: w.hp > 0)
close = group["wasp"].nearest(player.center, within=200)   # or None
n = group["wasp"].count_where(lambda w: w.hp > 0)
if group["wasp"].any(lambda w: w.hp <= 1):
    canvas.flash(0.2)
group["wasp"].filter(lambda w: w.hp <= 0).destroy()
mid = group["wasp"].centroid    # (x, y) or None
box = group["wasp"].box         # Box or None — frame_to(box) is safe when empty

nearest returns a member or None, not a list. filter returns a copy (it does not follow the group). centroid and box are None on an empty group.

Set operators between groups. The result is a copy: whoever joins later is not in it.

alive = group["wasp"] | group["drone"]    # union
hurt = group["wasp"] & group["hurt"]      # intersection
solo = group["wasp"] - group["elite"]     # difference
group["elite"] <= group["wasp"]           # subset
group["wasp"].issuperset("elite")         # superset
snapshot = group["wasp"].as_set()         # a Python set of the current members

Each operator has a method with the same effect, which also takes the tag's name: .union("drone"), .intersection(), .difference(), .symmetric_difference(), .issubset(), .issuperset(). .is_live tells whether the view still follows the group: True on group["wasp"] and on a formula group; False on a copy. For a combination that follows: Named live group.

Gives a name to a live combination: it is recomputed on every read. The expression has to stay inside lambda:, so that it is redone on every read.

group["enemies"] @= lambda: group["wasp"] | group["boss"]   # required: | & - give a copy; the lambda: redoes the expression on every read
group["enemies"] @= group["wasp"]                           # optional: a bare live group is an alias
group["enemies"] @= "wasp"                                  # optional: a bare tag string is an alias
group["enemies"] @= (group["a"] | group["b"])               # forbidden without lambda: raises an error with a hint to wrap it in a lambda

await until_empty("enemies")
group["enemies"].unlink()     # the name goes back to being an empty tag group

An alias without lambda only works for a live group or the tag's name. A union, an intersection or a filter has already been computed: @= refuses it (it does not freeze it silently). This does not use the @= link of fields: if two names depend on each other (A uses B and B uses A), the error only shows up on reading. .is_linked tells whether the name has a formula.

Similar, elsewhere: the active switch of an attack box is also linked with @= (sword["active"] @= lambda: hero.showing(STRIKE)) and is recomputed in each frame's collision step. See Attack boxes.

@collide does not follow a formula group — use the source tags. @click(group["…"]) follows the tag, like @collide: whoever joins later is clickable too.

Wait for the wave to end: await until_empty(...), in an async mode.

await until_empty("wasp")
await until_empty(group["wasp"])
await until_empty("enemies")      # a formula group too

It takes the name, group["wasp"] or a formula group — not the result of filter / | (a copy). Do not use until(lambda: group["wasp"].empty): use until_empty. See async wait.

Where else to look — Place · Appearance · Frame · Move

Place

Tools for placing objects. A Box is an invisible rectangular region: you measure it, shrink it (inset), slice it into strips (strip) and grids (grid), find its neighbor (beside) and create objects fitted into it with box=. Rect draws; Box only measures — it is not a game object.

Constructors / corners / inset / strip / beside → Box
Fleet / board → grid
Rect(box=) / Sprite / Text → box=
Screen in the world / HUD / leaving the level → Screen regions
Level made in the editor (Level, make()) → Level

Box

A Box is a rectangular region that does not show on the screen: it is for measuring and placing. You build it like a Rect (center= + width= + height=, a corner, p1= / p2=…) or from an object (ship.box), but it has no color, layer or group — and there is no empty Box().

zone = Box(center=(400, 300), width=800, height=220)
inner = zone.inset(24)
halo = zone.outset(24)
hud = zone.strip("top", 40)                 # strip inside
sidebar = zone.beside("right", width=120)   # neighbor outside
cell = canvas.game_view.inset(40).grid(4, 3).cell(0, 0)
Rect(box=cell, color="navy")

# the same models as Rect:
Box(top_left=(80, 640), width=160, height=80)
Box(p1=(100, 100), p2=(500, 300))
Box(p1=(100, 300), p2=(500, 300), height=40, anchor="square")
Box reference

Box(center=, width=, height=, angle=) · Box(source) · Box.from_graphic(graphic)

Constructors

CallMeaning
center=, width=, height=The usual way. angle= is optional.
top_left=, width=, height=Corner + size
p1=, p2=Opposite corners
p1=, vec=One corner (p1) and a vector to the opposite corner (vec), in design units
p1=, p2=, height=, anchor=Axis + thickness — the same as Rect ("cap" / "square" / "side_left" / "side_right")
Box(source)source is a Graphic (Rect, Sprite, Text…) or another Box. The same copy as graphic.box — the frame with its names (a Box is a Rect that does not draw)

Measuring a group

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
group["wasp"].boxNo parametersBox or NoneAn axis-aligned box that covers every member (a new Box), or None if the group is empty. Angle 0. It is not a Box constructor.

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.center .width .height .anglepoint or number(400, 300)read / writeGeometry. Corners: .top_left · .right_center · … — as in Rect, each name stays tied to its corner: after a rotation, .top_left is still the same corner, even if it is no longer at the top left on the screen. A Box made from another one (graphic.box, Box(b), inset, cells) keeps the names: cell (0, 0) of a board stays the same after you rotate or mirror it.
.left .right .bottom .topnumber80readSides. y up: top is the largest y. Read-only: to change the area, create another Box (e.g. box.outset(40)).
.col_index / .row_indexint or None0read / writeOn a grid cell. None on a standalone Box.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
inset(margin)Parameters: margin (number)BoxShrinks evenly inward. A copy. Room inside box=: box=cell.inset(8) — there is no padding= in the constructor. A negative margin raises ValueError.
outset(margin)Parameters: margin (number)BoxGrows evenly outward (the twin of inset). A copy, with the same center and angle. A negative margin raises ValueError. A collapsed source (a line or a point) gets an interior. It is not pad= / padding= (a fraction) — the margin is in units: frame_to(box.outset(40)).
strip(side, thickness)Parameters: side ("left"/"right"/"top"/"bottom"), thickness (number)BoxA strip inside, flush with a named side ("top" = the side of top_left / top_right). The strip has the thickness you ask for and spans the whole side of the Box. If the thickness is larger than the Box, the strip is the size of the Box, with no warning. A negative thickness or an unknown side raises ValueError. Compare: beside (outside); a grid for fleets.
beside(side, *, width=, height=, gap=0)Parameters: side; width/height optional; gap (number)BoxA neighbor outside, flush with a named side. Sizes you leave out are inherited; both left out → the same size. gap is the space between the sides. A negative size or gap, or an unknown side, raises ValueError. Compare: strip (inside).
grid(cols, rows, gap=0)Parameters: cols (int), rows (int), gap (number or pair)GridSlices the Box. gap is the space between cells. See Grid.
contains_point(x, y=None)Parameters: x (a point, or the number x with y)True/FalseGeometry only. It does not register clicks. For a board: g.cell_at(mouse.x, mouse.y).
rotate_to / rotate_byvalue (number); about= (point, optional); force=Falsethe same Box (changes it)Rotates the region in place and returns self — not a copy (unlike inset / outset). No time=: this is not Move's rotate_to (that one is for objects on the screen, with time= and a Handle). about= is the pivot (default: the center) — a tuple, Point, Vec2, Graphic or mouse, copied now. A grid made from it inherits the angle.

Box() raises an error. There is no default region. Four positional numbers do not work either: corners vs x, y, w, h. isinstance(box, Entity) is False. There is no @click / on_click on a Box. An inset / gap that is too large turns it into a line or a point with no warning — use .is_collapsed if you need to detect it. outset does not collapse; outset(m).inset(m) always gets the Box back, but inset(m).outset(m) only does when the inset did not squeeze it all the way down. strip = a strip inside; beside = a neighbor outside; a grid for fleets / equal cells.

Grid

A grid slices a Box into equal columns and rows — for fleets, boards, inventories. box.grid(8, 3) returns the grid; go through its cells with for or ask for one with .cell(col, row). Row 0 is the top one (the visual top of the Box).

zone = Box(center=(canvas.game_view.center.x, 520), width=820, height=220)
fleet = zone.grid(8, 3, gap=16)          # or gap=(gx, gy); the same as Grid(zone, 8, 3, gap=16)
for cell in fleet:
    Wasp(space, box=cell, height=40, group="wasp")

top_left = fleet.cell(0, 0)              # col, row
third = fleet.cell(2)                    # flat index: col = n % cols
for row_cells in fleet.rows:
    ...

hit = fleet.cell_at(mouse.x, mouse.y)    # None in a gap or outside
if hit is not None:
    piece = Rect(box=hit)
Grid reference
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
for cell in giterable—Row 0 first, left → right.
g.cell(col, row)col (int), row (int)BoxColumn first, like (x, y).
g.cell(n)n (int)BoxFlat: col = n % col_count, row = n // col_count.
.rows / .colslists—Lists of lists. Counts: .row_count / .col_count.
.cell_at(x, y)point or x, yBox or NoneThe inverse. On a rotated grid it converts to local coordinates first. A gap → None. A cell with zero area can still be reached with .cell(col, row), but cell_at never finds it.
cell.col_index / .row_indexint—Its place in the grid. There is no pointer back to g. The neighbor: g.cell(cell.col_index + 1, cell.row_index).
g[col, row]TypeError—Reserved. Use g.cell(col, row).

A grid on a Box with angle= makes its cells at the same angle. cell_at takes that into account. A click on the rotated board lands in the right cell.

box=

box= creates an object already fitted into a region (a Box, a grid cell): a Rect fills it, a Circle is inscribed in it, a Sprite fits inside it and keeps the image's proportions. With an explicit size, the object is only centered in it. To leave some room, shrink the region first: box=cell.inset(8).

cell = canvas.game_view.inset(24).grid(4, 3).cell(0, 0)
Rect(box=cell, color="navy")              # fills
Circle(box=cell)                         # inscribed (the shorter side)
zone = Box(p1=(200, 200), p2=(100, 400))
Sprite(box=zone)                         # fits whole, keeps the aspect
Sprite(box=cell, height=40)              # only centers; height wins
Text("Score", box=canvas.ui_view.grid(1, 8).cell(0, 0), layer="ui")

squares = panel.box.inset(8).grid(8, 8)
for cell in squares:
    Square(box=cell, color="gold")
Fit contract
Typebox= aloneWith an explicit size
Rect / EllipseFills (pose + size + angle)Mixing them raises an error
Circle / Square / regular N-gonInscribed (the shorter side). Circle does not inherit the angleOnly centers (radius= / length= / side=)
TriangleFills (the apex along the width; inherits the angle). With base_ratio=: fits, centered, with that proportionOnly centers (radius= / side=)
Sprite / SvgFits (the PNG's aspect; inherits the angle)Only centers (height= / width= / size=)
Textcenter= the center of the region (ui layer); align="center"; the region's width if left out; outside the columnDo not mix with center= / top_left= / top_center= / top_right=

A region that moves: pass a formula. box=cell fits once (a value copies); box=lambda: … fits again whenever something the formula reads changes (a formula links). It works on shapes (Rect, Square, Concave, Ellipse, Circle, RegularPolygon, Triangle) and on Sprite, Svg and SpriteButton.

shield = Rect(box=lambda: hero.box.beside("right", gap=8), color="cyan")
marker = Circle(box=lambda: board.cell(st.spot), color="gold")
banner = Rect(box=lambda: canvas.game_view.strip("top", 40), color="navy")

The shield follows the hero when it walks, turns or grows; the marker jumps to the cell that st.spot names; the banner follows the camera. Like any linked shape, it refuses move_by / rotate_by / scale_by (“its center follows its box= formula”). To let it go: force=True on the verb, or unlink_all() — it stays where it is. If the hero is destroyed, the shape is let go too, at its last place. A Sprite (or Svg) follows the region by changing its scale, so every frame of the animation keeps the same size as the others; with height=, only the center follows. Text does not take a formula in box= (its width decides where the lines break): link its center= instead.

Every object with a rectangular frame has .box — a copy of the frame, taken now, with the Graphic's names (rect.box.top_right is rect.top_right; sides on the screen: .left / .top / …): Rect, Square, Ellipse, Circle (the square of the diameter, turned toward the rim point p1), Sprite, Svg. Line / free Polygon / Track / Point raise TypeError. The layout verbs live on Box (panel.box.inset(8).grid(8, 8)), not on the Shape. To keep the pose inside a Box: confine.

box= does not mix with center= / width= on a Rect. box=region is a copy: the object does not follow the region afterward; to follow it, use box=lambda: region. A HUD after a pan: ui_view, not game_view. If the region shrank to a line or a point (an inset that is too large), the object is born invisible; check with .is_collapsed on the Box or on the object.

Screen regions

Three ready-made regions of the canvas: game_view (the part of the world the camera shows), ui_view (the window, for the HUD) and playfield (the play area, to know when something left it). You read them the same way; they are for different things.

Circle(box=canvas.game_view.inset(80).grid(3, 3).cell(1, 1))
hud = canvas.ui_view.strip("top", 80)
Text("SCORE", box=hud, layer="ui")
rail = canvas.game_view.strip("left", 120)
sidebar = canvas.game_view.beside("right", width=120)

# leaving the level — not layout:
canvas.playfield.pad = 0.4
@leave_playfield("bolt")
def leftover(shot):
    shot.destroy()

safe = canvas.playfield.inset(40)   # a Box; the playfield's .pad does not change
outer = canvas.playfield.outset(40)  # a larger halo; .pad does not change
band = canvas.playfield.strip("top", 80)  # a copy; .pad does not change
canvas reference
PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
canvas.width / .heightnumber2000readThe size of the design space. Set it in init(width=…, height=…) before run(). The OS window is something else: window_scale and canvas.display.
canvas.aspect_rationumber1.67readwidth / height.
canvas.game_viewnew Boxcanvas.game_viewreadA window on the world (what the camera sees). For ships, formations, “the top of the screen”. Each read is a new Box. With a rotated camera: it is the upright rectangle that holds the rotated view, larger than the screen.
canvas.ui_viewnew Boxcanvas.ui_viewreadA window on the view, [0, W] × [0, H]. HUD / layer="ui" / view Text. It does not move with the camera.
canvas.playfieldplayfieldcanvas.playfieldreadThe exit area for @leave_playfield, fixed in the world (default: the init space with a 25% margin on each side, so 1.5× larger; it does not follow the camera). It is not a Box. inset / outset / grid / beside / strip return Box copies and do not write .pad. Alias: canvas.bounds.

There is no canvas.center / canvas.screen / canvas.view. The center of what you see: canvas.game_view.center (world) or canvas.ui_view.center (HUD).

A Box cut from game_view in setup stays in the world when the camera moves. Usually that is what a formation wants. For a layout that follows the view, read game_view again in update. A HUD laid out in the world goes wrong after a pan. Leaving the level: @leave_playfield.

With a rotated camera, game_view is larger than the screen. It is the upright (unrotated) rectangle that holds the rotated view, so its corners, and the cells of a grid made from it, fall off the screen; confine(canvas.game_view) lets the object out through the corners. To keep it on the screen with a rotated camera, rotate the region too: Box(center=canvas.game_view.center, width=canvas.width / canvas.zoom, height=canvas.height / canvas.zoom, angle=-canvas.rotation).

Level

Reads a level file made in the level editor (python -m scena_editor). It only reads: Level("level1.json") creates nothing on the screen. Your code decides what each item becomes.

level1 = Level("level1.json")
for p in level1.group("platform"):
    block = p.make()                    # the Rect as it was drawn, in the group "platform"
    block.mass = STATIC
for e in level1.group("star"):
    Sprite("star_gold.png", size=28, center=e.center)   # a point is a place
level1["backdrop"].make()                  # image: the Sprite at the editor's size and rotation
pond = level1["pond"].make(color="steel blue")
area = level1["arena"].box              # or just the region (Sprite(box=), confine, a grid…)
start = level1["start"].center
route = level1["drone_route"].points      # a list of Vec2 for move_along
Level reference

Level(path) — a relative path is looked up like Sprite images: next to the script, in its media/ folder, in the current folder.

Level

MemberReturnsMeaning
Level(path)LevelReads the .json file the editor saved. path is the file name, looked up like images. A file that is not found raises ValueError with the folders it searched. A file Scena cannot read (invalid JSON, a malformed item, a version from a newer Scena) raises LevelFormatError, a ValueError that names the file and the item: except ValueError catches both.
level["name"]LevelItemThe item with that name (names are unique in a level). An unknown name raises ValueError, with a suggestion; if the name is a group's, the message says level.group(...).
level.group("g")list of LevelItemThe items that have the group g, in file order (drawing order). A group no item has raises ValueError — a typo does not become an empty list.
for item in level · len(level) · "name" in level—Every item, in file order. Guides (images that are only a reference in the editor) are not part of the level.
.names · .groupstuple of namesEvery name; every group in use (in order of first use).
.size · .box(width, height) · BoxThe level's area, from (0, 0) to size. .box is a new Box on every read — for canvas.playfield.set(level1.box), canvas.frame_to(level1.box), confine.
.pathtextThe absolute path of the file that was read.
level.sheet("name") · .sheetsSheet · tuple of namesThe level's sprite sheets (the file's sheets table). sheet("name") is the same Sheet for every frame of that sheet, created on first use: a clip registered on it plays on what make() creates. Creating it checks each item's frame: an unknown frame raises LevelFormatError with the item. An unknown name raises ValueError, with a suggestion. The editor only keeps the sheets some item uses: a sheet meant only for the code (the power-up boxes the code creates at the level's points) is gone on the next save — load it in code, Sheet("sheet.png", atlas="sheet.xml").

LevelItem — every item

MemberReturnsMeaning
.kindtext"rect" · "ellipse" · "concave" · "circle" · "line" · "polygon" · "regular_polygon" · "triangle" · "track" · "point" · "image"
.name · .groupstext or None · tupleThe name and groups given in the editor. An item can be in several groups.
.centerVec2The center. A line: its middle; a polygon or a track: the middle of the box around it; a point: the point itself.
make(**kwargs)the new shapeCreates the shape as it was drawn, in the item's groups: rect → Rect, ellipse → Ellipse, concave → Concave (with scoop and rim), circle → Circle, line → Line, polygon → Polygon, regular_polygon → RegularPolygon, triangle → Triangle (with base_ratio), track → Track (with the item's smooth; 0 if the file has none), point → Point, image → Sprite (the editor's size and rotation; a sheet frame → Sprite(item.sheet, frame=item.frame, …)). Other keywords are passed on (layer=, color=, visual=); group= adds to the item's groups. Geometry (center=, width= …) raises TypeError: it comes from the level. The same table as the editor's “Copy as code”.

LevelItem — by kind

KindFields.box
rect · ellipse.width .height .angleAn oriented Box (with the rotation)
concave.width .height .angle .scoop (text) .rim (Vec2)An oriented Box (the box)
image.width .height .angle; a whole image has .image (absolute path), a sheet frame has .sheet (the Sheet) and .frame (index or name) — asking for the other form's field raises AttributeError (a sheet's file would show every frame)An oriented Box
circle.radiusthe square around it
line.p1 .p2 (Vec2), .length, .angle (heading from p1 to p2; both as item.make() reads them)none — raises AttributeError with a hint
regular_polygon.radius (center to vertex), .n (sides), .angle (heading of vertex 0)none
triangle.radius (center to apex), .angle (heading of the apex), .base_ratio (base / side; 1 = equilateral)none
polygon · track.points (a new list of Vec2); a track also has .closed and .smooth (0 = straight lines, 1 = a curve; on a smooth track the points are the control points — move_along(item.make()) follows the curve)none
pointonly .centernone

The item in another model

make() creates the shape in the file's model: the rectangle by its center (center, width, height, angle), the line by its ends (p1, p2). The model decides what the shape stores and what it computes. In a Rect built by its center, width = 300 grows both ways, and top_left is computed: it takes neither = nor @=. For another model, write the constructor with the item's numbers; the Box from item.box has every named point.

b = level1["elevator"].box
door = Rect(top_left=b.top_left, width=b.width, height=b.height, angle=b.angle)  # grows from the corner
bridge = Rect(p1=b.bottom_left, p2=b.top_right, angle=b.angle)    # by two corners (copies)
beam = Rect(p1=b.left_center, p2=b.right_center, height=b.height, anchor="cap")  # by the axis
c = level1["rope"]
rope = Line(p1=c.p1, angle=c.angle, length=c.length, group=c.groups)  # pinned at p1: a pendulum
laser = Line(center=c.center, length=c.length, angle=c.angle)          # grows from the middle

These are copies, like every read from the level. make() puts the shape in the item's groups; here, pass group=item.groups. A concave one also takes scoop=item.scoop, rim=item.rim. The same goes for a shape that already exists, reading its parts (Rect(top_left=r.top_left, width=r.width, height=r.height, angle=r.angle)). The error message of a computed field already shows that line, ready to use.

The level and the window

The level's size (level1.size, the frame the editor shows) is the area of the world; the window is something else, and your code decides how one shows the other. Level only reads the file, so you can read the level before init() and open the window at its size: one unit of the level is one unit of the window, and the camera does not need to move. A level larger than the screen (the ninja level is 4000 × 750) fits in a window of any size you want, and the camera shows the right part: canvas.frame_to(level1.box) frames the whole level.

level1 = Level("level1.json")     # before init(): it only reads the file
w, h = level1.size
init(width=w, height=h)          # the window at the level's size

init(width=1280, height=720)     # or: any window...
canvas.frame_to(level1.box)      # ...and the camera frames the whole level

Frames from a sprite sheet

An image in the level can be a frame from a sheet (spritesheet): a grid (columns and rows, or the cell size) or an atlas (the coordinates in a .xml or .json file), the same cuts as Sheet. The level file stores the sheet once and, in each item, which frame it shows. Timing stays in the code: the clips go on the level's Sheet.

level1 = Level("level1.json")
for t in level1.group("ground"):
    t.make()                              # the frame, at the editor's size and rotation
level1.sheet("water").clip("ripple", [40, 41, 42], fps=6)
for a in level1.group("water"):
    a.make().play("ripple")                 # the same Sheet: the clip is on it

The level editor

The editor comes with Scena (pip install scena). In the terminal, either of these opens (or creates) the level: scena-editor level1.json or python -m scena_editor level1.json — the second always works, because it uses the same Python as your games.

An icon to open the editor with a double click: run scena-editor --shortcut (or python -m scena_editor --shortcut) once. On Windows it shows up in the Start menu and on the desktop; on macOS, in Applications (~/Applications); on Linux, in the applications menu. If you reinstall Python, run it again. Editor errors go to a log file, whose path shows in the status bar.

Tools (on the left, icons with their key in the corner): Rect (R), Ellipse (E), Circle (C), Line (L), Polygon (G), Triangle (D: Base ratio in the panel), Regular polygon (N), Track (A: Smooth in the panel), Concave (U: a box with a scoop; Scoop and Rim in the panel), Point (P), Image (I: a picture, or a sheet's .xml / .json atlas). Dragging draws; a click creates the shape with a side of 100 (96 or 128 on the grids from 8 to 64, so the corners land on the grid). Smooth and Base ratio have a slider, with the number next to it: dragging shows the shape changing, and Undo takes back the whole drag. On the top bar: Undo / Redo, Select (V) and Pan (H, or Space+drag). The panel on the right gives the name, groups (comma-separated), position and size. Shift while dragging: no grid. Cmd/Ctrl+C copies the items — and the code that creates them (Rect(center=…)) goes to the clipboard. The editor's numbers are the same as the code's.

Frames from a sheet: choose an atlas with the Image tool, or select an image and click Choose frame…. The sheet appears in place of the level, and the panel on the right shows the cut: the whole image, columns × rows, the cell size or the atlas. The mouse wheel zooms, dragging pans, F fits and Esc cancels. A click picks the frame, which keeps the image's center, rotation and scale: a strip of 17 cherries placed whole becomes one cherry of the same size. The status bar shows the frame under the pointer, or the Sheet message when the cut does not work.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
item.make() vs item.boxmake() = the shape drawn in the editor. .box = the region, for another use (Sprite("x.png", box=item.box), confine, a grid). Two purposes, not two spellings.Level(...) creates nothing on its own; neither does level.group(...).
Rect(p1=block, p2=…)The center of block as a point: a shape in place of a point counts as its center.It does not copy the block in another model. Read its parts: Rect(p1=block.p1, p2=block.p2, angle=block.angle).
The level's groupsLabels from the editor. make() applies them to the shape, so group["platform"] finds the blocks made this way.They are not live groups: level.group("g") reads the file, not the registry.
The editor's numbersThe same as the code's: design units, y up, center, counterclockwise rotation in degrees.There is no conversion. Changing a value you read (item.center) does not change the level: they are copies.

Where else to look — Draw · World · Geometry

Frame

What you read every frame: time (clock), the keyboard (keyp) and the mouse. Ask in update — “is the arrow key held?” — and act: that is the check, asked every frame. All three can also go in an @= formula. To run something once when a condition becomes true, see React.

Held / every frame → Frame
When it becomes true / leaves the screen → React
Bodies touch → Collision
In N seconds / every N → Schedule
This number goes from A to B → Move
This Entity is in this chapter → Mode
The whole map → Which to use

clock

clock is the game's clock: dt (seconds in this frame), time (seconds since the start) and the pause and slow-motion controls (paused, scale). Its times are already on the game's scale — in slow motion dt gets smaller; paused, it is 0. clock.real_dt / clock.real_time are real time (the wall clock), unscaled. e.time_scale makes a single Entity slower or faster. For a rhythm, “once every N seconds”: ready.

def update(dt):
    ship.move_by(0, 200 * clock.dt)

ship.on_update = lambda e, dt: e.rotate_by(40 * dt)
clock.paused = True
clock reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
clock.dt / .timenumber0.016readGame time: dt = seconds in this frame, time = seconds since the start. It shrinks in slow motion (scale) and is 0 while paused. At most 0.25 s per frame: after a freeze (a breakpoint, dragging the window) the world moves only that much — .time falls behind the wall clock.
clock.real_dtnumber0.016readReal seconds in this frame (wall clock): it ignores pause and slow motion and has no 0.25 s cap. Useful for widgets and for measuring FPS.
clock.scalenumber1read / write1 normal, 0 paused, 0.5 slow motion.
clock.pausedboolFalseread / writeShortcut for scale == 0. False brings back the previous scale. The pause starts on the next frame: the frame in which you press P already has its dt, so its on_update functions, timers and tweens still advance once. After that the on_update functions keep being called, with dt = 0: a key read there (keyp.once("W")) still acts during the pause. To freeze the object, start its on_update with if clock.paused: return.
e.time_scalenumber1read / writeAn extra multiplier on this Entity (timers, tweens, wait, on_update). Default 1.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
e.on_updateParameters: e (object), dt (number)—fn(e, dt) every frame for this Entity, even during await. In the class: def on_update(self, dt).
In @= (reactive)

clock can go in a formula: name it in a lambda. The formula then depends on the whole clock (clock.time is not a field that links on its own) and is recomputed every frame.

from math import cos, sin
moon["center"] @= lambda: (
    earth.center.x + 200 * cos(clock.time),
    earth.center.y + 200 * sin(clock.time),
)
st["pulse"] @= lambda: abs(sin(clock.time * 3))
You canYou can't
field @= lambda: … clock.time … (also .dt, .frame, .scale, …)field @= clock.time — a bare number → TypeError; use lambda
@when(lambda: clock.time > 5) (Scena checks the condition every frame)clock["time"] @= … — time/dt are not fields you link with @=
Only clock.dt in update — no extra costship.angle = lambda: clock.time * 40 — use ship["angle"] @= lambda: …

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
A formula with clock.time only updates when something changesupdated every frame: each frame advances the clock, so a formula that reads clock.time is re-evaluated every frame. If no formula reads clock, this costs nothing. The first dt counts from the start of run() (after setup), not from init.—

chance / ready / recently. A one-shot roll (a 30% drop): chance. A rate / cooldown: ready. Remembering a value for X seconds: recently.

Keyboard

keyp tells you, in update, the state of the keyboard. keyp("A") is True while A is held (Shift held with it does not get in the way; Ctrl / Alt / Cmd do); keyp.once("A") only on the frame A is pressed (to jump, to shoot once); keyp.only("A") requires that no other key is held; keyp("CTRL+R") reads a shortcut. It also goes in an @= formula (below).

def update(dt):
    if keyp("LEFT"):
        player.move_by(-200 * dt, 0)
    if keyp.held("A"):
        player.move_by(-280 * dt, 0)
    if keyp.only("SPACE"):
        shoot()
    if keyp.once("R"):
        canvas.reset_view()
    if keyp.once("CTRL+R"):
        restart()
    if flag1 and flag2 and keyp.once("SPACE"):
        act()
keyp reference
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
keyp("A")Parameters: key (key name)True/FalseA held, without Ctrl/Alt/Cmd (those make shortcuts). Shift does not get in the way: “hold Shift to run” still reads keyp("RIGHT") and keyp.once("SPACE"); with Shift and R, keyp("R") and keyp("SHIFT+R") are both True. Another plain key held at the same time changes nothing: with LEFT and RIGHT held, keyp("LEFT") and keyp("RIGHT") are True (only keyp.only requires the key to be alone, without Shift either).
keyp.held("A")Parameters: key (key name)True/FalseA held; modifiers ignored.
keyp.once("A")Parameters: key (key name)True/FalseTrue only on the frame A is pressed. The first read uses up the press: after that it gives False until the key is released and pressed again. A press nobody read on that frame does not show up later: in if armed and keyp.once("SPACE"), a SPACE pressed while armed was False does not count when armed becomes True. To keep the press, keep it yourself: if keyp.once("UP"): st.wants_jump = True.
keyp.only("A")Parameters: key (key name)True/Falsekeyp("A") and no other physical key — not even Shift: keyp.only("R") is not Shift+R.
keyp("SHIFT+A")Parameters: key (shortcut, e.g. "SHIFT+A")True/FalseShortcut: True while Shift and A are held together. Another plain key held at the same time does not get in the way; one extra modifier makes it False — in a shortcut, Shift counts too: keyp("CMD+Z") is not Cmd+Shift+Z.
"SPACE" "ESC" "LEFT" "F1"Key names (str)—The other special keys: "ENTER" "TAB" "BACKSPACE" "DEL" "INS" "HOME" "END" "PAGEUP" "PAGEDOWN", the arrows ("UP" "DOWN" "LEFT" "RIGHT") and "F1"…"F12". Modifier families: "SHIFT" "CTRL" "ALT" "CMD". Punctuation is "K1"…"K12" (table below). Upper or lower case does not matter. An unknown name fails right away: keyp("ESCAPE") → ValueError suggesting "ESC"; keyp(5) → TypeError. keyp["A"] is not a query: TypeError asking for keyp("A") or keyp.once("A").
mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_LEFT)Parameters: button (mouse button, int 0–7)True/FalseA button by number (Mouse.BTN_LEFT / BTN_RIGHT / BTN_MIDDLE). A press that a widget (or a SpriteButton) took reads False until the button is released, just as a focused TextInput hides keys from keyp (mouse). mouse.press("left") → TypeError with the hint.
Punctuation keys (K1–K12)

A punctuation key has a number, not a character: keyp("K11"), key == "K7". The name is the key's position on the keyboard — the same in every layout. What is printed on the key changes (on ABNT2, K7 is Ç). keyp(".") or keyp("PERIOD") → ValueError suggesting "K11".

def update(dt):
    if keyp.once("K10"):       # comma (US and ABNT2)
        previous_camera()
    if keyp.once("K11"):       # period
        next_camera()
    if keyp("CTRL+K3"):        # Ctrl + the = key
        canvas.zoom_by(1.02)
