"K1"left of 1`'
"K2"right of 0--
"K3"2nd right of 0==
"K4"right of P[´
"K5"2nd right of P][
"K6"above Enter (US) / left of Enter (ABNT2 and other ISO)\]
"K7"right of L;Ç
"K8"2nd right of L'~
"K9"left of Z (ISO keyboards only)—\
"K10"right of M,,
"K11"2nd right of M..
"K12"3rd right of M/;

Limits of the physical keyboard: the ABNT2 /? key (right of K12) has no name — the system does not identify it. On an Apple ISO keyboard, the keys left of 1 and left of Z arrive swapped (K9 ↔ K1). The numeric keypad and Caps Lock have no name: keyp and on_key do not see them.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
I want the typed character (?, :, ç)on_char(char) — it follows the layout and Shift. keyp is a position: game controls.keyp("?") — ? is Shift + K12 only on US.
In @= (reactive)

keyp can go in a formula: pressing or releasing a key makes Scena recompute the formulas that read it. In a formula, use the “held” reads (keyp("D"), held, only, a shortcut) — not once.

c.center["x"] @= lambda: 1200 if keyp("D") else 800
gate["open"] @= lambda: keyp.held("SHIFT")
# “when pressed”: @when, not once inside @=
@when(lambda: keyp("Y"))
def on_y():
    restart()
You canYou can't
field @= lambda: … if keyp("D") … / held / only / shortcutkeyp.once inside @= — the lambda may be re-evaluated; once uses up the press
@when(lambda: keyp("Y")) — fires when it goes from False to True@when + keyp.once together — @when already fires only when it goes to True
Just reading in update — no extra cost while no formula uses keypkeyp["A"] @= … — keyp has no fields to link; it is only read

Held: update or @=. Pressed once: keyp.once in update, or @when(lambda: keyp("…")).

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
keyp.once at the start of an anda check that uses up the key press. To combine conditions, put once last: if flag1 and flag2 and keyp.once("SPACE"): fires once, on the frame the key is pressed, only when both flags are already True. If once comes first, the and uses up the press even with a flag False.—

A press one or more frames before the condition (jumping just before landing): recently("jump", keyp.once("UP"), hold=0.12). The request stays alive for hold. The note above only covers the same frame.

keyp.once sees the press even if the key was already released by the same read (a slow frame). keyp("A") does not: it only says what is held now.

Keys already held when the window opens count as held: keyp("A") is already True, but keyp.once("A") does not fire — there was no press.

Keys with a focused TextInput. A focused TextInput keeps the text and editing keys (letters, digits, space, arrows, Enter, Esc, Tab…) and Cmd/Ctrl + A / C / X / V / Z / Y: callbacks and keyp do not see them. The other keys go through to the game — Cmd/Ctrl + another letter (keyp.once("CMD+S") works), F1–F12, Page Up / Down, and Shift / Ctrl / Alt / Cmd alone — and the box saves its text first, like an Enter, but without losing focus and without running on_submit: what the box shows is what the game reads. Shortcuts ("CTRL+R") in the key callbacks: see Callbacks. To react when a game condition becomes true: @when. Bodies overlapping: Collision.

Mouse

mouse tells you where the pointer is and which buttons are pressed, in the same world coordinates as the objects (the camera is already taken into account). It is a point itself: move_to(mouse), no (mouse.x, mouse.y) needed. To click or drag an object, use Click / drag. It also goes in an @= formula (below).

def update(dt):
    if mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_LEFT):
        marker.move_to(mouse)

def on_mouse_scroll(xoffset, yoffset):
    factor = 1.1 if yoffset > 0 else 1 / 1.1
    canvas.zoom_by(factor, about=mouse)

mouse is a point: it works wherever the API expects a place (move_to(mouse), query_point(mouse), about=mouse…). That copies the position as it is now. To follow it: Circle(center=lambda: mouse) or center @= mouse. Both numbers at once: x, y = mouse (also a copy).

mouse reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
mouse.x / .ynumber300readThe pointer's position in design units, in world space (the camera is already taken into account). Read once per frame: after canvas.pan_by / zoom_by in the same update, mouse.x is still the value from before the camera moved, until the next frame. x, y = mouse copies both at once.
mouse.dx / .dynumber0readHow far the pointer moved since the previous frame, in units.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
mouse.press()No parametersTrue/FalseAny button (except one a widget took, as in the row below).
mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_LEFT)Parameters: button (mouse button: Mouse.BTN_LEFT / RIGHT / MIDDLE)True/FalseThat button. A press a widget took (dragging a Slider, holding down a Button or a SpriteButton, even a disabled one) reads False until the button is released: the brush does not paint under the slider or the tool icon. A press on another object (draggable, @click, a Sprite with on_click) is still True.
mouse.click_pos(button)Parameters: button (mouse button)point(x, y) of the last click. A click on a widget or under a modal menu does not count.
In @= (reactive)

mouse is reactive (like clock / keyp). The whole pointer links directly (center @= mouse). .x / .y / .press are properties — name mouse in a lambda. Same rule as the keyboard: held (a state) works; “just pressed” does not.

canvas is reactive too: lambda: canvas.game_view.center, lambda: canvas.zoom or lambda: canvas.layers["back"].view.left follow every camera move and every layer scroll (canvas.ui_view only changes with init).

cursor["center"] @= mouse
cursor.center["x"] @= lambda: mouse.x
st.aiming = 0.0
st["aiming"] @= lambda: 1.0 if mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_LEFT) else 0.0

# still fine in update (movement / one-shot gesture)
def update(dt):
    if mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_RIGHT):
        canvas.pan_by(mouse.dx, mouse.dy)
You canYou can't
["center"] @= mouse / field @= lambda: mouse.x / (mouse.x, mouse.y) / mouse.press(…)field @= mouse.x — a bare number → TypeError; use lambda or @= mouse on the whole point
@when(lambda: mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_LEFT))mouse.dx / .dy in @= — a delta (like keyp.once); read it in update
Just reading in update — no extra cost while no formula uses mousemouse["x"] @= … — mouse has no fields to link; it is only read

["center"] @= mouse is placing. Since it places (it does not travel), the object goes through the walls of resolve(). To click or drag an object: Click / drag. mouse.x / .y are in world space; a HUD object (the "ui" layer) is pinned to the window, so these coordinates do not work on it directly: with the camera panned / zoomed, button.contains_point(mouse) answers in the world and gets it wrong. To know whether the pointer is over a HUD object, read button.pointer_hover (click and hover already use the view).

@= on mouse / mouse.x is live on the first drawn frame. The engine samples the pointer when the window opens (and again if the camera moves while the cursor stays still). Circle(center=mouse) or center=(mouse.x, mouse.y) in the body of the script is still (0, 0): there is no window at init. mouse.dx / on_mouse_move do not fire on that sample.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
The order in which things get the clickfor press/scroll: widgets → shapes (top, then the rest) → the script's callback. on_mouse_move runs alongside; it is not exclusive.exclusive

Where else to look — Reactive · React · Move

Move

Move, rotate and scale objects — at once or over a stretch of time (time=), in a straight line, along a curve or held inside a region — and animate any field from one value to another (tween). To call a function after a while: Schedule. For a sequence of steps with waits: Mode.

move_to / rotate / scale → move / rotate / scale
Parameters that take time (time= / ease= / loops=…) → Time parameters (time=)
Travel along a curve → move_along
Hold inside a region → confine
Interpolate an Attribute → tween

move / rotate / scale

Verbs that change the position, angle and size of a Graphic (Shape, Sprite, Text). A SpatialFx moves by its .center — see SpatialFx. Without time= the change happens at once and the verb returns the object itself. With time= it happens gradually over those seconds and the verb returns a Handle; it also takes ease= / loops= / yoyo= / then= / on_done= / force= (see Time parameters). Moving and rotating can also travel by speed: speed= instead of time= (units or degrees per second), and the duration comes from the distance.

Absolute (destination)Relative (delta)
Movemove_to(x, y) — Vec2 / Point, about=move_by(dx, dy) — Vec2, polar angle= / distance=, just distance= (forward)
Rotaterotate_to(θ) — short arcrotate_by(dθ) — as written
Scalescale_to(s)scale_by(f)
Along a curvemove_along(track, time=) or move_along(track, speed=)

Collision: place × travel. At once (= / *_to without time=) it places — it goes through the wall. move_by, move_along and move_to(…, time=) (or speed=) travel — the resolve() wall stops them midway, and the @collide of a fast traveler checks the path (Fast objects). Rotating in place and scaling (rotate_* / scale_*, with or without time=) are never stopped by the wall: it only pushes the object away afterwards, if it was left touching. Rotating around another point (rotate_by(…, about=)) travels: the center moves, and the wall stops it. Reset / respawn: hero.center = spawn_point. See Place × travel.

An absolute place. Without time= it places. With time= it travels — each frame it covers a piece of the way, and a wall can stop it midway. With speed= instead of time=, it travels at that speed (units per second): far away takes longer, close by arrives soon. By default the center reaches the destination; about= picks another point of the shape.

c.move_to(400, 200)                 # x, y
c.move_to(Vec2(400, 200))           # Vec2 as the 1st
c.move_to(p)                        # Point as the 1st
c.move_to(400, 200, time=1.2, ease="ease_out")
c.move_to(400, 200, time=1.0, loops="forever", yoyo=True)
missile.move_to(target, time=1.2, face=True)
hero.move_to(mouse, speed=220)               # on a click: walk to the pointer
drone.move_to(drone.dock, speed=300, ease="ease_out")   # all of them return at the same pace

move_to(x, y, *, time=None, speed=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, face=False, then=, on_done=, about=, force=False) · move_to(point, *, …)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
x, y1st · 2ndnumber400The destination as two coordinates.
point1stpointThe destination as a single argument: any point — a tuple (x, y), Point, Vec2, a Graphic (its center counts) or mouse. It does not take angle= / distance= (those belong to move_by).
about=name=point or NoneThe point that lands exactly on the destination (not the one that stays fixed). Default: the shape's center. With face=True, the rotation is around this point.
time parametersname=—time= or speed= (the distance from the traveling point to the destination, measured at the call; a None axis does not count) · ease= · loops= · yoyo= · face= · then= · on_done= · force=.

Shifts the object from where it is — an offset, not a destination. It always travels: a resolve() wall stops it midway. Write the offset in one of these ways, one per call: dx, dy · a Vec2 · angle= and distance= · just distance=, toward where the object points. With time= (or speed=), the offset is computed at the start and does not change during the trip.

c.move_by(40, 0)                        # dx, dy
c.move_by(Vec2(40, 0))                  # Vec2 as the 1st
c.move_by(angle=90, distance=40)        # polar (both together)
ship.move_by(distance=200 * dt)         # forward (no angle=: uses ship.angle)
ship.move_by(distance=-80 * dt)         # reverse: backs up without turning
c.move_by(200 * dt, 0)
c.move_by(0, 80, time=0.4)
c.move_by(40, 0, time=0.5, loops="forever", yoyo=True)
bolt.move_by(angle=45, distance=500, time=1.0, face=True)
guard.move_by(300, 0, speed=60, loops="forever", yoyo=True)   # patrols at 60 per second

move_by(dx, dy, *, time=None, speed=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, face=False, then=, on_done=, force=False) · move_by(Vec2, *, …) · move_by(angle=, distance=, *, …) · move_by(distance=, *, …)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
dx, dy1st · 2ndnumber20Cartesian offset.
Vec21stVec2The delta as a single argument. A Point raises TypeError — use move_to. A tuple (dx, dy) is not accepted.
angle=, distance=name=number90Polar. Degrees, 0 = +x. Without angle=, it moves where the object points: it reads angle at the time of the call (like raycast(length=)); a negative distance backs up and the direction does not change. angle= without distance= raises TypeError. Do not mix with dx/dy in the same call.
time parametersname=—time= or speed= (the size of the offset ÷ speed) · ease= · loops= · yoyo= · face= · then= · on_done= · force=. No about=.

Turns the object to the angle θ (degrees, counterclockwise, 0 = to the right). Without time= it turns at once; with time= it turns gradually the shortest way (at exactly 180° apart, it turns counterclockwise). With speed= (degrees per second), the duration is that short arc ÷ speed. A resolve() wall does not interrupt the turn: it only pushes the object away afterwards, if it was left touching.

c.rotate_to(45)
c.rotate_to(180, time=0.6, ease="ease_in_out")
c.rotate_to(90, time=0.5, loops="forever", yoyo=True)
turret.rotate_to(aim_angle, speed=90)   # the turret turns at 90° per second

rotate_to(θ, *, time=None, speed=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=, about=, force=False)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
θ1stnumber45Absolute angle.
about=name=point or NoneThe point the object turns around; it stays still. Default: the object's center.
time parametersname=—time= or speed= (degrees per second) · ease= · loops= · yoyo= · then= · on_done= · force=.

Turns dθ more degrees from the current angle (positive = counterclockwise, negative = clockwise). It can go past 180°: 360 makes a full turn. .angle accumulates, without wrapping back to 0–360 (50°/s for 8 s reads 400); to compare directions, use % 360.

c.rotate_by(30 * dt)
c.rotate_by(360, time=1.2)
c.rotate_by(45, time=0.4, loops=4, yoyo=True)
wheel.rotate_by(-720, speed=180)         # two turns at 180° per second: 4 s

rotate_by(dθ, *, time=None, speed=None, ease="linear", loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=, about=, force=False)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
dθ1stnumber30Degrees to add.
about=name=point or NoneThe point the object turns around; it stays still. Default: the object's center.
time parametersname=—time= or speed= (degrees per second; the size of dθ ÷ speed, also with about=) · ease= · loops= · yoyo= · then= · on_done= · force=.

Changes the object's size to value times its original size (1 = original, 2 = double, 0.5 = half), the same in width and height.

c.scale_to(1.5)
c.scale_to(0.5, time=0.3, ease="ease_out")
c.scale_to(1.05, time=0.45, ease="steps", loops="forever", yoyo=True)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
value1stnumber1.5Absolute factor (1 = original size).
about=name=point or NoneThe point the object grows or shrinks from; it stays still. Default: the object's center.
time parametersname=—time= · ease= · loops= · yoyo= · then= · on_done= · force=. No speed=: a scale is a ratio, not a distance.

Multiplies the current scale. With time=, the factor is frozen at the start.

c.scale_by(2)
c.scale_by(0.5, time=0.25)
c.scale_by(1.1, time=0.3, loops="forever", yoyo=True)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
factor1stnumber1.2Relative factor (2 = double the current one).
about=name=point or NoneThe point the object grows or shrinks from; it stays still. Default: the object's center.
time parametersname=—time= · ease= · loops= · yoyo= · then= · on_done= · force=. No speed=: a scale is a ratio, not a distance.
.angle / .scale / reset_rotation 
c.angle = 45
c.scale = 1.5
c.reset_rotation()
turret["angle"] @= lambda: dial.value
ship["scale"] @= lambda: 1.0 + 0.15 * st.pulse

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.angle / .scalenumber15read / writeAbsolute state. angle is the heading — where the object points (0 = +x, counterclockwise) — and it is a field, like width: =, @= and the constructor parameter do the same thing, and the point the object was positioned by stays still (center, top_left, p1, vertex; a Rect p1=, p2= tilts). Where the direction comes from the points (Line p1=, p2=, Rect anchor=, Ellipse by its foci, Circle by its rim point, Polygon), changing angle turns it around the center. Sprite / Svg / Text / Point / Track are positioned by the center (Text with an anchor: by the anchor). The verbs rotate_to / rotate_by turn the whole object around the center (or about=). scale is a shortcut for scale_to around the center. An Entity that is not a Graphic (like Entity()) has no real angle: reading it raises AttributeError, and writing it only creates an own field with that name, without turning anything. .scale multiplies the drawing and the collider: .width / .height stay the size you gave (a Sprite with height=40 and scale_to(1.08) still reads height 40); the size on screen is .box.
.rest_headingnumber90readThe angle at which the object has “no rotation” — where the art points; reset_rotation() goes back to it. Shape: 0. Sprite: the art's direction (art_angle), with the flip already counted — see Facing sprites.
.tiltnumber · contact · "ground""ground"read / writeSprite. Tilts only the drawing, without turning the collider. See Tilt.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
reset_rotation(*, time=None, speed=None, ease="linear", then=, on_done=, about=, force=False)Parameters: time (number), speed (degrees per second), ease (str), then, on_done, about (point), force—Undoes the rotation: brings the object back to the rest_heading angle (Shape: 0; Sprite: the art's direction). It also zeroes .tilt. It does not clear flips. It takes the same time parameters as rotate_to (speed= included), without loops= / yoyo= (a single destination).

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
move_by(p) with a Pointa TypeError. A destination is move_to(p). A delta: dx, dy, Vec2 or angle=/distance=. A bare tuple does not go into move_by. Polar does not exist in move_to.a delta given as a Point
move_by(distance=…, face=True) turns toward where it goesa TypeError. Without angle= the direction already is the angle; face= would turn the object by its own motion (with a negative distance, a U-turn on every call). To back up: drop face=. To turn around: rotate_by(180) first. Or pass angle=.turning
move_to(..., about=, face=True) turns around the centera turn around the about= point — otherwise the anchor would leave the destination the moment it rotates. Among the move verbs, only move_to has about=.the center
turret["angle"] @= … turns around any pointa link (@=) that writes the field: the positioning point stays still (or it turns around the center, where the direction comes from the points). For another pivot, call the verb with about=.rotate_to(…, about=)
x.angle = 30 does the same as x.rotate_to(30)the same only on an object positioned by its center. A Rect top_left= keeps its top_left with angle =; rotate_to turns it around the center — like top_left = versus move_to.—

Time parameters (time=)

The parameters every verb that takes time accepts: how long it lasts (time=) or, instead, how fast it goes (speed=), with which curve (ease=), how many times it repeats (loops=, yoyo=) and what to do at the end (then=, on_done=). They apply to move_to, move_by, rotate_to, rotate_by, scale_to, scale_by, move_along, reset_rotation (without loops= / yoyo=), tween and the camera (without force=). speed= applies only to the verbs that cover a distance: move_to, move_by, move_along, rotate_to, rotate_by, reset_rotation and, on the camera, pan_to / pan_by.

h = ship.move_to(400, 200, time=1.2, ease="ease_out")
ship.rotate_by(360, time=1.0, loops="forever")
ship.scale_to(1.2, time=0.3, loops=4, yoyo=True)
ship.move_to(600, 200, time=1.0, on_done=lambda: play_sound("pop"))
hero.move_to(mouse, speed=200)          # 200 units per second: far away takes longer
turret.rotate_to(90, speed=45)          # 45 degrees per second

Without time= or speed= (except move_along, which requires one of the two, and tween, which requires time=): it happens at once and returns the object. With time= or speed=: it interpolates and returns a Handle. time= and speed= together raise TypeError: both say how long it lasts. ease= / then= / on_done= / loops= / yoyo= require time= or speed= (without them there is no curve: rotate_by(10, ease="ease_in_out") raises an error). start= exists only in tween — to place and then travel with a pose verb, use two lines (center = … and then move_to(..., time=)). The contract for the end: When it ends.

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
time=name=number or NoneNoneSeconds for one lap. Without it: at once. With it: it interpolates and returns a Handle. In tween it is required; in move_along, pass time= or speed=.
speed=name=number > 0 or NoneNoneA speed instead of a duration: units per second (in move_to / move_by / move_along / pan_to / pan_by) or degrees per second (in rotate_to / rotate_by / reset_rotation). The duration is the distance ÷ speed, measured once, at the call: in move_to, from the traveling point to the destination (a None axis does not count; with about=, from that point); in move_by, the size of the delta; in move_along, the track's length × the portion in span; in rotate_to, the short arc. After that it is the same trip as with time=: the destination does not change if the target moves, and a track that grows later does not change the duration. With ease=, speed is the average speed (in the middle it goes past it). With loops=, it applies per lap (per leg with yoyo=). A zero distance ends on the next frame, with on_done. 0, a negative number, nan or text raise an error. It does not exist in scale_*, tween or the other camera verbs (scale and zoom are ratios, not distances): there, speed= raises TypeError.
ease=name=curve name or function"linear"The curve. Default "linear". Names: linear · ease_in · ease_out · ease_in_out · quad · inv_quad · smoothstep · sigmoid · bounce · elastic · steps · xpsin · erratic, or your own function that takes t from 0 to 1 (the time already elapsed) and returns how much of the way is done (0 to 1). An unknown name → ValueError with the list. spring / wobble do not go here — only in remap(…, modifier=). With loops= / yoyo=, the curve runs forward in each leg (it is not mirrored in time).
loops=name=1, N or "forever"1Same spelling as move_along / play_sound. Default 1. "forever" never fires then= / on_done= — stop it with handle.cancel() or destroy.
yoyo=name=boolFalseOdd laps reverse direction (start and end swap) instead of starting over. Needs loops > 1 (or "forever"); with loops=1 it raises an error. A finite loops=N: it lands at the start if N is even, at the end if N is odd. In move_along, it reverses the span, not the phase.
face=name=boolFalseOnly in move_to / move_by / move_along. Optional: writes .angle in the direction of travel (the straight line or the tangent). Delta ~0 / no motion: it keeps the rotation. With yoyo (and in move_along also with span=(1,0)) it flips 180° the other way. It does not require time= in move_to / move_by.
then=name=mode functionThe mode to enter when the tween ends (finite laps). Pass the mode's function (leaving, self.diving), without (). It is not a callback.
on_done=name=function or NoneNoneA callback when the tween ends (without changing mode). Pass a function to call. The same as passing fn to after. Do not use it together with then=.
about=name=point or NoneNoneA reference point for the motion. It applies to rotate_* / scale_* / reset_rotation / move_to, and on the camera to zoom_* / rotate_*. Default: the object's center (camera: the center of the view). In rotate_* / scale_* the point stays fixed; in move_to it is the point that lands exactly on the destination. move_to(..., about=, face=True) turns around that same point, not the center.
force=name=boolFalseOnly in the object verbs (move / rotate / scale, tween, move_along) — the camera has none. If the field the verb needs to change is linked with @=: False (default) raises LinkedAttributeError; True removes the link (its own and its parts', like center.x), shows a warning and goes on. An escape hatch, not everyday use. See Persistent drivers.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
time= and duration are the same thingtwo different things: a pose verb takes time= (the trip's seconds); a transient or a screen overlay lasts duration (the seconds the effect stays). sprite.flash(duration) and canvas.flash(intensity) do not have the same first argument: on the sprite it is the duration; on the canvas, the intensity.synonyms
speed= and h.speed are the same thinga request and a reading: speed= asks for the trip's average speed, turned into a duration at the call. h.speed reads how far the object moved this frame, per second. With ease="linear" the two match; with a curve, h.speed starts below and goes past the request in the middle.always the same number
move_to(target, speed=) chases the targeta destination copied at the call, as with time=. If the target moves, the object arrives where the target was. To chase a target that moves, at a steady speed, call approach in update, every frame: enemy.move_to(approach(enemy.center, player.center, 120)).chasing
time= and speed= togethera choice of one: time= fixes the duration and the speed comes from the distance; speed= fixes the speed and the duration comes from the distance. Both together raise TypeError.a combination
The Handle of a trip writes .vela reading only: with time= or speed=, h.velocity / h.speed / h.heading tell what this frame moved, in units per second — but they do not write .vel. For physics: crate.vel = h.velocity. Whatever stands on the platform does not need it: resolve already carries it along. See Handle..vel

move_along

Makes the object travel along a curve: a Track, the outline of any Shape, or a ready-made shape by name ("eight", "circle"…). time= is how long one lap lasts; or pass speed= (units per second along the track) and the lap lasts the length ÷ speed. It always travels: a resolve() wall stops the object on the way. To go to a point in a straight line: move_to(..., time=).

# first step: a string = a floating preset (loops=1)
ship.move_along("eight", time=2)
ship.move_along("circle", time=4, loops="forever")
# a size / your own track: a full Track
wasp.move_along(Track.eight(width=90, height=40), time=2.5)
ship.move_along(Track.circle(center=(400, 300), radius=120), time=4, loops="forever")
bug.move_along(hexagon, time=3, phase=0.2)
ship.move_along(Track(vectors=[(80, 0), (0, 50), (-30, 20)], smooth=0), time=1.2)
moon.move_along(orbit, time=6, face=True, loops="forever", yoyo=True)
# the same speed on tracks of different sizes
small.move_along(Track.circle(radius=60), speed=80, loops="forever")
big.move_along(Track.circle(radius=200), speed=80, loops="forever")

move_along(target, *, time=None, speed=None, ease="linear", span=(0, 1), phase=0, loops=1, yoyo=False, face=False, at=None, then=, on_done=, force=False)

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
target1stTrack, Shape or strThe track. A Track; a Shape (the object follows its outline, wherever the Shape is, even if it moves); or the name of a ready-made shape, at the default size and placed where the object is: "circle" · "eight" · "star" · "wave" · "spiral" · "arc" · "line" · "shuttle". "zigzag" raises an error (use "eight"). For another size: Track.eight(width=…). A point / (x, y) → TypeError; use move_to(..., time=).
span=name=(u0, u1)(0, 1)Which stretch of the track to cover, from 0 (start) to 1 (end): (0, 1) is the whole lap, (0, 0.5) only the first half, (1, 0) goes backwards — only on this trip; the track does not change.
phase=name=number0.15How far ahead on the track this object starts, as a fraction of the lap (0 to 1): 0.25 starts a quarter of the way along. For a line of objects on the same track, give each one a different phase= in a for (see the example below). yoyo= does not change phase=.
at=name=point or NoneWhere the start of the stretch (span) is put — any point, copied now. Default: where the object is when the trip starts. It only works for tracks with no fixed place (floating ones: the ready-made names, a Track.eight(width=…) with only a size, or Track(…, floating=True)). On a track with a fixed place (made with center= / start=, or a Shape's outline) it raises TypeError — wrap it with Track(source, floating=True).
time parametersname=—time= or speed= (one of the two; with speed=, one lap lasts track.length × the size of the span ÷ speed, measured at the call — phase= does not change the math) · ease= · loops= (default 1) · yoyo= (reverses the span) · face= (tangent) · then= / on_done= (at the end of finite laps) · force=. No about=.
TopicRule
Fleetgroup["wasp"].move_along(…) calls it on each member and returns a list of handles. A different phase per member: the for with phase=. To wait: await parallel(*handles). See Acting in bulk.
An open preset in a loop"wave" / "spiral" / "arc" / "line" with loops="forever": pass yoyo=True — otherwise the object jumps at the seam of the open path. Closed ones ("eight", "circle", "shuttle", …) wrap around on their own.
Same key as move_toA move_along and a move_to(..., time=) on the same object cancel each other: the last one wins.
The followed Shape goes awayIf the Shape whose outline the object follows is destroyed, the object keeps going along the last shape that outline had. The trip is only cancelled if the Shape goes away before the trip's first frame.
HandleIt reports what this frame moved: h.velocity (units per second), h.speed, h.heading (the tangent — the same as face=), h.u (the track parameter) and h.lap (the lap, starting at 0; loops="forever" keeps counting). With speed= and ease="linear", h.speed reads the requested speed. It does not write .vel.
 
# fleet: a list of handles
handles = group["wasp"].move_along(track, time=4)
for i, w in enumerate(group["wasp"]):
    w.move_along(track, time=4, loops="forever", phase=i * 0.15)
await parallel(*handles)

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
move_along(point) / move_along((x, y))a TypeError. To glide to a point: move_to(..., time=). move_along is a curve: a Track, a Shape's outline, or a preset name.a straight line to the point
ship["center"] @= lambda: track.cursor travelsplacing: it writes the point every frame and goes through walls. To travel: move_along.traveling

confine

Keeps an object inside a region (a Box or a Graphic): when it goes past the edge, confine holds it there (exactly on the edge: with the default by="center", the center sits on it), bounces it or takes it to the opposite side (Asteroids style). It is a call you make in update, right after moving. For walls that push, use resolve; to know when something left the play area, @leave_playfield.

PLAY = canvas.game_view.inset(40)

class Ship(Sprite):
    def on_update(self, dt):
        self.move_by(dx, 0)
        sides = self.confine(PLAY)          # by="center", action="clamp"
        if sides:
            canvas.shake(2)

# platform: the sprite's box stays inside
enemy.confine(platform_box, by="box")

# the ball bounces off the edges (needs .vel)
ball.vel = Vec2(220, 140)
ball.move_by(ball.vel.x * dt, ball.vel.y * dt)
ball.confine(arena, action="bounce")

# Asteroids-style wrap
ship.confine(canvas.game_view, action="wrap")

g.confine(region, *, by="center", action="clamp") → frozenset

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
region1stBox or GraphicPLAYThe region where the object must stay. It can be rotated: the sides ("left" / "right" / "top" / "bottom") turn with it (as in inset / grid / contains_point). It also takes Rect / Square / Ellipse / Circle / Sprite / Svg (the same contract as box=). The region is always a rectangle: an Ellipse or a Circle counts by its frame (the ellipse's rectangle, rotated with it; the square of the diameter, rotated toward the rim point p1), not by its curve.
by=name=str"center"What is compared to the region. See the by= tab.
action=name=str"clamp"What to do on crossing the effective edge. See the action= tab.

Returns a frozenset of the region's local edges it acted on in this call ("left" / "right" / "top" / "bottom"), or an empty one if nothing happened. In a rotated region, "left" is the local left — the same orientation contract as Grid / Box. Use the return value to react (a shake, a sound, flipping something else); there is no callback.

Which part of self must respect the region.

ValueMeaning
"center" (default)Only the center. The same as the hand-written pattern (if x < 40: center.x = 40). On a Sprite with Sheet(anchor="bottom"), the center is the feet: they are what stays on the edge.
"box"The object's outline stays entirely inside. For that, the region shrinks by half the outline's width and height, measured along the region's sides: the frame of a Rect / Square / Sprite / Svg / Text, the radius of a Circle, the true ellipse of an Ellipse, the vertices of a Triangle / RegularPolygon / Polygon, the ends of a Line, the path of a Track. The measure follows the rotation: a triangle that turns while touching the wall is pushed as it turns, and stays entirely inside. An object bigger than the region: it is held at the center on that axis (a remainder, not an error) — the same spirit as Box.inset.
"overlap"The opposite of "box": the object may stick partly out; the action only fires once its outline has left the region completely (the Asteroids ship: ship.confine(canvas.game_view, by="overlap", action="wrap") vanishes entirely before coming back on the other side). For that, the region grows by half the outline's width and height.
 
# patrol on a platform: the sprite does not “fall” halfway off
enemy.confine(platform, by="box")

# let it leave until it disappears, then wrap / destroy
sides = shot.confine(view, by="overlap", action="wrap")

For a Sprite, graphic.box is the rectangle of the drawn image (the size you asked for with height= / box=), not the silhouette. The silhouette is only hitbox_shape="auto", in collision. Line / free Polygon / Track / Point have no .box, but by="box" / "overlap" work on them: they are measured by their points (the ends, the vertices, the path; a Point is itself).

What happens when the reference has crossed the effective edge.

ValueMeaning
"clamp" (default)Stops the reference at the edge. It does not touch .vel.
"bounce"Holds it at the edge (like "clamp") and flips the sign of self.vel on the local axis crossed (measured along the region's sides, even when rotated). Requires self.vel to be set already — otherwise TypeError with a hint. The ball comes back at the same speed (it does not lose strength). To bounce weaker, read the return value and reduce .vel yourself.
"wrap"Takes the object to the opposite edge, keeping how far it went past (15 beyond → it comes in 15 inside the other side), with no visible jump.
 
ball.vel = Vec2(220, 140)

def on_update(self, dt):
    self.move_by(self.vel.x * dt, self.vel.y * dt)
    sides = self.confine(arena, action="bounce")
    if "bottom" in sides:
        play_sound("thud")

A single string (action=), not a bounce= + wrap= combo — this is not collision resolution.

The frozenset of edges is the hook for reacting.

sides = hero.confine(PLAY)
if "left" in sides or "right" in sides:
    hero.flash(0.15)
# empty → it did not touch the edge this frame

The names follow the region's own sides. With angle=30, "top" is the “upper” edge of the tilted region, not the world's +y. The same way Grid.cell_at already thinks of an oriented Box.

confine@leave_playfieldresolve
RoleHolds / wraps / bounces the pose nowTells you when the center leaves the playfieldPushes apart bodies that collide
WhenIn your update / on_updateA step of the frame (after collision)A step of the frame (collision)
RegisteredNo — just the callYes (group or method)Yes (resolve(a, b))
Changes the pose?YesNo (callback only)Yes (stops the body at the wall and pushes it away)

Do not use confine and a tween / move_along / resolve() wall on the same axis — they are separate authorities with no defined precedence. Cleanup when the shot leaves the world: @leave_playfield.

Contract

Method

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
g.confine(region, *, by=, action=)Parameters: region (Box or Graphic), by (str), action (str)frozensetKeeps the object in the region. Writes the center (and .vel if action="bounce"). The returned edges follow the region's sides.

Errors

CaseError
An unknown by= / action=TypeError with the allowed list
action="bounce" without self.velTypeError — hint: self.vel = Vec2(…)

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Calling confine(PLAY) once makes it hold forevera call that acts only on that frame: call it in update / on_update, after moving.a rule registered once (like resolve or @leave_playfield)

A region that shrank down to a point (for example, an inset bigger than the region) is not an error: the object stays at its center, as in the rest of Box.

tween

tween(field, value, time=) takes a field from its current value to value in time seconds. The value can be a number, a tuple / list of numbers, a Vec2, a Color (the value changes gradually, in a straight line, from the current one to the final one — like lerp) or a point. For position, angle and size, prefer their own verbs (move_to…). A new tween on the same field cancels the previous one. It takes the time parameters of the move verbs: time= (required) / ease= / loops= / yoyo= / then= / on_done= / force=. Only here: start= (the initial value; without it, the current value). What to do at the end: When it ends. An object's color, visible and flips cannot be tweened (TypeError with the recipe): animate a color field and link the object's color to it. Neither can glow. line_width and a Sprite's alpha are numbers and can be tweened.

tween(ship["radius"], 80, time=0.4, ease="ease_out")
tween(ship.center, (400, 200), time=1.2)
tween(ship.center, (400, 200), time=1.2, start=(0, 0))
ship.tween(ship["hp"], 0, time=0.6)
# TypeError: tween(ship["color"], …) is not allowed — animate a color field and link:
st.tint = Color("red")
tween(st["tint"], Color("blue"), time=1)
ship["color"] @= lambda: st.tint
tween reference

Options

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
time=number—parameterHere: seconds, required (without time=, TypeError). It interpolates. The full rule: time parameters.
ease=str or function"linear"parameterHere: the tween's curve. time parameters.
start=same type as to(0, 0)parameterThe initial value. Without it: it uses the current value at the moment of the call. With it: the interpolation starts there — the same format as to (number, point, Color, …). Only in tween, not in move_to / rotate_to / scale_to.
loops=1, N or "forever"1parameterHere: laps. "forever" never fires then= / on_done=. Requires time=. time parameters.
yoyo=boolFalseparameterHere: odd laps reverse direction. Needs loops > 1 or "forever". time parameters.
then=mode functionparameterHere: the mode to enter at the end. time parameters.
on_done=function or NoneparameterHere: a callback at the end. time parameters.
force=boolFalseparameterHere: a field linked with @=: False raises LinkedAttributeError; True removes the link and warns. time parameters.
name=str or None"pulse"parameterSlot: a new tween with the same name=, on the same object (or bare, in the same place), replaces the previous one instead of adding another. Without name=: each call is a new tween.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
tween(target, to, *, time, ease="linear", start=, loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=, force=False, name=)Parameters: target (the target, Attribute or Point), to (same type as the current value), time (number), ease (str), start (same type as to), loops, yoyo, then, on_done, force, nameHandleThe target: a field (ship["radius"], ship["hp"]), a field of st (st["t"]; st.t is the number and raises an error) or a Point (ship.center). Color and glow cannot be a target. to must match the current value — a number, a flat tuple/list, Vec2, Color, a point (Graphic, mouse: copied now). start= is optional (the same format as to). It goes from the start to to gradually, in a straight line (like lerp). An incompatible type raises an error right away. time= is required.
e.tween(target, to, *, time, ease="linear", start=, loops=1, yoyo=False, then=, on_done=, force=False, name=)Parameters: target (the target, Attribute or Point), to (same type as the current value), time (number), ease (str), start (same type as to), loops, yoyo, then, on_done, force, nameHandleThe same, on this Entity. It survives a mode change; it dies on destroy.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
tween(…) in the mode's body survives the changeowned by the mode: a bare tween(…) in the mode's body belongs to the mode and stops when the mode ends. e.tween belongs to the object and keeps going. See scope and cancelling.—

tween(shape.center, …) places. It writes the point every frame, like center =. The resolve() wall does not stop it midway. To travel (the resolve() wall stops it midway): move_to(..., time=), move_by(..., time=) or move_along. The same goes for center @= (including track.cursor).

yoyo=True with loops=1 raises an error. There is nothing to bounce back. With a finite loops=N and yoyo: it lands at the start if N is even, at the end if N is odd. A linked target: force=True (a warning + unlink) or unlink first.

Where else to look — Schedule · Collision · Draw · Time parameters (time=)

Schedule

Do something N seconds from now (after) or every N seconds (every), limit how often an action can happen (ready), and remember that something happened a moment ago (recently). To run something when a condition becomes true, see @when.

after / every → after / every
Cooldown → ready
Time window → recently
then= / on_done= → When it ends
What a tween returns → Handle
The whole map → Which to use

after / every

after(seconds, function) calls the function once, after that much time; every(seconds, function) calls it again at each interval — the first time after one interval, not right away. It fires on the first frame where the time has already passed: with 1/60 s frames, after(0.5) is frame 30 and every(0.25) is frames 15, 30, 45… A frame longer than the interval fires as many times as it should: the rhythm does not depend on the FPS. An after that sets itself again inside its own function is not a steady rhythm: each round starts on the frame where the previous one fired, so the intervals become “at least p” and the delay adds up (up to one frame per round). For a rhythm that changes (invaders that speed up), use every(p, step, name="march") and, only when the rhythm changes (an invader died), call it again with the new p: the name replaces the previous one. The same goes for movements chained with on_done (move_by(…, time=0.12, on_done=next_hop)): each step starts on the frame where the previous one ended. For a path of several steps at a steady rhythm, use move_along on a Track. The time is game time: pause and slow motion apply. Ignore the Handle it returns, keep it to cancel, or give a name= — calling again with the same name replaces the previous one. Inside a mode, bare after / every stop when the mode ends; e.after / e.every keep going (scope and cancelling).

after(2.0, boom)
every(1.2, drop, name="spawn")
ship.after(0.4, then=diving)
h = after(3.0, then=leaving)
h.cancel()
h.pause()
h.resume()

At the module level. The Handle lives in fn.handle.

@after(2.0)
def boom():
    explode()
# boom.handle.cancel()

@every(1.2, name="drop")
def drop():
    spawn()

In a class, @after / @every apply to each object: the timer starts when the object is created and belongs to it (it survives a mode change and stops at destroy).

class Wasp(Sprite):
    @every(2.4, name="fire")
    def volley(self):
        shoot(self)

    @after(0.4)
    def armed(self):
        self.mode = self.diving
after / every reference

Options

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
then=mode functionparameterOnly in after: the mode to enter when the time is up. time parameters.
on_done=function or NoneparameterOnly in after: the function to call when the time is up (the same as fn). time parameters.
name=str"spawn"parameterSlot: a new timer with the same name=, on the same object (or bare, in the same place), replaces the previous one instead of adding another. Without name=, each call is a new timer.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
after(delay, fn=None, *, then=, on_done=, name=)Parameters: delay (number, seconds), fn (function), then (mode function), on_done (function), name (str)HandleOnce, after delay seconds: calls fn (or on_done=, which is the same) or enters the mode then=.
every(interval, fn, *, name=)Parameters: interval (number), fn (function), name (str)HandleRepeats. No then= and no on_done= (it never ends).
e.after / .everyParameters: delay or interval (seconds), fn (function)HandleOn this Entity, always. An fn that asks for a parameter with no default value receives the object (ball.after(4, vanish) with def vanish(ball)); with no parameter, it receives nothing. It survives a mode change; it dies at destroy / cancel_process. See scope.
@after / @everyDecorator — schedules the function—At the module level: the timer starts right away (it counts game time, which runs from run() on: @every(0.4) first calls 0.4 s after the start); the Handle is in fn.handle. On a class method: it starts when each object is created. Without parentheses (@every above the def) it raises an error with the right spelling; the same goes for @when, @on_change, @collide_with and @exit_mode.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
on_done= and then= togetherone or the other: fn / on_done= calls a function; then= changes the mode. Both together raise an error. after(d, boom) ≡ after(d, on_done=boom). Don't mix @every with @collide / @when / @on_mode on the same def.—
every(0, fn) for every framea ValueError. Every frame is on_update (Entity) or update(dt) (script) — both receive dt. The interval must be > 0.EVERY_FRAME or an interval of 0

ready

ready(name, interval) is a cooldown: it returns True once per interval — “can I shoot again yet?”. The rhythm is exact on average: what one frame overshoots counts toward the next, so two Trues in a row can come a little closer than the interval when it is not a whole number of frames. The first call already returns True. It counts game time (pause applies). Called every frame (button held), it keeps the rhythm at any frame rate; after a while without calls (the button was released, even for one frame), it gives True once again, with no burst, and the rhythm restarts from that True.

def update(dt):
    if ready("fire", 0.18):
        shoot()
    if keyp.once("R"):
        ready.reset("fire")
ready reference

ready(name, interval)

Parameters: name (str), interval (number, seconds). Returns True/False.

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
ready(name, interval)Parameters: name (str), interval (number, seconds)True/FalseTrue when the interval is up. The name is the slot. Passing the interval again updates the period.
e.ready(name, interval)Parameters: name (str), interval (number, seconds)True/FalseThe same reading, in a slot of this Entity. Two enemies with self.ready("fire", …) don't share a cooldown. It is not a Handle — it dies with the instance; destroy / cancel_process don't touch it.
ready.reset(name)Parameters: name (str)—Resets: the next question returns True.
ready.disable(name) / .enable(name)Parameters: name (str)—Pauses / resumes the slot. Disabled → always False.
ready.remove(name)Parameters: name (str)—Deletes the slot. The next call with an interval creates it again (and returns True).

A one-off roll (30% drop): chance. ready is an interval, not a probability. A callback N seconds from now: after / every. Remembering a boolean for a moment: recently.

recently

recently(name, value, hold=) remembers for a moment that something was true: it returns True if value was true at some point in the last hold seconds. Use it to give the player some slack — jumping right after running off a ledge (coyote time), pressing jump a little before landing — or for “was hit a moment ago”.

def update(dt):
    on_ground = "bottom" in hero.touching_sides
    # Coyote: stays "on the ground" for 80ms after leaving the ledge.
    can_jump = recently("on_ground", on_ground, hold=0.08)
    # Buffer: UP up to 120ms before landing still counts.
    if recently("jump", keyp.once("UP"), hold=0.12) and can_jump:
        hero.vel.y = JUMP
        recently.reset("jump")        # jumped: use up the buffer and the coyote,
        recently.reset("on_ground")   # or the boost comes back on the next frames
recently reference

recently(name, value, hold=0.1)

Parameters: name (str), value (anything — it counts as true if if value: would pass), hold (number, seconds). Returns True/False.

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
recently(name, value, hold=)Parameters: name (str), value (anything), hold (number)True/FalseTrue if value is true now, or was in the last hold seconds. The name is the slot. Passing hold again updates the window.
e.recently(name, value, hold=)Parameters: name (str), value (anything), hold (number)True/FalseThe same reading, with the memory of this Entity. In a fleet with self.recently("hit", …), the ships don't mix up their memories. It is not a Handle — it dies with the instance.
recently.reset(name)Parameters: name (str)—Forgets: the next question is False until value is true again.
recently.remove(name)Parameters: name (str)—Deletes the slot. The next call creates it again.

recently returns True on every frame while the window lasts, not just once. It is meant for states and animation. An action that changes movement can't be repeated without harm: setting vel.y = JUMP again on each frame of the window undoes those frames' gravity, and the jump goes higher (in the example above, about 150 instead of 115) — that is why the example calls recently.reset when jumping. Nor is it for what must happen only once (creating an object, playing a sound, adding points): use keyp.once / @when. A periodic cooldown: ready.

When it ends

Verbs that take time — after, move_to(…, time=), tween, transients, play_sound, fades — accept a trigger for when they end: on_done= calls a function; then= changes the mode. This section covers only that; the rest of each verb is in its own section.

then= expects a mode: the mode's function (leaving, self.diving), without (). It is not a callback.

on_done= expects a callback: a function to call, without changing the mode.

after(0.4, then=diving)
ship.move_to(400, 90, time=0.8, then=leaving)
ship.tween(ship["radius"], 80, time=0.4, on_done=boom)
ship.dissolve_out(0.4, on_done=ship.destroy)
canvas.fade_out(0.5, on_done=load_next)
Wherethen= (mode)on_done= (callback)
afterEnters that mode.Calls the function. The same as passing fn.
pose / tween with time=Enters that mode (a finite number of loops). loops="forever" never fires.Calls the function (a finite number of loops). loops="forever" never fires.
transientNot available.Calls when the effect ends — also when a new effect on the same channel replaces it midway.
play_soundEnters that mode.Calls at the natural end (not on cancel, nor after the owner has ended).
canvas.fade_out / fade_inNot available.Calls when the fade finishes. After fade_out the screen stays covered until you call fade_in.
play(clip, next=)Chains a clip (min_hold= / resume= in the Sprite's Clip panel). It is not this contract.

then=ship.destroy does not destroy: destroy is not a mode. To remove the object at the end: on_done=ship.destroy, after(0.2, ship.destroy), a dying mode, or await and then destroy(). A new transient on the same channel replaces the old one and calls the old one's on_done right away (with no sign that it was cut short).

Handle

A Handle is the object that verbs which take time return — after, every, tween, move_to(…, time=), move_along, play_sound, wait. It stands for that task while it runs: keep it to cancel (h.cancel()), pause, read the progress, or wait for the end with await h in an async mode. If you need none of that, ignore the return value. .elapsed / .remaining are in world seconds. In move_along and in move_to / move_by with time=: also .velocity / .speed / .heading. In play_sound: .volume / .pan / .pitch / .level.

h = after(2.0, boom)
h.remaining   # 2.0, then counts down
h.cancel()
if h.done:
    pass

pen = every(0.03, stamp).pause()
pen.resume()

@every(1.2, name="drop")
def drop():
    spawn()
drop.handle.cancel()

async def diving(e):
    await e.move_to(player.center.x, 90, time=0.8)
    await wait(0.2)

# take on the velocity of the travel (you write .vel)
h = platform.move_along(rail, time=4, loops="forever")

def drop_crate():
    crate.vel = h.velocity        # the crate leaves at the platform's velocity
Handle reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.doneboolTruereadIt has already finished (successfully or cancelled).
.cancelledboolFalsereadIt was stopped by cancel / a mode change / destroy.
.pausedboolFalsereadFrozen with pause(). True only while alive and frozen. Read-only.
.elapsednumber1.2readGame seconds since the task started (or since the last firing of every).
.remainingnumber0.8readThe opposite of .elapsed: seconds left until the end (after / wait / tween) or until the next firing (every). 0 if it has already finished or was cancelled. Read-only.
fn.handleHandledrop.handlereadModule-level decorator: the Handle of that @after / @every.

Motion readings

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.velocityVec2Vec2(80, 0)readUnits per second on this frame (world); after the end, it keeps the last frame's (the on_done reads the arrival velocity). Only in move_along / move_to(..., time=) / move_by(..., time=). It does not write Graphic.vel. Read-only.
.speednumber80readThe magnitude of .velocity. Read-only.
.headingnumber90readDegrees, counterclockwise from +x (like .angle / face=). On the track: the tangent; in move_to / move_by: the direction of the delta. Read-only.
.unumber0.25readWhere the object is on the track, from 0 (start) to 1 (end), already counting span= / phase=. Only move_along. Read-only.
.lapinteger0readThe number of the current lap, starting at 0. loops="forever" keeps counting. Only move_along. Read-only.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
await hNo parametersWaits (use await)In an async mode or a task. A Handle that is already .done goes through at once. A cancelled one raises Cancelled. A task returns the value of its return.
.cancel()No parameters—Stops now. Safe to call twice, even after destroy.
.pause()No parametersthe Handle itselfFreezes this task's clock (every / after / wait / tween / play_sound). Calling it again does nothing. Returns self. On until / parallel / race it raises TypeError.
.resume()No parametersthe Handle itselfUnfreezes. It does not bring back a Handle that was cancelled or has finished. Calling it again does nothing. Returns self.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Handle(...)made by the verb: after, every, tween, wait, move_to(..., time=), play_sound. Keep what it returns: h = after(2.0, fn)something you build by hand — Handle(...) gives a TypeError that says so

Cancelled is a BaseException. except Exception does not catch it. There is no cancel("spawn") by string: the slot is name=; a specific task is its Handle.

Don't write h.remaining = …. TypeError. To renew the duration, after(2.0, fn, name="tail") (the slot replaces it). To stop, h.cancel().

Don't write h.paused = …. TypeError. Use h.pause() / h.resume(). Pausing the world is clock.paused; parking the Entity is e.active = False.

.velocity does not write the Graphic's .vel. Copy it if the physics needs it: crate.vel = h.velocity (not for whatever rides on top: resolve already carries it along). Only bounce= (collision), confine(…, action="bounce") and your own code write .vel. after / every / rotate_* / scale_* / tween raise AttributeError (they have no velocity). A Handle that is already .done or cancelled keeps the last frame's (useful in on_done).

Where else to look — Move · Mode · React · Sound

Mode

A mode is the chapter of behavior an Entity is in: in formation, diving, dying. Each mode is a function; e.mode = e.diving enters it (the function runs). Whatever the chapter starts (timers, movements, sounds) stops on its own when the chapter ends; see Scope and cancelling. For an action that finishes and moves on to another mode, use then=. For a sequence of steps with waits, use an async mode.

Enter a chapter → mode
wait / parallel / race → async / wait
A sequence on the side, or one nobody owns → tasks
Cancel the chapter → Scope and cancelling
The whole map → Which to use

mode

e.mode is the current mode (the function) or None. Write it to switch: the old mode ends and the new one starts. Compare with ==. Writing the same mode again does nothing; to restart it, use goto_mode.

@on_mode
async def diving(e):
    await e.move_to(player.center.x, 90, time=0.8, ease="ease_in")
    await wait(0.2)
    e.mode = leaving

wasp.mode = diving
class Wasp(Sprite):
    @on_mode
    def entering(self):
        self.move_to(self.slot_x, self.slot_y, time=1.0, then=self.formation)

    @on_mode
    def formation(self):
        every(2.0, self.shoot)          # gone when the mode changes
        after(3.0, then=self.diving)    # same

    @on_mode
    async def diving(self):
        await self.move_to(player.center.x, 90, time=0.75)
        await wait(0.12)
        self.mode = self.formation

wasp.mode = wasp.entering

class Director(Entity):
    def setup(self):
        self.mode = self.directing

    @on_mode
    async def directing(self):
        while True:
            self.start_wave()
            await until_empty("wasp")
            await wait(1.4)
Mode reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
e.modemode or Nonee.mode = e.divingread / writeThe current function, or None. Compare with ==. The same mode does nothing.
e.mode_timenumber1.2readSeconds in this chapter. Resets to zero on entering / re-entering.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
e.goto_mode(fn)Parameters: fn (the chapter's function)—Always exits and enters (same mode or not).
@on_modeDecorator — marks only—Marks the function as a mode, for whoever reads the code and for the debug tools. It changes nothing at run time: e.mode = fn works with or without it.
@exit_mode(formation)Parameters: enter_fn (the chapter's function, e.g. formation)—Decorator: the marked function runs when the Entity leaves the formation mode (by a mode change, then= or e.mode = None). Use it for appearance and own fields; the mode's timers and movements already stop on their own. The function is a plain one (def), not async.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
self.mode = self.diving()The mode is the function, not the call: self.mode = self.diving. Assigning the same mode does nothing; force it with goto_mode. then= is When it ends, not a callback. With no mode set, .mode is None.calling the function

async / wait

In an async def mode, await pauses the chapter until something happens (a time with wait, a condition with until, a group becoming empty with until_empty, other tasks finishing with parallel / race) and then goes on to the next line. It only works inside an async mode or a task (or a function they call with await); in update or in a @collide, start the sequence with run_task(…) or use after.

await wait(0.4)
await until(lambda: ship.hp <= 0)
await until_empty("wasp")
await parallel(h1, h2)
i = await race(h1, h2)   # 0 or 1; cancels the other

async def pause(s):
    await wait(s)

async def diving(e):
    await pause(0.4)
Wait reference
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
await wait(0.4)Parameters: delay (seconds)Waits (use await)Pauses. Without await it does not block: error. Only in the async code the mode or the task is running, helpers included.
await until(lambda: ship.hp <= 0)Parameters: pred (condition, function)Waits (use await)Waits until the function returns True (Scena checks it every frame). Pass a function (lambda: …) or a field (until(st["over"])), not the condition already computed: a bare True/False raises TypeError, and so does st.over (that is the value). Same script rule as wait.
await until_empty("wasp")Parameters: group_or_id (name or the group)Waits (use await)Empty group. Takes the name, group["wasp"] (a live view, not a copy), or a formula group. Do not use until(group.empty).
await parallel(h1, h2)Parameters: h1 (Handle), h2 (Handle), …Waits (use await)Waits for all of them. Cancelling cancels the rest. Pass the Handle to parallel / race before the next await.
await race(h1, h2)Parameters: h1 (Handle), h2 (Handle), …integerThe first one to finish; cancels the others. Result: an index starting at 0.
set_watchdog(enabled=False)Parameters: enabled (on, True/False)—By default, an async mode stuck in a loop with no await is stopped with an error (the watchdog). set_watchdog(False) turns that check off; only for demos and performance measurements.

wait(0.4) without await does not pause the script. It returns a Handle and the rest runs on. Outside an async mode or a task (update, on_update, @collide, a sync mode) it is a TypeError. Inside, without await (and without passing it to parallel / race), it is a TypeError naming the line and the missing await. Outside async code, start the sequence with run_task(…) or use after(…).

Only modes and tasks are async. Scena runs an async mode and a task (run_task) as a script; everything else it only calls. That is why async def setup, async def on_update, an async @every / @when / @collide / on_click / on_done=, or after(1, lambda: self.walk()) with an async walk are a TypeError: the body would never run. The same goes for a function Scena asks a question: a filter (group["x"].filter / any / all / count_where, nearest(where=)), the condition of until / @when, the target of @on_change, resolve(only=) and a @= formula: the answer of an async function is not a value. Write a plain def and start the sequence from it: as a task (self.run_task(self.intro), run_task(intro)) or as a mode (self.mode = self.intro). An async helper is fine when the mode or the task calls it with await. Calling an async function without await (self.intro() alone on a line) runs nothing: Scena warns (SCENA WARNING) with the line.

tasks

A task is an async def sequence that runs alongside everything else without being a mode: run_task(reveal) runs reveal() right away up to the first await and carries on over the next frames. Use it for a button that sets off an animation in steps, a power-up that lasts a few seconds while the ship changes modes, a countdown on the screen.

A loop with await wait(p) goes around once every p seconds at least, always on a whole frame: wait(0.02) waits 2 frames at 60 Hz (0.033 s) and 3 at 144 Hz (0.021 s), so “move 5 every 0.02 s” moves faster on faster screens. For speed, move with dt in update (or on_update) or use @every, which keeps the remainder between rounds.

async def reveal():
    await panel.move_to(600, 300, time=0.5)
    await wait(0.2)
    await parallel(panel.rotate_by(90, time=0.3),
                   caption.move_by(0, 40, time=0.3))

start_btn.on_click = lambda: run_task(reveal, name="reveal")   # another click restarts it

class Ship(Sprite):
    @collide_with("powerup")
    def grab(self, item, info):
        item.destroy()
        self.run_task(self.triple_shot, name="power")      # survives mode changes

    async def triple_shot(self):
        self.shots = 3
        await wait(4)
        self.blink(2.0)
        await wait(2)
        self.shots = 1

Mode or task?

A mode is what the object is doing, one at a time; entering another cancels the previous one. A task is extra work (a power-up, a blink, a countdown) or a sequence on the screen that does not belong to a single object. Several tasks run together.

Owner

The same as for after: an object's method (run_task(self.flicker)) or a lambda that uses self → the task belongs to that object and ends at destroy; inside a mode's body → it belongs to the mode and ends when the mode exits; a loose call → it belongs to the current Act (to the whole game, if called at the top of the file). panel.run_task(reveal) gives the task to panel (it survives the panel's mode changes) and calls reveal(panel) if reveal takes a parameter. Arguments: run_task(lambda: reveal(panel, 2)).

Clicked again?

  • run_task(reveal) on every click: the runs go on together.
  • run_task(reveal, name="reveal"): a new click cancels the run in progress (and what it started) and starts over.
  • To ignore clicks while it runs, keep the Handle: if h is None or h.done: h = run_task(reveal).

What a task starts is its own

An after, a wait, a movement or another task started inside the task ends with it: cancelling the task (h.cancel(), name=, the owner destroyed, the Act changed) cancels that work. A task that finishes normally lets that work go on. The first part (up to the first await) runs right away, where you called run_task; the rest runs in the frame's process step, like an async mode.

A task at the top of the file, before run(). Its first part runs there, at the top: what it makes belongs to the top of the file and survives Act changes, and a change_act in it raises an error (the game has not started yet). Start with await wait(0) so the rest runs once the game is going. Such a task belongs to the whole game: a tween on an st field that it starts goes on after change_act (st belongs to no Act) — keep the Handle and cancel it, or give it name=.

Task reference
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
run_task(fn, *, name=None)Parameters: fn (async function, or a lambda that calls one), name (slot, text)HandleRuns fn as a task. Owner as with after. name=: a new task with the same name cancels the one running.
e.run_task(fn, *, name=None)Parameters: fn (async function), name (slot, text)HandleThe task belongs to e: it ends at destroy / cancel_process and survives mode changes. fn receives e if it takes one parameter.
await hNo parametersthe value the task returnsWaits for the task to end (in an async mode or another task). Also works in parallel(h1, h2) / race(h1, h2).
h.cancel()No parameters—Stops the task and what it started. h.done, h.elapsed as on any Handle; h.pause() does not work on a task (pause the owner with active = False).

run_task(reveal()) with parentheses is a TypeError. Pass the function; for arguments, run_task(lambda: reveal(panel, 2)). A plain def function is refused too (call it directly or use after), and so is a mode (@on_mode): enter it with self.mode =.

When what the task is waiting for is cancelled from outside, the task stops and Scena warns with the reason: the object that was moving was destroyed, another movement took the same property. If that is expected, put try: … except Cancelled: around the await; for the task to end along with the object, start it on the object: panel.run_task(reveal). Cancelling the task itself (owner destroyed, name=, h.cancel()) is silent.

A task waiting on an until that never becomes true gives no warning: the game goes on and the sequence simply does not continue. To see what each task and each mode is waiting for, for how long and on which line: Ctrl+Shift+6 or show_processes(). A wait of 5 s or more on an until shows up as SLOW.

Scope and cancelling

A mode is a chapter of behavior. Everything you start while that chapter is running goes away when the chapter ends, unless you say otherwise with e.after / e.every / e.tween / e.run_task.

What a mode is

A mode is the function in e.mode: the Entity's current chapter (formation, diving, dying…). Entering the chapter runs the body once; leaving cancels that chapter's work and calls @exit_mode, if there is one. Compare with ==. For an action that finishes and moves on to another mode, use then=. For a sequence of steps with waits, use an async mode with await.

The one rule

What the mode starts while it is running belongs to the mode and goes away when you leave. Outside the mode's body (setup, on_update, @collide, @when, loose script) there is no “current chapter”: the work belongs to the object you call it on (ship.after: the owner is ship) or, for a loose call, to the whole game (if made at the top of the file) or to the current Act (if made later; see Acts).

For work to survive a mode change, call it on the object explicitly: ship.after(…), ship.every(…), ship.tween(…). These live until destroy or cancel_process.

What cancels (and what does not)

These calls, in the mode's body, take on the chapter's scope and are cancelled on a change:

  • after / every (loose call)
  • wait / until / until_empty / parallel / race
  • tween(…) (without the e.)
  • move_to / move_by / move_along / rotate_* / scale_* with time=
  • play_sound (loose call)
  • run_task(…) (loose call) and what that task starts
  • the mode's async script

These are not cancelled on a mode change:

  • e.after / e.every / e.tween / e.play_sound / e.run_task: Entity scope (they die at destroy / cancel_process; at destroy, a sound that ends on its own finishes playing)
  • script timers (module level, no mode running): these go away when the Act changes (change_act, see Acts) if they were created after the top
  • transients (blink, flash, dissolve_out, …) and sprite.play
  • event functions (@collide, @when, on_click)
Where / howScopeMode change
In the mode's body: after / every / wait / tween / move_*(time=) / …"mode"cancels
e.after / e.every / e.tween / e.run_taskalways the Entitydoes not cancel (dies at destroy / cancel_process)
after(…, bomb.destroy) of another Entity, from inside the modethat other Entitynot cancelled with this mode
The Entity's setup / on_update / @collide: after(0.1, self.shoot) or a lambda / inner def that uses self (after(0.1, lambda: self.set_color("red")))the Entity (self)does not cancel (there is no surrounding mode); dies at destroy: a destroyed enemy does not shoot afterward. Exception: in on_destroy the lambda belongs to the script and runs after the death
loose script at the top of the file (after(…), play_sound(…), tween(…))"game": the whole gamedoes not cancel; lasts the whole game
loose script after the top (update, event functions, an Act's setup)"act": the current Actdoes not cancel; goes away at change_act
transients / playoutside the schedulerdoes not cancel

Sound is the exception: when the owner ends, a sound that ends on its own finishes playing. This holds for a mode change, destroy() and change_act. play_sound("boom.wav") right before self.destroy() or change_act(…) is heard in full. Only sounds that would never end are cut: loops="forever", a name= slot (music, ambience), a paused sound, the mic monitor. A sound with a fade_out in progress ends on its own: the fade finishes. The on_done / then= of a sound whose owner has ended does not run. h.cancel() and cancel_process() cut everything. Every cut has a ramp of ~5 ms (no click).

cancel_process(): restart without destroying

Keeps the Entity; cancels everything it has in progress (timers, tweens, movements with time=, sounds, both the mode's and the Entity's own) and sets mode to None without firing @exit_mode or on_destroy. Own fields, tags, active, on_update and @when stay. Transients: clear_transients().

I wantI use
Pause a Handle (it stays pending)h.pause() / h.resume()
Pause the Entity's timers (they stay pending)e.active = False
Cancel timers, tweens, sounds and the modee.cancel_process()
Remove for goode.destroy()
Leave the mode with exit hookse.mode = None
 
# Restart: destroy the disposable fleet; restart what stays
group["wasp"].destroy()
group["bolt"].destroy()
player.cancel_process()
player.clear_transients()
player.hp = 3
player.active = True
avatar.goto_mode(avatar.playing)       # force re-enter; playing is a mode of the class
director.goto_mode(director.directing)

There is no global reset_all for the author. A Handle you kept becomes .cancelled (you can ignore it or cancel it again).

Usage patterns

@on_mode
def formation(self):
    every(2.0, self.shoot)              # gone when leaving formation
    after(3.0, then=self.diving)        # same
    self.move_along(track, time=2.4, loops="forever")  # same

@on_mode
def hurt(self):
    # i-frames: must survive if the mode changes midway
    self.after(0.7, lambda: self.untag("hurt"), name="hurt")

A loose call in the mode = the chapter. self.after / self.every = the Entity. The two are not synonyms.

@exit_mode and try/finally

The chapter's timers and movement already cancel on their own. Use @exit_mode for what is not a Handle: appearance (glow, visual…), own fields, flags:

@on_mode
def charging(self):
    self.glow = True
    after(0.5, then=self.diving)   # cancels on its own if you leave early

@exit_mode(charging)
def charging_exit(self):
    self.glow = False              # appearance: needs @exit_mode

This works for a sync or an async mode. The exit hook is always a plain function (not async).

In an async mode, try/finally also works when the cleanup needs to sit next to the setup (rare: most Handles go away on their own):

@on_mode
async def formation(self):
    self.glow = True
    try:
        every(2.0, self.shoot)
        while True:
            await wait(5.0)
            if chance(0.5):
                self.mode = self.diving
                return
    finally:
        self.glow = False   # also runs if the mode is cancelled

Prefer @exit_mode for appearance / own fields (one place, every way out). Prefer not to cancel a Handle by hand: the mode's scope already does that. destroy() and cancel_process() do not fire @exit_mode; use on_destroy for “the Entity is gone”, or set e.mode = None first if you need the exit hooks, then cancel_process() for whatever is left.

Where else to look — Schedule · Entity · React

Acts

An act is one part of the game — title, level, game over — written as a class, class Play(Act); change_act moves from one to the next, with no cleanup code for you to write. What the top of the file creates stays on the stage for the whole game. What an act creates leaves with it, and what it changes goes back to how it was. Acts are optional: a game without acts (run()) works as always.

Write an act → Act
Start / change / restart → change_act
What leaves, what comes back, what stays → The stage and the act
Score, lives, level → Game data
@when, @collide and fades in an act → Act rules

Act

An act is a plain class. setup(self) builds it; on_update, @when and modes run the logic of this act. No cleanup code: everything it created leaves on the change.

# ---- the stage: top of the file, lasts the whole game ----
def new_game():                   # the data of a game that starts
    st.score = 0
    st.lives = 3

st.best = 0                       # lasts across games
new_game()                        # run(Play) directly also finds st ready

class Hero(Sprite): ...           # classes are just definitions

# ---- acts ----
class Title(Act):
    def setup(self):
        Text("GALAGA", center=(500, 500), font_size=72)

    def on_update(self, dt):
        if keyp.once("SPACE"):
            new_game()
            change_act(Play)

class Play(Act):
    def setup(self):
        Hero(center=(500, 70))
        scoreboard = Text("", top_left=(20, 760))
        scoreboard["text"] @= lambda: f"Score {st.score}   Lives {st.lives}"

    @when(lambda self: st.lives == 0)
    def lost(self):
        self.after(1.5, lambda: change_act(GameOver))

class GameOver(Act):
    def setup(self):
        Text("GAME OVER", center=(500, 400))
        self.after(8, lambda: change_act(Title))

run(Title)
In an act class
WriteMeaning
setup(self)Builds the act. No parameters — data comes from st.
on_update(self, dt)Per-frame logic of this act.
@every / @after / @when / @on_changeRules of the act: switched on when it starts, gone when it ends.
self.mode = self.fleetA mode of the act (chapters inside an act).
self.after(…) / self.play_sound(…)Owned by the act: they stop on the change (a sound that ends on its own plays to the end).
self.notice = Text(…)The act's memory — only for an object that a later method uses.
on_destroy(self)Runs first on the change, with the act's objects still alive. Rarely needed: everything else leaves and goes back on its own.

The simple way is plain classes: class Play(Act), and what repeats goes in an act that reads st (st.round) or in a function at the top called from setup. An act can inherit from another (class Boss(Play)): the base's on_update, @every and @when apply once in the child act, and the base's setup runs only if the child calls super().setup(). No __init__, no setup(self, lives). An act has no body: @collide_with, class-level @leave_playfield, on_click and on_collide raise an error when the class is defined. So do self.destroy(), self.active, self.tag(…), self.visible and self.cancel_process() — the message says what to use.

In 0.6.0, Scene and change_scene were renamed Act and change_act; with from scena import * the old names no longer exist (NameError): replace Scene with Act and change_scene with change_act.

change_act

run(Title) starts with the first act. change_act(Play) changes at once: the previous act leaves, the new one is built, and the next line already runs in the new one. Always a new act — change_act(Play) inside Play restarts it.

class Play(Act):
    def on_update(self, dt):
        if keyp.once("R") and st.lives > 0:
            change_act(Play)            # restarts: always a new Play

    @on_mode
    async def fleet(self):
        build_fleet()
        await until_empty("enemy")
        st.round += 1
        change_act(Play)                # last line: the mode stops here

Make change_act the last thing. After it, the previous act's objects are dead and whatever you create already belongs to the new act (the same advice as for destroy()). It works anywhere a call works: update, a timer, @when, @collide, on_done=, the last line of an async mode. The same key press does not carry over to the new act: keyp.once is used up by whoever reads it first.

MistakeFix
Play()You don't build acts by hand: change_act(Play) — or run(Play) for the first one.
change_act(Play()) / change_act("Play")Pass the class: change_act(Play).
change_act(Play, lives=2)Only the act. Data goes in st: st.lives = 2, then change_act(Play).
change_act before runThe game has not started yet: run(Title).
change_act in a game started with run()To use acts, start with run(Title).
change_act in an on_destroy during a changeAn error that names the hook and the act that was leaving; the change ends in the act asked for first. Act flow belongs in the act: an @when of the act.

The stage and the act

The top of the file builds the stage: it stays for the whole game and works in every act. Everything created after that — by any code, even a shot fired from Hero.on_update — belongs to the current act and leaves with it.

On an act changeWhat
LeavesObjects (Shape, Sprite, Text, SpatialFx, Entity, widgets) — on_destroy runs. Timers, tweens, sounds and camera tweens with no owner on the stage — but a sound that ends on its own plays to the end (without on_done); a "forever" loop, one with name= and a paused one are cut off. Bare @when / @on_change / @collide / @leave_playfield written in setup. Post and background created in the act. Formula groups (group["targets"] @= …) created in the act. A collision tag that no remaining rule names stops enrolling members (an object that only that tag put into collision leaves it; a collidable = True you wrote stays).
