A camera movement with time=, whoever owns it. The script's ready / recently slots. Pending shake / flash / explosion_at. @= links between objects that leave together go away silently.
Goes back to what the top left (or to the default)Camera, canvas.background, canvas.effects and the background (list and .enabled), canvas.playfield, clock.scale / clock.paused, collision.resolve_enabled, collision.floor, canvas.layers.default, set_defaults, the resolve pairs, the top's formula groups, the HUD column (the act's next Text or widget without y always starts in the same place).
Staysst. Objects on the stage and their timers (radio.play_sound(…)) — except what the act handed them: a method of the act (or a function that reads the act's self) in hero.every(…), hero.on_update or hero.mode leaves with the act. A stage timer or sound whose name= the act reused is paused during the act and comes back after the change — whether reused in a bare call, on the act itself (self.every(…, name=), self.play_sound(…, name=)) or with a method of the act as the callback. A stage task (run_task at the top) does not pause: reusing its name in a bare call in the act (no owner: run_task, after, every, tween, play_sound) is an error that gives the fix (another name, or cancel() on it first). With an owner (hero.run_task(…, name=), self.every(…, name=)) it is another slot, and the stage task keeps going. Layers on the stage (a layer created in the act leaves with it; restarting the act creates it again). Preferences: the audio volume, fx_quality, post_fx_scale, display, framerate, ui.scale / ui.font. The fade (fade_out / fade_in).

Rule of thumb: if it should start from scratch every time, create it in setup. If it should survive every act, create it at the top. Music played at the top carries across acts; music played in setup stops on the change.

I need…How
Data that carries across acts (score, high score, did they win?)st
Act music that fades out softly on the changeKeep the Handle and start the fade in the act's on_destroy: self.music.fade_out(0.5). It finishes fading in the new act.
Something started mid-game that outlives the act (music turned on by a key)An owner at the top: radio = Entity(), then radio.play_sound(…) / radio.after(…) from anywhere.
An object in every act, shown only laterCreate it at the top and hide it on the next line (panel.visible = False); an act shows it (panel.visible = True). The state is the object's own: the change does not hide it again.
An object created inside an act that becomes part of the stageThere is no such thing: it goes away on the change → move it to the top.

Ownerless work (bare after(…), play_sound(…), tween(…)) has h.scope == "game" when it starts at the top and "act" after that — "act" work leaves on the change. The SCENA WARNING for ownerless work says <game> / <act> the same way.

An @= that the act makes on a stage object (hud["text"] @= lambda: f"Score {st.score}" in setup) belongs to the act: on the change the link leaves and the field goes back to what it was before — the stage's link, if there was one, or the value (hud.text goes back to ""). Restarting the act links it again without a warning, and the next act can write hud.text = "SHIPS". This also holds when the formula read an object of the act or the act itself (self.score).

Game data

Everything the next act needs to know lives in st. A new game is a function at the top (new_game()), called at the top and by the act that starts a game. An act change never clears st.

st.won = True
change_act(GameOver)               # GameOver.setup reads st.won

class Play(Act):
    def setup(self):
        st.score_on_entry = st.score   # in case a restart should undo points

Restarting (R) keeps st as it is: the lives and score so far. Whatever must be undone is saved on entry, in plain sight in the code.

Entities find each other by group, never through the act: group["hero"].nearest(self). The act does not keep the hero — the HUD and the losing rule read st.

self.enemies = group["enemy"] is an error on any Entity: look a group up where you use it; don't store it. Fields hold any value except a function; a stored object that has died reads as false (if self.notice:). A hero at the top of the file belongs to the stage: it keeps lost lives and tags, and shows up on the title — create it in setup.

Act rules

A rule (@collide, @when, @on_change…) applies according to the moment it is registered, not where it is written: at the top of the file, the whole game; in an Entity class, that object; inside setup, only this act.

@collide("shot", "enemy")            # top: the whole game (idle where there are no shots)
def hit(shot, enemy):
    shot.destroy()

class Practice(Act):
    def setup(self):
        @collide("enemy_shot", "hero")      # only in this act
        def harmless(shot, hero):
            shot.destroy()

The top's update and on_key_down run in every act. An act's logic goes in its on_update; the act's keys and mouse go in there too (keyp.once("R"), mouse.press()). A def update(self, dt) or def on_key_down(self, key) inside the act class would never run: it is a TypeError on the class line, with the act's spelling.

@when fires when the condition turns true (false → true). A condition that is already true when the act starts never fires: restarting Play with st.lives == 0 would leave the act stuck. Guard the change (keyp.once("R") and st.lives > 0) or check the state in setup.

Transitions

You put fades together yourself — there is no fade= on change_act. The fade belongs to the stage and carries across the change:

canvas.fade_out(0.5, on_done=lambda: change_act(Play))     # previous act

class Play(Act):
    def setup(self):
        canvas.fade_in(0.5)                                  # new act

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
Act × modeA mode is a chapter of one object's behavior (self.mode = self.dive; the same mode again does nothing; then= enters a mode). An act is the part of the game the player is in (change_act(GameOver); always new; owner of everything created in it). An act can have modes.There is no then= for acts, no stack of acts, no pause act — pausing is clock.paused = True.

Where else to look — Mode · Scope and cancelling · st · Camera

Sound

Playing a file is play_sound("laser.wav"). It returns the same Handle as in Schedule — cancel, await, on_done, then=, name=. The sound belongs to whoever played it, like a timer (scope and cancelling): the mode, the Entity, or the whole game / the current Act — and when that owner ends, a sound that ends on its own finishes playing. Sound("x.wav") only loads the file (like Sheet): it does not play or show up on its own. Effects (echo, filter…) go on the Handle while the sound plays; to apply them once and keep the result, use Sound.bake.

Play / audio data / bake → play_sound
Master volume, level, spectrum, amp_db → audio
Capture / record → Microphone · mic.record
Filters / echo / distortion → effects

play_sound

play_sound plays a sound file (or a Sound already loaded, or the microphone) and returns a Handle to control that playback: volume, pause, fade, effects. Sound("x.wav") only loads the sound, without playing it. h.pause() holds the sound; h.resume() continues it.

import random
play_sound("laser.wav")
play_sound("hit.wav", volume=0.6, pan=-0.2, pitch=1.05)
h = play_sound("laser.wav", on_done=ship.destroy)

play_sound("theme_a.mp3", name="music", loops="forever")
play_sound("theme_b.mp3", name="music", loops="forever", crossfade=1.0)

laser = Sound("laser.wav", volume=0.7)
play_sound(laser, pitch=random.uniform(0.95, 1.05))   # live rate (changes the duration)
crunch = laser.bake(Distortion(), transpose=3, pitch=1.1)
play_sound(crunch)   # PCM already processed — cheap

class Ship(Sprite):
    @on_mode
    def flying(self):
        play_sound("thrust_loop.wav", loops="forever")   # stops when the mode ends

    @on_mode
    def cruising(self):
        self.hum = self.play_sound("engine.wav", loops="forever")  # outlives the mode

    @exit_mode(cruising)
    def cruising_exit(self):
        self.hum.fade_out(0.3)

The two name="music" above swap because they run in the same place. The slot is per place (slot): a bare call in an act's setup and a bare call inside one of the act's modes are two slots, and both songs play. For music in an act that switches between phases: self.play_sound("theme.ogg", name="music", loops="forever") in the act, always.

play_sound reference

Function / audio data

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
play_sound(source)Parameters: source (file path, Sound or Microphone); volume (1 = original; can go above 1), pan (−1 left … 1 right), pitch (1 = normal; 2 = an octave higher and twice as fast), loops=1 (int or "forever"), fade_in (seconds rising from silence), crossfade (with name=: seconds of mixing with the sound that was playing in that name=), on_done, then, nameHandlePlays. Who owns it: in a mode's body → the mode; e.play_sound → the Entity; a bare call → the whole game (at the top of the file) or the current Act (later — see Acts). When the owner ends, a sound that ends on its own finishes playing; a "forever" loop / name= / a paused sound are cut. A missing / corrupted file: silence for its nominal duration + a warning in the banner (once per asset). The Handle keeps running — on_done and loops still behave. A clip still being recorded raises RuntimeError — mic.stop() or await first.
Sound(path)Parameters: path (str); volume (its default volume); stream (True/False, optional)SoundAudio data. Does not play. Short clips (< 8 s) go into memory; long ones stream. stream= forces the choice. No .effects.
Sound.bake(*fx, transpose=0, pitch=1)effects from the catalog; transpose (semitones, same duration); pitch (rate, changes the duration)SoundApplies transpose, pitch and the effects once and returns a new Sound, already processed — playing that Sound costs nothing extra. Order: transpose → pitch → effects; the Echo/Reverb tail is included in the new sound.
e.play_sound(src)Same as play_soundHandleAlways Entity scope: survives a mode change; stops at destroy (a sound that ends on its own finishes playing).

On the sound Handle

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.volume / .pan / .pitchnumber0.6read / writeChange the sound right away, while it plays. Volume can go above 1; Scena only keeps the sum of all sounds from clipping. Pan −1…1. Pitch 1 = normal (rate — changes the duration; cheap). On a mic monitor, pitch is ignored.
.fade_to(v, time=)methodh.fade_to(0.2, time=0.4)methodVolume ramp. World clock (follows clock.scale), like any tween.
.fade_out(time=)methodh.fade_out(0.3)methodRamps to 0 and stops (a natural end: on_done fires). It is not cancel. No Echo/Reverb tail afterward.
.levelnumber 0…10.4readHow loud this sound is right now, from 0 (silence) to ~1 (the maximum), already smoothed (audio.level_tau). For bars: amp_db(.level).
.spectrum(bins=8)list[0.1, 0.8, …]methodSplits this voice's sound into bins bands, from the lows (~40 Hz) to the highs (~16 kHz); each value (0…1) says how much sound is in that band right now. Smoothed like .level (audio.level_tau). A sound-only attribute: on a Handle that is not a sound it raises AttributeError with the hint — the same goes for .volume, .pan, .pitch, .fade_to, .fade_out, .level, .effects.
.effectsstackh.effects.add(LowPass())readSee effects. Only on the Handle / mic — not on Sound.

From the generic Handle

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
.remainingnumber0.4readTime until the audible end (clip + Echo/Reverb tail, if any). Same contract as the Handle — not specific to sound.

Sound("laser.wav") does not play. It only loads the file. Use play_sound. A fade is never automatic: if you want one, write fade_in= / .fade_out() / crossfade=. When the mode ends, a sound that ends on its own finishes playing; a sound with loops="forever", with name= or paused is cut right away (with a ~5 ms ramp, no click).

on_done fires only at the natural end (the Echo/Reverb tail included). .cancel(), .pause(), a mode change and name= (a cut) do not fire it. loops="forever" never ends on its own. Live pitch= ≠ transpose= in bake (the latter keeps the duration).

audio

audio is the game's sound as a whole: overall volume, mute, and meters of what is playing (level, spectrum) — for bars that jump with the music. amp_db converts those readings to the scale the ear hears, ready for a bar's height.

audio.volume = 0.8
audio.level_tau = 0.08

play_sound("theme.mp3", loops="forever")

N = 8
bars = [Rect(width=18, height=4, color="cyan") for _ in range(N)]

def update(dt):
    spec = audio.spectrum(bins=N)
    for i, bar in enumerate(bars):
        bar.height = 8 + 160 * amp_db(spec[i])   # floor=-60 by default
        bar.center = (80 + i * 28, 120 + bar.height / 2)
audio reference
PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
audio.volumenumber0.8read / writeMaster gain. 0 silences everything without cancelling any Handle.
audio.mutedboolFalseread / writeTrue silences everything; False goes back to the volume from before.
audio.level_tauseconds0.08read / writeHow long the smoothing of level / spectrum takes to catch up with the sound, in seconds (in the mix, in each sound and in the mic). Smaller = jumpier bars. ≤ 0 raises ValueError.
audio.levelnumber 0…10.4readHow loud the whole game's sound is right now (all sounds added together), from 0 (silence) to ~1 (the maximum), already smoothed. Read-only. For bars: amp_db(audio.level). Link it: bar["width"] @= lambda: 300 * amp_db(audio.level) follows the sound, once per frame. The h.level of a play_sound links the same way.
audio.spectrum(bins=8)list8 numbersmethodSplits the game's sound into bins bands, from the lows (~40 Hz) to the highs (~16 kHz); each value (0…1) says how much sound is in that band right now. You only choose the number of bands (bins=).
amp_db(x, floor=-60)number 0…1amp_db(audio.level)functionConverts a 0…1 reading (level or a spectrum value) to the ear's scale (decibels), also 0…1, ready for a bar's height: 1 stays 1; anything floor decibels below the maximum (default −60) or lower becomes 0. Values ≤ 0 give 0; values above 1 stay at 1.

.level / .spectrum are linear (0…1). For bars, use amp_db. Otherwise the lows drown out the rest. The smoothing is built in; there is no need to average in update.

Microphone

Microphone() opens the computer's microphone — nothing is captured before that. With it you measure the voice's volume (mic.level), listen live (play_sound(mic)) and record (clip = mic.record(); the clip plays after mic.stop() or await).

mic = Microphone()          # the system's default input
print(mic.level)
bar = Rect(top_left=(20, 20), width=0, height=10)
bar["width"] @= lambda: 300 * amp_db(mic.level)   # follows the voice
play_sound(mic)             # listen live (with mic.effects)
mic.effects.add(Echo())     # only on what you hear live — the recording has no echo

clip = mic.record()         # Sound, still recording
mic.stop()                  # clip ready; the mic stays open
play_sound(clip)

h = play_sound(clip)
h.effects.add(Echo())       # effect on playback
play_sound(clip.bake(Distortion()))

clip = await mic.record(seconds=2)
mic.close()                 # releases the device; not the same as stop()
Microphone reference
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
Microphone(backends=None)Parameters: backends (list of miniaudio.Backend; advanced — tests / diagnostics)MicrophoneOpens the system's default input. No device: a SCENA WARNING and a silent mic (.level stays 0). A recording with seconds= still ends, full of zeros, so the await does not get stuck. There is no choice of input or output device.
.record(seconds=None)seconds (of captured samples, not of game clock); on_done, thenSoundStarts recording a clip without the effects in mic.effects (they only apply to what you hear live). It does not play yet. seconds= must be finite, > 0 and ≤ 30 (ValueError otherwise). Without seconds=, it records until stop() or the 30 s cap. At the cap: a normal end + one warning per mic. Already recording, or the mic is closed: RuntimeError. Who owns it: in a mode's body → the mode; a bare call → the whole game (at the top of the file) or the current Act (later — see Acts). on_done / then= run on the next frame, only at a natural end.
.stop()No parameters—Ends the recording and keeps the clip. The mic stays open. The clip plays on the very next line; on_done waits for the next frame. With no recording running: RuntimeError — call record() first.
.recordingboolboolRead-only. True while recording.
.availableboolboolRead-only. True while a microphone is open; False with no microphone (the mic is silent, .level 0) or after close(). To offer another control: if not mic.available: ….
.level / .spectrum(bins=8)bins in spectrumnumber / listSame smoothing as audio.level_tau. Linear 0…1 — use amp_db for bars. A formula (@=) or a @when that reads the level follows the voice, once per frame. The mic must exist when the formula is linked: the @= learns what it follows at that moment.
.effectsStack—Live stack of the monitor. It does not go into the recording. Effects on the clip: h.effects on playback, or clip.bake(...).
.close()No parameters—Calling it again does nothing. Releases the device and zeroes .level / .spectrum. If it was recording, it keeps the audio already captured and does not fire on_done. Quitting the application closes every open microphone the same way.
clip.durationsecondsnumberGrows while recording (samples ÷ 44100). Stays fixed once the recording ends. Read-only.
await clipthe Sound returned by record()the same SoundWaits for the recording to end and returns the same clip, ready to play. await on a Sound loaded from a file raises TypeError.

How a recording ends

EndingKeeps the audioon_done / then=
mic.stop()yes — playable on the very next lineon the next frame
seconds= reachedyeson the next frame
30 s capyeson the next frame, plus a warning
the mode ends / destroy() / mic.close()yesno

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
clip right after record()a Sound still being made. play_sound / bake raise RuntimeError.playable — mic.stop() or await first.
mic.stop()ends the recording; the mic stays open.mic.close() (releases the device).
mic.effects applies to everythingmic.effects changes only what you hear live (play_sound(mic)).the recording — the clip always comes out without those effects.

pitch= on the mic monitor is ignored (it only makes sense for files). The monitor is the live play_sound(mic). The clip, once ready, takes pitch= and bake.

effects

Sound effects change how a sound sounds while it plays: muffled, like a radio, with an echo, in a room, distorted. Every playing sound (the Handle from play_sound) and the microphone monitor have an .effects stack: .add(…) puts an effect on, .remove() / .clear() take it off, .enabled = False turns it off without removing it. The parameters change live (lp.cutoff = 1500).

For a sound you play many times, always with the same effect, compute it once with Sound.bake(…): the result is a new Sound, already processed, that plays at no extra cost.

h = play_sound("shoot.wav")
h.effects.add(LowPass())
lp = h.effects.add(HighPass())
lp.cutoff = 1500
lp.enabled = False
lp.remove()
h.effects.clear()

# Once, then every play is cheap:
crunch = Sound("shoot.wav").bake(Distortion(), Wavefold(), transpose=3, pitch=1.1)
play_sound(crunch)
Catalog reference
NameParametersWhat it does
LowPass(cutoff=300)cutoff: cutoff frequency, in HzMuffles: lets the lows through and cuts the highs above cutoff — a sound “behind a wall”, or underwater. The lower the cutoff, the more muffled.
HighPass(cutoff=2000)cutoff: cutoff frequency, in HzThe opposite: cuts the lows below cutoff — the thin sound of a radio or a telephone.
Echo(delay=0.25, decay=0.6)delay: seconds between repeats · decay: how much of the volume each repeat keeps (0 to 0.95)Echo: the sound comes back several times, quieter each time. After the file ends, the echo goes on until it fades away.
Reverb(size=1.0, mix=0.6)size: size of the room (0.05 to 1.5) · mix: how much of the room you hear (0 = none, 1 = only the room)Ambience: the sound in a room, a cave or a hall. It also keeps sounding a little after the end.
Distortion(drive=8)drive: how hard the sound is pushed (greater than 0)“Dirty” distortion, like a guitar or a blown speaker. It changes the character, not the volume.
Wavefold(drive=3)drive: how many folds per peak (greater than 0)A metallic, arcade sound. More drive, brighter.

.enabled = False turns the effect off: it sounds exactly as it would without it. .remove() twice does nothing. cancel and fade_out stop the sound without waiting for the Echo/Reverb tail. Leaving the mode does not cut a sound that ends on its own: it finishes playing, tail included (when the owner ends). Sound has no .effects; use bake.

Where else to look — Handle · Mode · Reactive

React

Run code when something happens — an event, which runs once, at that moment: a condition becomes true (@when), a value changes (@on_change), a key is pressed (script callbacks), the mouse clicks an object, something leaves the play area. To read the keyboard every frame: Frame. Objects touching: Collision.

A bool became True → @when
A value changed → @on_change
Key / mouse / setup / update → Script callbacks
The Entity's setup / on_update / on_destroy → Entity callbacks
Click on an object → Click / drag
Left the playfield → @leave_playfield
Bodies touch → Collision
Held / every frame → Frame
In N seconds → Schedule
This Entity is in this chapter → Mode
Widget (Button.on_click, linked value) → UI
The whole map → Which to use

@when

@when(condition) runs the function once when the condition turns from False to True — “when HP reaches 0, die”. The condition is checked every frame; while it stays True, the function does not run again.

A Python expression (player.hp <= 0) is evaluated now, when the decorator runs. For Scena to check the condition every frame, pass a function: lambda: …. A bool field (st["alive"]) can go in as is at module level. In a class: lambda self: ….

st.hp = 3
@when(lambda: st.hp <= 0)
def on_death():
    player.destroy()

@when(lambda: keyp("Y"))
def on_y():
    restart()

unregister_event(on_death)

It needs a lambda. The expression must return True or False — otherwise TypeError.

It fires when the condition turns from False to True. While it stays True, it does not fire again.

@when(lambda: player.hp <= 0)
def on_death():
    player.destroy()

@when(lambda: keyp("Y"))
def on_y():
    restart()

A bare expression (@when(player.hp <= 0)) is evaluated once, when the decorator runs — it is not checked again. At module level a bool field works too: @when(st["alive"]) (with brackets: st.alive is the current value).

In a class: lambda self: …. A bare field (st["hp"]) works only at module level.

class Ship(Sprite):
    @when(lambda self: self.hp <= 0)
    def on_death(self):
        self.destroy()
Contract
PartMeaning
@when(cond)Bool. It needs a lambda (a True/False expression). It fires when the condition turns from False to True. While it stays True, it does not fire again. At module level, a bool field: @when(st["alive"]).
When it is checkedEvery frame, and after writes to own fields / State. flush() runs the pending checks now, without waiting for the end of the frame.
Methodlambda self: …. It applies to every object of the class, from the moment it is created.
Several @when on the same defFine: both expressions fire the same body. Mixing with @on_change is a TypeError.
Mixing with @every / @collide / @on_modeTypeError.
unregister_event(fn)Removes every @when / @on_change from that function.
until / wait / parallelAn async wait in Mode. Not an event. until also needs a callable: lambda: ship.hp <= 0.

Do not combine @when with keyp.once. @when already fires only when the condition turns True. A widget linked to a formula: the gesture does nothing (that is Reactive, not an event).

@on_change

@on_change(value) runs the function every time the value changes, and can receive the new value. It works for any type: number, text, tuple.

It takes a field (st["wave"], st["pos"]) or a lambda. Without brackets, st.wave is the current number and raises an error. An object's field needs a lambda: a bare c.radius takes the current number. In a class: lambda self: ….

st.pos = (0, 0)
@on_change(st["pos"])
def on_pos(value):
    marker.center = value

@on_change(lambda: c.radius)
def on_radius(value):
    ring.radius = value

It fires when the new value is != the previous one. Callback: no args, or one arg (the new value).

st.wave = 1
@on_change(st["wave"])
def on_wave(value):
    spawn(value)

@on_change(lambda: c.radius)
def on_radius(value):
    ring.radius = value

In a class: lambda self: …. A bare field (st["hp"]) works only at module level. Callback: def fn(self) or def fn(self, value).

class Ship(Sprite):
    @on_change(lambda self: self.hp)
    def on_hp(self, value):
        self.flash(0.12)
Contract
PartMeaning
@on_change(target)Any value. Something reactive in Scena (an Attribute) or a lambda. It fires when the new value is != the previous one. Callback with 0 or 1 arg (the new value).
When it is checkedEvery frame, and after writes to own fields / State. flush() runs the pending checks now, without waiting for the end of the frame.
Methodlambda self: …. It applies to every object of the class, from the moment it is created. Callback: def fn(self) or def fn(self, value).
Several @on_change on the same defFine: both expressions fire the same body. Mixing with @when is a TypeError.
Mixing with @every / @collide / @on_modeTypeError.
unregister_event(fn)Removes every @when / @on_change from that function.

An object's field needs a lambda. @on_change(c.radius) receives only the current number and raises TypeError: write @on_change(lambda: c.radius).

Script callbacks

Functions with fixed names that you define in the script; run() calls them: setup when the window opens, update every frame, on_key_down / on_mouse_click… when there is input. To know whether a key is held, keyp in update is usually simpler (Frame). Click on an object: Click / drag. In a class: Entity callbacks.

def setup(canvas):
    canvas.fx_quality = "high"

def update(dt, canvas):
    if keyp("RIGHT"):
        player.move_by(200 * dt, 0)

def on_key_down(key):
    if key == "ESC":
        canvas.reset_view()

def on_mouse_click(x, y, button):
    marker.move_to(x, y)

def on_mouse_scroll(xoffset, yoffset):
    factor = 1.1 if yoffset > 0 else 1 / 1.1
    canvas.zoom_by(factor, about=(mouse.x, mouse.y))

The engine sends the full tuple and drops what the function does not ask for. update(dt) and update(dt, canvas) both work. The same goes for on_mouse_up(x, y, button) vs. the version with click_x, click_y.

The keyboard sends only key — there is no second mods parameter. Modifiers are keys of their own: "SHIFT", "CTRL", "ALT", "CMD". A shortcut: keyp("CTRL+R"). Never key == "CTRL+R".

Signatures
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
setupParameters: canvas (the canvas)—Once, with the window open. Not the Entity's setup(self).
updateParameters: dt (number), canvas (the canvas)—Every frame, after input. Take only dt if you do not need the canvas. In the script the name is update, not on_update.
on_key_downParameters: key (str)—A key was pressed. A friendly name in capitals, the same as keyp's (punctuation arrives as "K1"…"K12" — table). An ordinary key arrives only with no Ctrl / Alt / Cmd held: Ctrl+R does not call on_key_down("R") — use keyp("CTRL+R"). Shift does not block: with Shift held, SPACE calls on_key_down("SPACE"). key == "ESCAPE" → ValueError suggesting "ESC".
on_key_upParameters: key (str)—A key was released. The same key. It arrives only for a key whose on_key_down arrived (a shortcut like CMD+S sends neither of the two for "S"); it arrives even if a modal menu opened in between or if the act changed while the key was held (walking right up to the door, the on_key_up("RIGHT") arrives in the new act).
on_keyParameters: key (str)—On the press and, while the key stays held, on each auto-repeat. The same key. A key pressed before change_act does not repeat in the new act (its on_key_up arrives).
on_charParameters: char (str)—A Unicode character.
on_mouse_downParameters: x (number), y (number), button (number: Mouse.BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT…)—A mouse button went down; x, y in the world. Who receives it first: widgets, then objects, then this function.
on_mouse_upParameters: x (number), y (number), button (number: Mouse.BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT…), click_x (number), click_y (number)—The button was released; x, y is where it was released, in the world. click_x, click_y (optional) is where the button was pressed — useful for measuring the drag. You can leave both out and keep x, y, button. It also arrives when the act changed with the button held; then there is no on_mouse_click or on_mouse_drag in the new act.
on_mouse_clickParameters: x (number), y (number), button (number: Mouse.BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT…)—A click (press+release in the same place). World. Not shape.on_click.
on_mouse_double_clickParameters: x (number), y (number), button (number: Mouse.BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT…)—A double click. World.
on_mouse_moveParameters: x (number), y (number)—The mouse moved; x, y in the world. It runs alongside the other mouse events, without blocking them.
on_mouse_dragParameters: x (number), y (number), button (number: Mouse.BTN_LEFT, BTN_RIGHT…)—A drag with a button held. World. Not shape.on_drag_to.
on_mouse_scrollParameters: xoffset (number), yoffset (number)—The mouse wheel turned (yoffset > 0 = up). Who receives it first: the widget under the pointer (it keeps the wheel; a Slider changes its value), then an object held with wheel_rotate, then this function. An object without wheel_rotate does not hold the wheel.
post_drawParameters: skia_canvas (Skia canvas), scene_image (image)—Escape hatch: you draw the final screen image yourself, in place of the whole post-processing effect list (Post). Not an event.

A shortcut is not an event name: never key == "CTRL+R". A focused TextInput: see Keyboard. Button.on_click (receives the button, or nothing) is UI.

The script has no other way to receive events besides the ones in this section and in the map at the top: @when / @on_change, click on an object, @leave_playfield, collision, reading every frame in Frame, @= in Reactive, timers in Schedule, @on_mode in Mode, widgets in UI.

Entity callbacks

Methods with fixed names that Scena calls on an Entity: setup when it is born, on_update every frame, on_destroy when it is destroyed. They work on every Entity (Shape, Sprite, SpatialFx and the Entity() with no drawing). Write them as methods of the class or assign a function to the object (ship.on_update = …). The script's names (setup(canvas), update) are something else — Script callbacks.

class Ship(Sprite):
    def setup(self):
        self.hp = 3

    def on_update(self, dt):
        self.rotate_by(40 * dt)

    def on_destroy(self):
        canvas.burst_at(self)

ship.on_update = lambda e, dt: e.rotate_by(40 * dt)
Signatures
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
setupParameters: self (this object)—Once, after the constructor. Own fields are born here: self.hp = 3. Not the script's setup(canvas).
on_updateParameters: self (this object), dt (number)—Every frame, on this Entity, even during await. On an instance: fn(e, dt). See Frame.
on_destroyParameters: self (this object)—Once, from inside destroy(). It does not fire on a mode change.
on_click / on_hover / on_hover_exitParameters: self (this object)—Shape, Sprite and Text (hover on widgets too). The method already turns on clickable (for the click) or makes the object a hover target, like assigning on the instance. See Click / drag.
on_drag_to / on_drag_overParameters: self (the dragged object), to_shape (the droppable underneath, or None), pos (point)—On the dragged object. The method turns on draggable. self is already the object being dragged: the method does not receive the piece again (def on_drag_to(self, piece, target, pos) raises TypeError when the object is created).
on_drop_byParameters: self (the target), from_shape (the dragged object), pos (point)—On the target. The method turns on droppable.
on_collide / on_collide_stay / on_collide_exitParameters: me (object), other (object), info (CollisionInfo)—Shape, Sprite and SpatialFx. See Collision.

Click / drag / hover

Clicking, dragging, dropping and hovering the mouse over a Shape, Sprite or Text (and a Button). Just declare the gesture's function: it turns on the right property (clickable, draggable…) by itself. Who receives the click, from top to bottom: widgets → ui → top → other layers → script.

Three ways to write the same gesture: a decorator (@click, @hover, @drag_to…), a callback on the object (shape.on_click = fn — an alternative to the decorator) and the properties alone (clickable / draggable). Every Graphic (Shape, Sprite, Text) has these properties and callbacks; SpatialFx does not. The gesture's function can receive the target or ask for nothing — that is why the same function serves a Shape and a Button. A parameter with a default value does not receive the target, so lambda f=f: choose(f) in a loop works.

@click(c1, c2, box)
def on_click(shape):
    shape.set_color("gold")

reset = Button(label="Reset")

@click(reset, restart_icon)   # Button and Shape: the same function
def restart():
    st.score = 0

@click(group["click_group"])
def on_group(shape):
    shape.set_color("gold")
@drag_to(token)
def on_drag(from_shape, to_shape, pos):
    from_shape.center = pos

@drag_over(token)
def on_over(from_shape, to_shape, pos):
    zone.set_color("yellow" if to_shape is zone else "gray")

@drop_by(zone)
def landed(from_shape, to_shape, pos):
    from_shape.center = zone.center

One hover target at a time: the topmost one under the cursor, among widgets, ui and the world. Entered → @hover; left → @hover_exit. Every entry has exactly one exit.

@hover(group["cards"])
def lit(card):
    card.set_color("gold")

@hover_exit(group["cards"])
def unlit(card):
    card.set_color("gray")

Three different tests, each answering one question — do not swap one for another:

if ship.contains_point(mouse):
    ...  # this object (by its drawing), in the world. Also contains_point(x, y)

def on_update(self, dt):
    self.set_color("gold" if self.pointer_hover else "gray")  # a state, not an event

hits = collision.query_point(mouse)  # without group=: registered hitboxes

The exit is immediate: hiding, destroying, moving out from under the cursor, clickable = False, a widget on top or a modal Menu. The entry waits for the mouse to move: a shape that slides under a still cursor only gets hover on the next movement. A shape with only @hover does not block clicks: the click goes through to the one below.

# wheel turns it while the button is held on the body
rect.wheel_rotate = True
rect.show_handles()
rect.show_points()

a1 = Anchor(120, 620)
a2 = Anchor(280, 660, color="dark red")
Line(p1=lambda: a1.center, p2=lambda: a2.center)
a = Circle(center=(900, 150), radius=55, color="red")
b = Circle(center=(930, 170), radius=40, color="green")
# only within the same layer
b.move_to_front()
a.move_to_back()

hud = Rect(center=(930, 170), width=85, height=65, layer="top", color="navy")
Decorators

They turn on the right property on the target (clickable, draggable, droppable) and tie the function to the gesture. The target is a Graphic (Shape, Sprite or Text), not a SpatialFx. @click also takes a Button; @hover / @hover_exit take any widget. Slider / CheckBox / DropDown / TextInput in @click raise an error: use @on_change(w.data). @click(group["…"]) follows the tag, like @collide: it turns on the current members and anyone who joins later (group=, add_to_group), and turns off anyone who leaves. A refused member raises an error before any member is turned on (and a refused object that joins later raises an error on the line that put it in the tag). A function set by hand (card.on_click = f) is not replaced when the object joins or leaves the tag (the decorator, when it runs, sets its own on the members at that moment). Made inside an act, it goes away with the act. A union (group["a"] | group["b"]) or a .filter(…) is a snapshot: it turns on only the members of that moment. No target (@click()) or no parentheses (@click above the def) raises an error: without parentheses, Python would hand the function itself to @click and it would never run. Above a method in a class it also raises an error, because there is no object there yet: in a class, the gesture is the method with the fixed name (def on_click(self); or, for another name, self.on_click = self.tapped in setup). In an act, write @click(start_btn) inside setup.

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
@click(c1, c2)Function receives: target (Shape, Sprite, Text or Button)—Turns on clickable. A click on the body, with the left button (the right one does not fire it: use mouse.press(Mouse.BTN_RIGHT) or on_mouse_down).
@hover(card)Function receives: target (object)—The cursor entered: the object became the hover target. It does not turn on clickable.
@hover_exit(card)Function receives: target (object)—It stopped being the hover target (the cursor left, or it vanished, was destroyed, was covered).
@drag_to(shape)Function receives: from (object), to (object or None), pos (point)—The drag of this shape was released. The values arrive by position: a function with 2 parameters receives (from, to) — the point is the 3rd (def dropped(card, target, pos)).
@drag_over(shape)Function receives: from (object), to (object or None), pos (point)—During the drag, on each mouse movement (not every frame): to is the target under the piece, or None outside any target.
@drop_by(zone)Function receives: from (object), to (the target), pos (point)—Turns on droppable. Something was dropped on it.

from, to and pos in the three drag decorators:

ParameterPassType (default)Meaning
from1stShapetokenThe shape being dragged.
to2ndShape or NonezoneThe topmost droppable under the pointer: first those on the ui layer, then those in the world, wherever the drag comes from — the seed from the inventory (layer="ui") lands in the world's flower bed, the world's stone lands in the HUD's trash can. None if there is none.
pos3rdpoint(mouse.x, mouse.y)(x, y) where the pointer is (over) or was released (to / drop), in the space of the object that owns the function: in drag_to / drag_over the dragged object's (that is why from_shape.center = pos works), in drop_by the target's (Plant(center=pos) is born in the flower bed). World for world objects, screen (view) for layer="ui"; with no camera the two are the same.
 
@drag_to(token)
def on_drag(from_shape, to_shape, pos):
    from_shape.center = pos
    if to_shape is zone:
        from_shape.set_color("gold")
Callbacks

An alternative to the decorators. The same gestures, the same signature. A property on the object: assigning it also turns on the flag. Use one or the other — the last one written wins.

token = Circle(center=(200, 200), radius=24, color="coral")
token.clickable = True
token.on_click = lambda shape: shape.set_color("gold")

token.draggable = True
def on_drag(from_shape, to_shape, pos):
    from_shape.center = pos
token.on_drag_to = on_drag
MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
on_clickParameters: shape (object)—Same as @click(shape). shape.on_click = fn or a method in the class.
on_drag_toParameters: from (object), to (object or None), pos (point)—Same as @drag_to(shape). On the dragged shape, on release.
on_drag_overParameters: from (object), to (object or None), pos (point)—Same as @drag_over(shape). On the dragged shape, during the drag.
on_drop_byParameters: from (object), to (the target), pos (point)—Same as @drop_by(zone). On the droppable target, on release.
on_hoverParameters: shape (object)—Same as @hover(shape). Makes the shape a hover target without making it clickable.
on_hover_exitParameters: shape (object)—Same as @hover_exit(shape).
On every Graphic

Every Graphic (Shape, Sprite, Text) has these methods and properties. SpatialFx does not — it is not a Graphic. Widgets are UI.

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
clickableboolTrueread / writeAccepts clicks. A decorator / callback turns it on by itself.
draggableboolTrueread / writeDrags the whole body.
droppableboolTrueread / writeA drop target. @drop_by turns it on.
pointer_hoverboolTruereadRead. True on the hover target: the topmost clickable / draggable / on_hover object under the cursor. A state, updated once per frame. A decoration with none of these is always False (and does not block). Not contains_point.
pointer_pressedboolTruereadRead. True while the left button, pressed on this shape, stays held and the cursor is over it (releasing there would click). It goes False when the cursor leaves and back to True when it returns; while dragging it stays True. It ends on release and when the shape goes away (visible = False, active = False, destroy()), stops being clickable / draggable, or a modal menu opens. Good for a "pressed-in" look.
wheel_rotateboolTrueread / writeTrue: with the mouse button held over the object, the mouse wheel turns it. Independent of draggable.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
contains_point(x, y=None)Parameters: x (a point, or the number x with y)True/FalseDoes this object contain the point? Drawing geometry (the same shape the click tests). Point, tuple, mouse, Graphic. The point is in the world: on an object on the "ui" layer with the camera panned / zoomed / rotated, contains_point(mouse) is not the click — use pointer_hover. Sprite: the current frame's alpha, not the PNG's rectangle or the hitbox. Circle: the painted slice (pie or segment). Rect corner_radius: the click follows the corner; collision stays the rectangle.
show_handles() / show_points()No parameters—show_handles() shows the free points that define the shape (corners, center, ends) as drag handles: dots you drag with the mouse to change the shape. show_points() only marks all the points, with no dragging, to check the geometry. An Anchor is born as a drag handle, on the top layer.
move_to_front() / move_to_back()No parameters—Order within the layer. An object on layer="top" stays above those on the "default" layer (the default one), whatever the order.
 
token = Circle(center=(200, 200), radius=24, color="coral")
token.clickable = True
token.draggable = True
token.on_click = lambda shape: shape.set_color("gold")

zone = Rect(center=(500, 300), width=120, height=80, color="navy")
zone.droppable = True

An invisible object does not click. Who receives the click: widgets → objects on the ui layer → world. pointer_hover comes from clickable / draggable / on_hover. There is no hoverable: @hover already makes it a target. Three tests: contains_point = this drawing; pointer_hover = the topmost target; collision.query_point without group= = registered hitboxes.

@leave_playfield

@leave_playfield runs a function when an object's center leaves the play area (canvas.playfield) — to destroy the shot that left the screen, to lose a life when the star falls.

@leave_playfield("bullet")
def leftover(shot):
    shot.destroy()

canvas.playfield.pad = 0.4
# or explicit:
canvas.playfield.set(left=-40, bottom=-40, right=1040, top=840)
# or a Box:
canvas.playfield.set(canvas.game_view.outset(300))

The rectangle is the playfield, fixed in the world — it does not follow the camera. It is not canvas.game_view (the window). Laying out ships / HUD: Place.

A moving camera (runner, flappy): the playfield falls behind. Make it follow the window with one line per frame, in update: canvas.playfield.set(canvas.game_view.outset(300)).

Only an object that was inside can leave: an object born outside the playfield that moves away (the shot of a tower the camera left behind) never fires @leave_playfield and stays alive forever. Create it inside the area (shoot only when the tower is on screen) or destroy it after a while (shot.after(3, shot.destroy)).

Default (no need to set it): the design rectangle with pad=0.25 on each side (1.5×, centered). It only takes effect when some @leave_playfield is in use.

Two @leave_playfield("bullet") both run, in the order they were written (like @collide). One made inside an act goes away on the act change.

canvas.playfield reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
canvas.playfield.pad = 0.4number0.4read / writeA fraction on each side (size × (1+2p)). 0.0 would be exactly the screen's limit. Negative shrinks inside the design rectangle.
.left .right .bottom .topnumber-40read / writeSides. y up: top is the largest y. Writable one by one.
.width .height .centernumber or point120readDerived, read-only. .center has .x / .y.
.padnumber0.4read / writeA number if the mode is pad; None if the sides are explicit. Negative = an area smaller than the design; pad <= -0.5 collapses to the center (it does not flip the sides).

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
canvas.playfield.set(box) / canvas.playfield.set(left=, bottom=, right=, top=)Parameters: box (Box) — or left (number), bottom (number), right (number), top (number)—An axis-aligned rectangle, in the world: a Box (read once) or the four sides, all required. Both together: error.
.inset(margin) / .outset(margin) / .grid(…) / .beside(…) / .strip(…)same as BoxBox / GridCopies for layout. They do not write .pad. See Place.

Ctrl+Shift+7 draws the playfield (cyan) when some @leave_playfield is in use. Alias: canvas.bounds.

At module level: one or more group names. Objects that join the group later are watched too. Callback: fn(item).

@leave_playfield("bolt", "sting")
def leftover(shot):
    shot.destroy()

@leave_playfield("star")
def missed(star):
    star.destroy()
    st.lives -= 1

In a class: no group names. It applies to every object of the class, from the moment it is created. Callback: fn(self).

class Bolt(Sprite):
    @leave_playfield
    def leftover(self):
        self.destroy()

It fires only after the center has been inside once. A spawn outside does not count. Do not mix it with @collide / @every on the same def. You do not have to destroy: you can park, lose a life, reappear on the other side. Do not use the playfield to position the fleet — that is Box / game_view. To keep the pose inside a region (clamp / bounce / wrap): confine.

Where else to look — Frame · Collision · Mode · Reactive

Collision

Know when two objects touch (@collide) and make one stop against the other — walls, floors, platforms (resolve). Only what you enroll takes part, by naming it in a @collide or a resolve(). Shape, Sprite and SpatialFx use the same system. To know whether something left the play area: @leave_playfield; where two outlines cross: intersections.

A function that runs when two bodies touch → Detect (@collide / @collide_with / on_collide)
What the collision function receives → CollisionInfo
Wall, floor, bounce → Make it solid (resolve / .mass / bounce=)
On the floor? → Touching (touching_sides)
Which block am I standing on? → Touching (touching_contacts)
Will I fall if I walk on? End of the platform → Floor ahead (floor_below)
Dash, your own controller → Manual resolution
Who is here / radius → Queries
collidable / collider shape → What collides
Debug overlay → Debug

Detect

@collide calls a function of yours when two objects (or groups) touch. Say which two — @collide("bullet", "enemy") — and write the function that reacts: a function in the module, a method of the class or a property on the object. All three forms have the same three phases: started touching, still touching, stopped touching.

Just touching counts. Two objects that share a border already touch (that is what keeps an object resting on the floor “touching”). In a grid of same-size cells (snake, Tetris, match-3), the head touches the neck right at the start: make each cell 1 or 2 units smaller than the grid step.

@collide("bullet", "enemy")
def on_hit(me, other, info):
    other.destroy()

@collide_stay("zone", "player")
def inside(me, other, info):
    other.hp -= clock.dt

@collide(player, ANYTHING)
def bump(me, other, info):
    other.flash(0.1)

Without a named pair (or on_collide / ANYTHING), no collision function runs. Each of the pair's two sides is a group name (tag), an object, group["tag"], ANYTHING or a hitbox part — or a list of them. Anything else (5, None, a dict, an effect) raises TypeError right away, in @collide and in resolve / unresolve. Group names see whoever joins later; an object passed directly leaves the pair when it is destroyed (destroy()), and the new object you create in its place does not join — prefer the group name if the Entity dies and comes back.

PhaseWhenFunctionMethodObject
enterFirst frame of overlap.@collide(a, b)@collide_with(b)on_collide
stayEach following frame they still overlap.@collide_stay(a, b)@collide_with_stay(b)on_collide_stay
exitThey stopped touching. info.point is None.@collide_exit(a, b)@collide_with_exit(b)on_collide_exit

ANYTHING is the wildcard: that side × everything enrolled. Callback: fn(me, other) or fn(me, other, info) — me is the object of @collide's 1st argument, other that of the 2nd; info is a CollisionInfo.

Several handlers on the same contact all run, even if one of them destroys one of the two: the ones after it receive the already dead object (you can read it; destroy() again does nothing). So a Bullet with @collide_with("enemies") that does self.destroy() and an Enemy with @collide_with("bullets") that destroys itself and adds a point give the same score, whichever is created first — and the same holds for a module function together with a method. That contact's exit waits for the remaining handlers: on a contact you always see the enter, then the exit (a counter with += 1 on enter and -= 1 on exit goes back to zero, whichever handler destroys). The destroyed object's own exit hooks (its on_collide_exit, its class's @collide_with_exit methods) and the exits of its other contacts run at the moment of destroy(), while it still exists. An object that died in a contact does not start another one in the same frame: a bullet hits only one enemy. On an act change in the middle of the contact, the handlers of the act that left do not run.

Each rule has its own contact. A rule's enter runs when the rule starts to apply to the two — because they started touching, or because one of them got the tag while they were already touching (hero.tag("shield") inside the lava fires @collide("shield", "lava")), or because the rule was created at that moment — and its stay comes from the next frame on. The exit runs when the rule stops applying: they separated, or one of them lost the tag (untag), even if another rule still joins the two. That is why a rule does the same thing with or without other rules for the same pair. Removing the tag and adding it back in the same frame changes nothing; a tag given inside a handler counts from the next frame on.

Fast object. An object that travels (move_by, move_to(…, time=), move_along, or turning around another point with rotate_by(…, about=)) more than half its own thickness in a frame is checked along the frame's whole path, not only where it stopped. A fast bullet does not pass through the enemy, at any frame rate. If the path crosses several, the nearest one's enter runs first: destroying the bullet there stops the others. The contact with an object already passed lasts one frame (enter now, exit on the next); info.point is where it hit and info.depth is 0. Placing (center = …, move_to without time=, @=, tween) is not checked along the path — for that, use raycast from the previous position to the new one. Spinning in place is not either: a blade that spins very fast can skip a thin object between two frames.

A function in the module. Both sides in the call. Scope: the pair.

@collide("bullet", "enemy")
def on_hit(me, other, info):
    other.destroy()

@collide_stay("zone", "player")
def inside(me, other, info):
    other.hp -= clock.dt

@collide_exit("player", "door")
def left_door(me, other, info):
    me.set_color("cyan")

A class method. self is the class's object; other is the target. The target follows the same rules as a side of @collide (tag, shape, ANYTHING). Scope: self × the target.

class Wasp(Sprite):
    @collide_with("bolt")
    def on_hit_bolt(self, bolt, info):
        self.hp -= 1

    @collide_with_stay("acid_pool")
    def in_acid(self, pool, info):
        self.hp -= clock.dt

Callback: fn(self, other) or fn(self, other, info).

A property on the object — Shape, Sprite and SpatialFx. Scope: this object × any other enrolled one. A plain Rect is not enrolled: the bullet that passes through the alien with nothing happening needs bullet.collidable = True (or its own on_collide, or a @collide with both groups).

ball.on_collide = lambda me, other, info: me.set_color("yellow")
def drain(me, other, info):
    other.hp -= clock.dt                 # a lambda can't do -=; use def
ball.on_collide_stay = drain
ball.on_collide_exit = lambda me, other, info: me.set_color("cyan")

class Probe(Circle):
    def on_collide(self, other, info):
        self.flash(0.1)

Assigning enrolls the object and declares an ANYTHING interest: it is the same as @collide_with(ANYTHING) (and _stay / _exit). As a class method: fn(self, other) or fn(self, other, info). It does not filter the other side — for a specific pair, use @collide(a, b). Only one per phase on the object: the last one written wins.

on_collide = None removes that callback's ANYTHING interest: the engine stops testing this body against all the others, unless @collide_with(ANYTHING) or @collide(…, ANYTHING) still declares it. The module's @collide(a, b) functions keep firing.

Order. You can combine the forms. On the same contact, the object's function (on_collide) runs first, then the pair's function (@collide); if both exist, both fire (with @collide_with(ANYTHING) and on_collide in the same class, Scena warns once).

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
@collide and @collide_with on the same defTypeError. A plain function uses @collide(a, b); a method uses @collide_with.two spellings of the same decorator
A collectible / sensor in a resolve()A collectible / sensor is only @collide, never resolve(). A coin pushes no one. See Make it solid.solid
Outlines that crossDetect is about bodies overlapping. Outlines crossing: intersections. Leaving the playfield: @leave_playfield.@collide

CollisionInfo

CollisionInfo is the collision function's third parameter (info): it tells where the two objects touched, in which direction and how much they overlap, on that frame. You don't build one — Scena hands it to you. It exists without resolve(): it comes from @collide, on_collide and test_collision.

@collide("bolt", "wasp")
def boom(me, other, info):
    canvas.explosion_at(info.point, amount=0.8, shake=False)
    # or: canvas.explosion_at(*info.point, amount=0.8, shake=False)
    # or: canvas.explosion_at(info, amount=0.8, shake=False)
    other.destroy()

@collide_stay(player, "ramps")
def on_ramp(me, other, info):
    if abs(info.slope_angle) <= 45:      # the threshold is the script's call, not the engine's
        player.vel = info.slide_along(player.vel)
    else:
        ...                               # too steep — treat it as a plain wall

info.a is me and info.b is other. info.point is the useful place for VFX — the middle of the contact points (info.points). Enter / stay always have a point (without an exact contact point, a point on the object's border is used). Exit has no point (points empty → point is None — the engine does not keep the last stay).

CollisionInfo reference

Contact

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning

info.a_hitbox / info.b_hitboxHitbox or Noneinfo.b_hitbox is hurtreadEach side's part (add_hitbox); None = the body. With a part, push_apart / bounce_apart / resolve raise TypeError (a part only detects).
info.normalVec2info.normalreadFrom a toward b (unit length). Zero if there is none.
info.depthnumberinfo.depthreadHow much they overlap. 0 when a fast object has already gone past the other.
info.pointpoint or Noneinfo.pointreadA usable (x, y) — the middle of the contact points. Enter / stay: always a tuple (at least a point on the object's border). None only on exit. Fast object: the place of impact, even if the object is already further on.

info.sidestr or Noneinfo.side == "bottom"readThe side of a in the contact: top/bottom/left/right.

Slope

NameType / signatureReturnsMeaning
info.slope_anglenumberinfo.slope_anglereadThe surface's angle in degrees (0 = flat floor). Continuous — not the 4 buckets of side.

Methods that push (info.resolve, push_apart, bounce_apart, mtv_split, velocity_split, reflect_velocity): Manual resolution.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
VFX at info.points[0]That is a corner of the face. Use info.point. canvas.explosion_at / burst_at / ripple_at / wave_at / bubbles_at / fireworks_at / zap_at / hit_at / debris_at take (x, y) or a point (tuple, Point, Vec2, Graphic, info). None does nothing — on exit, explosion_at(info.point) is silent; *info.point on exit raises TypeError.the last contact, kept
In the collision function, me.vel / other.vel already reflect the impactStill the ones from update(dt): resolve() runs later. info keeps no velocity — read it on the bodies. info.bounce_apart() / info.resolve(bounce=…) inside it write .vel right away.the velocity after the impact
Fast bullet: info.point is where the bullet isWhere it hit. The bullet stays where the frame took it (Scena does not pull it back): for the explosion, use info.point, not me.center.the bullet's position

Make it solid

resolve(a, b) enrolls a pair to separate on its own every frame: it follows the path of the movement and stops at the point of impact, then slides along the surface. Detection (@collide) and resolution are separate enrollments.

Stacks. Two crates one on top of the other stand; three or more movable crates stacked up (or a crate much heavier than the light ones under it) can sink a little into each other, more so at low frame rates: resolve does not promise stacks. Keep stacked crates at similar masses, or make the stack a single object, or STATIC if it should not move.

wall = Rect(center=(400, 300), width=200, height=30, group="walls")
wall.mass = STATIC

player.mass = 1.0

resolve(player, "walls")          # enroll + detect + push
resolve(player, "walls", bounce=0.0)  # + zero the velocity along the normal

# reset: places, does not travel — a wall in the way does not stop the hero
player.center = start_pos

unresolve(player, "walls")

.mass decides who gives way in the push. STATIC does not give way: floor, wall, platform.

Every frame, Scena follows the movement path of the enrolled pair and stops at the impact, slides along the surface and undoes whatever overlap is left. The sides are objects or group names (whoever joins the group later is in too). Default mass 1.0; <= 0 raises an error. Two equal masses push each other half and half.

Pieces laid side by side are rarely perfect: a rotated row of blocks, a rounded coordinate. In a world with a floor (collision.floor = True), an object on the floor that walks against the side of a still piece rising up to 2 above its feet climbs that step and keeps walking. A bigger step is a wall. In the air there are no steps: hitting the corner from the side is a wall.

A collectible or sensor is not solid: only @collide. A coin pushes no one:

@collide("hero", "star")
def caught(me, star, info):
    star.destroy()
    st.score += 1

resolve(hero, ANYTHING) makes everything enrolled solid, including coins, bullets and sensors: the hero pushes the coin instead of passing through it (the coin's @collide keeps firing). There is no way to mark a body “not solid”: name the solid groups, resolve(hero, ["walls", "crates"]). ANYTHING is for when everything in the world is solid (a world made only of blocks and walls).

A floor that must not give way is STATIC. When neither body is STATIC, the push is split by mass, whichever was created first: a crate of mass 1 moves half the step of the player pushing it, one of mass 50 barely moves. That holds for floors, walls and platforms too: left at the default mass 1, they give way under a hero of mass 1 (the hero's gravity sinks the floor). A platform you move with move_by that should carry whoever is on top is STATIC.

Whoever is on top rides along, in a world with a floor (collision.floor = True). An object resting on top of another one in the resolve (its "bottom" side touching) moves with it in the frame, sideways and up and down, with move_by, time= or move_along, at any frame rate; its own movement adds to that (walking on the elevator). A wall in the elevator's path holds back whoever is on top. An object that jumps or bounces stops riding along. A pushed crate does not carry the one above it: only a platform (STATIC, or without .vel) carries.

Don't copy the elevator's velocity to whoever is on top. hero.vel.x += elevator_vel (or hero.vel = h.velocity) makes the hero move twice: resolve already carries it along.

A STATIC never gives way: a stack of heavy crates does not sink the bottom one into the floor, and a light ball hit by a heavy one does not go through the floor or a thin wall. The crates of a stack can still sink a little into each other and jitter (Scena is not a physics engine). Two objects born inside each other separate along the side where they overlap, whatever the .vel.

bounce= says what happens to .vel on contact. Leaving it out is not the same as 0.

CallEffect
resolve(a, b)Position only: stops at the impact; neither reads nor writes .vel.
resolve(a, b, bounce=0.0)Position + an inelastic impulse along the normal: removes the component going in and keeps the tangent one (walking on a slope).
resolve(a, b, bounce=1.0)Elastic. > 1 = super bounce. Only runs if the moving body has a .vel.

“No bounce” in everyday speech usually means bounce=0.0; leaving the parameter out is position only. .mass decides who absorbs the impact; bounce= decides how much of the normal velocity survives. Two equal masses with bounce=0 end up moving together — not a bug.

There is no friction. Surfaces are smooth: bounce=0 removes only the velocity going into the wall, and the sideways velocity stays forever — the ball slides down the slope and a stack never comes to rest. Brake it yourself in on_update(self, dt): self.vel.x *= 0.5 ** dt (loses half the sideways velocity per second, the same at any frame rate).

ball = Circle(center=(200, 200), radius=15)
ball.mass = 1.0
ball.vel = Vec2(180, 0)

floor.mass = STATIC
resolve(ball, floor, bounce=1.0)   # elastic
resolve(ball, wall, bounce=0.0)    # inelastic — zeroes the normal component of .vel

There are two patterns for zeroing the velocity against a wall:

collision.floor = True   # a world with gravity (A world with a floor)

# A — the engine zeroes the normal velocity on contact
resolve(player, "walls", bounce=0.0)

# B — position only in resolve; you handle the velocity (same recipe as the slope)
resolve(player, "walls")

def update(dt):
    player.vel.y -= GRAVITY * dt
    ...
    for c in player.touching_contacts:
        if c.side == "top" and player.vel.y > 0:
            player.vel.y = 0.0   # head against the ceiling — the other one is above
    player.move_by(player.vel.x * dt, player.vel.y * dt)

.vel is None until you assign it; the script moves with move_by(vel * dt). move_along / move_to(..., time=) / move_by(..., time=) do not write .vel — to take on the travel's rate: crate.vel = h.velocity (Handle). Whoever is on the platform already rides along; don't copy its velocity.

Broken on contact. Destroying (or parking) the partner in @collide does not cancel the bounce: with resolve(ball, "brick", bounce=1) and a @collide(ball, "brick") that does brick.destroy(), the ball breaks the brick and bounces back from where it touched, as off a whole brick: on this frame the dead brick still holds the ball, but it does not move or count as a contact. Breaking it on the next frame (a flag in @collide, the destroy() in update) gives the same bounce. Only the part coming head-on changes: whatever grazes past or moves away keeps the same velocity. With bounce=0, a floor that vanishes when the hero lands holds the fall on that frame, and on the next one the hero falls. At the seam of two bricks the ball touches both at once, and both respond together: it bounces straight back, whatever order they were created in.

In a game with gravity, the world has a floor: collision.floor = True. An object that touches what is below it stands on it.

collision.floor = True              # this world has a floor (the gravity is yours)
resolve("hero", "ground", bounce=0)

With a floor, resolve treats a body's bottom side as its feet: an object that was on the floor at the start of the frame is pulled back to a floor within reach (it walks down a slope without hopping, and does not flicker between “on the floor” and “in the air” on short frames), a moving platform carries whoever is on top, a step of up to 2 is climbed by walking, and an object standing on a slope does not slide.

Without the line (the default), the world has no floor: a game seen from above (racing, maze, RPG), in space or without gravity. No side is special, and rotating the whole world rotates all movement with it: a car that scrapes a wall below it leaves that wall the way it leaves a wall beside it.

A platformer without collision.floor = True. The hero does not ride along with the elevator, slowly slides down the slope and, on 120 Hz screens, flickers between “on the floor” and “in the air” (the jump sometimes fails). floor_below and tilt = "ground" in a world without a floor warn once (SCENA WARNING).

In a world with a floor, the pair's bounce= decides when an object on the floor leaves it:

bounce=Sticking to the floor
omitted, 0 or up to 0.5 — walkersSticks. It leaves the floor only when, on the same frame, the velocity (.vel) points away from the floor and the body actually moves away from it (as in a jump). Walking up a slope or being carried by an elevator gives a large upward velocity, and the object still stays on the floor.
above 0.5 — balls, projectilesDoes not pull back a real bounce: the engine trusts the leaving velocity.

That is why resolve(ball, "wall", bounce=1) bounces and resolve(hero, "ground", bounce=0) stays steady. There is no “stick” option — bounce= already states the intent.

Placing jumps straight to the spot; traveling goes along the path. A wall only stops what travels.

Places (goes through the wall)Travels (the wall stops it midway)
center =, move_to / rotate_to / scale_to without time=, tween(shape.center, …), center @= (including track.cursor)move_by, move_to(..., time=), move_by(..., time=), move_along

@collide follows the same split: an object that travels fast is checked along its whole path (Fast object); a placed one, only where it stopped. Reset / respawn: hero.center = start_pos or an instant move_to — don't turn off collision.resolve_enabled for that. Sliding to a point and stopping at the wall: move_to(..., time=). See Move.

only= says on which sides of a the pair holds. Any other first contact passes through until the two separate. A platform you jump through from below is only="bottom".

resolve(hero, "thin", bounce=0.0, only="bottom")   # jump through from below, stand on top
resolve(hero, "thin", bounce=0.0, only={"bottom", "left", "right"})  # the sides hold
resolve(hero, "door", only="left")                 # one-way door

# drop down through the platform: DOWN + jump
def update(dt):
    st.drop_down = recently("drop_down", keyp("DOWN") and keyp.once("UP"), hold=0.15)
    ...

resolve(hero, "thin", bounce=0.0,
        only=lambda c: c.side == "bottom" and not st.drop_down)
With only="bottom"What happens
Jumps up from belowThe head hits ("top"): passes through.
The top of the jump ends inside the platformKeeps passing through and falls back down: it did not get past the top.
Gets past the top and fallsThe feet touch ("bottom"): stands on it.
Walks against the sidePasses through (as in Mario). To hold, list the sides.
Walks over adjoining blocks with a step of up to 2Climbs the step and stays on top (does not pass through). A bigger step is a side: passes through.
Standing on topA normal floor: touching_sides, coyote, tilt = "ground", elevator.
Falls very fastScena checks the frame's whole path: it catches the top and does not pass through.

The sides are those of a, the same words as a.touching_sides: "bottom" = standing. One side works, or a list / tuple / set (order does not matter). All four sides = no filter. A function receives the contact (TouchingContact, seen from a: .side, .other, .normal) and returns True to hold. It runs inside the collision, several times per frame: only read state. Effects (playing a sound, breaking the plank) go in @collide, which keeps firing while the object passes through. Scena checks: in resolve(), a function that writes (st.x = …, hero.vel.y = 0, destroy(), recently(…), keyp.once(…), chance(…), creating an object) raises TypeError pointing at the line; whatever escapes that reading (code without source) raises RuntimeError when it runs. Compute in update(), store it in st and only read it here — like st.drop_down in the example.

The side is that of the first contact, the same one a solid platform would use. Falling diagonally and touching the corner from the side passes through, just as it would slide down the wall of a solid platform.

Don't confuse

Looks likeIt isIt is not
only="top" for a jump-through platformonly="bottom": the side is the hero's (the feet), not the platform's.the platform's side
The same platform in "platform" and "thin", with only= on just one of themValueError: two registrations disagree. Give the one-way platforms a group of their own.the first one wins
resolve("crate", "crate", only="bottom")ValueError: a group against itself sees each contact from both sides. Use {"top", "bottom"}, {"left", "right"} or a function.stackable crates
only= on a slope steeper than 45°The sides are 45° bands of the world. For a steep one-way slope, use a function with c.normal.“on top” of the slope

Removing a pair: unresolve(a, b), with the same sides as resolve.

unresolve(player, "walls")
collision.resolve_enabled = False   # advanced: turns off all resolution

collision.resolve_enabled = False turns off, for every pair, stopping along the path, separating and sticking to the floor. @collide, queries and raycast go on; touching_* stays empty while it is off. It is not the way to reset (see Place × travel).

resolve reference

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
STATICconstantwall.mass = STATICread / writeImmovable — floor, wall. float("inf").
shape.massnumber1.0read / writeWeight in the push. Default 1.0. <= 0 raises an error.
shape.velVec2 or Noneball.vel = Vec2(0, -200)read / writeThe body's velocity. None until assigned. Read and written by resolve(..., bounce=). It is not linked with @= (the engine writes to it): to follow state, write it every frame — ship.vel = vec_from_angle(st.a * 30, 10) in on_update. Pose tweens do not write it — the Handle reports the rate (Handle).
collision.floorboolTrueread / writeDoes the world have a floor? Default False (seen from above, space, no gravity: no side is special). True in a game with gravity: an object that touches what is below it stands on it (slope, elevator, step). See A world with a floor. Resets on an act change.
collision.resolve_enabledboolTrueread / writeAdvanced. False: no pair stops along the path, separates or sticks to the floor. @collide, queries and raycast go on. touching_* is emptied while it is off.

Methods

MethodSignatureReturnsMeaning
resolve(a, b, bounce=, only=)Parameters: a (object or group name), b (object or group name), bounce (number, optional), only (side, list / set of sides or function of the contact, optional)—Registers the pair. Every frame: stops the movement at the impact, slides along the surface, undoes whatever overlap is left. Without bounce= → does not read .vel. With it: 0 inelastic, 1 elastic, >1 super bounce. only=: only these sides of a hold; the rest passes through (One-way). Calling the same pair again replaces bounce= and only=.
unresolve(a, b)Parameters: a (object or group name), b (object or group name)—Cancels the enrollment. Same sides as resolve.

Touching

touching_sides says which sides of the object rest against something solid, as of the last collision check (the previous frame's) — only pairs in resolve(), not sensors. It is the platformer's "am I on the ground?", and a platformer is a world with a floor (collision.floor = True): that is what keeps "bottom" steady on short frames and on slopes.

collision.floor = True              # a world with a floor (A world with a floor)
player["grounded"] @= lambda: "bottom" in player.touching_sides

def update(dt):
    if keyp("SPACE") and player.grounded:
        player.vel.y += JUMP
    player.tilt = "ground"   # slope: tilts only the drawing (Facing sprites)

for c in player.touching_contacts:
    if c.side == "bottom":
        dust_at(c.point)

# which block am I standing on? (None in the air)
standing_on = next((c.other for c in player.touching_contacts if c.side == "bottom"), None)
touching reference
PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning
touching_sidesfrozenset{"bottom"}readSides in contact with a resolve() pair. Reactive when a formula depends on it (e.g. grounded @=).
touching_contactstupleplayer.touching_contactsreadOne TouchingContact per resolve() pair. Not reactive. Table below.

Each item of touching_contacts (TouchingContact)

Properties

PropertyType (typical value)Read/WriteMeaning

.sidestr or None"bottom"read"top" · "bottom" · "left" · "right" — the side of this body that touches.
.slope_anglenumber22readAngle of the surface in degrees (0 = flat ground). Sprite.tilt = c with the "bottom" anchor turns to that angle and sets the drawing against the plane, along the normal only. tilt = c.slope_angle only turns.
.normalVec2c.normalreadUnit normal (this body → the other).
.tangentVec2c.tangentreadUnit tangent to the surface.
